audits.title: Follow-up Audit Report on New York City Public Schools’ Efforts to Maximize Medicaid Reimbursement Claims for Special Education Services
audits.plain_title: Schools left an estimated $431.6 million in Medicaid money unclaimed
audits.agency: Department of Education (New York City Public Schools)
audits.what_they_audited: A follow-up to a 2021 audit that found the school system was not seeking Medicaid reimbursement it was entitled to for special education services. Auditors checked whether New York City Public Schools carried out the 30 earlier recommendations and measured how much reimbursement went unclaimed in fiscal years 2023 through 2025.
audits.background: Federal law requires the school system to provide the special education services spelled out in each student's individualized education program, and Medicaid reimburses school districts for 10 types of covered services delivered to Medicaid-enrolled students, with the state and city splitting the money evenly. A claim fails if even one documentation requirement is not met.

findings.plain: Auditors estimate the city failed to claim about $431.6 million in Medicaid reimbursement for special education services in fiscal years 2023 through 2025.
findings.quote: the City failed to claim approximately $431.6 million in Medicaid revenue during Fiscal Years 2023, 2024, and 2025

findings.plain: The school system claimed reimbursement for only 54% of the documented occupational, physical and speech therapy sessions it provided to Medicaid-enrolled students, largely because it failed to collect required paperwork. That gap cost at least $273.4 million over the three years.
findings.quote: NYCPS only claimed reimbursement for 54% of all documented OT, PT, and ST services provided to Medicaid-enrolled pre-K to Grade 12 students

findings.plain: There is no record of 16.2% of the therapy services that students' education plans required. Either children missed services considered medically necessary or the services happened but were never documented, which would add up to $132.8 million more in lost reimbursement.
findings.quote: NYCPS lacks any record of providing 16.2% of all OT, PT, and ST services that were mandated for eligible students with IEPs

findings.plain: The school system still chooses not to seek reimbursement for seven of the 10 service types Medicaid covers, including psychological counseling, evaluations, special transportation and skilled nursing. Auditors conservatively put the added cost at $25.4 million.
findings.quote: It is still NYCPS’ policy not to claim for seven of the 10 service types for which Medicaid reimbursement is available

findings.plain: Of the 30 recommendations from the 2021 audit, the school system fully implemented three, partially implemented eight and did not act on the other 19.
findings.quote: NYCPS has fully implemented only three recommendations and partially implemented eight others, leaving a total of 19 that were not acted upon

findings.plain: Cooperation with the audit was poor. The school system took 52 business days on average to hand over requested information and denied auditors direct access to its record systems.
findings.quote: On average, it took NYCPS 52 business days to provide requested information or documentation

numbers.label: Estimated Medicaid money left unclaimed over three years
Lost on therapy services provided but never claimed
Share of documented therapy sessions actually claimed
Prior recommendations not acted on, out of 30

recommendations: Create an interim action plan with milestones to strengthen claim checks and cut unclaimed services while the new MedSys claiming system is being built.
Set up routine monitoring, such as sample-based reviews, so every therapy session has the required written order or referral before claims are submitted.
Periodically review the licenses and national provider identifier numbers of existing employees and promptly fix wrong or incomplete provider records.
Keep working to collect parental consent forms and add monitoring, such as sample-based reviews, to check compliance.
Record every service session in the two tracking systems, determine whether unrecorded services were delivered but not logged or never delivered, and act on what it finds.
Meet documentation and claiming requirements for all covered services for K-12 and eligible preschool students, file claims within the allowed window and resubmit correctable claims.
Do a cost-benefit analysis of expanding claiming to more of the covered services and develop a staged expansion plan.
Revisit the still-unimplemented recommendations once the Medicaid team is fully staffed and the new special education system is rolled out.
Promptly give auditors the information and documents needed to complete legally authorized audits.
audits.agency_response: New York City Public Schools agreed with four of the nine new recommendations, partially agreed with four and disagreed with one. It also questioned the audit's sample size, an argument the auditors rejected as inconsistent with government auditing standards.

audits.title: Elder Abuse Services, Training, and Coordination
audits.plain_title: How the city monitors elder abuse services
audits.agency: New York City Department for the Aging
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the New York City Department for the Aging effectively oversees the provision of elder abuse services. The audit covered April 2019 through April 2025.
audits.background: The Department for the Aging's Elder Justice Program contracts with six community-based providers, at a cost of about $12.6 million for 2023 through 2025, to serve and protect people age 60 and older who have been abused by someone in a trusting relationship. Program standards set deadlines for contacting, assessing and following up with clients, with faster action required in high-risk cases.

findings.plain: Providers did not always meet required timelines for contacting, assessing and following up with clients. In 17 of 41 sampled cases the referral described high-risk conditions such as physical violence or no access to food, and in none of them did case workers act within the required time frame.
findings.quote: For all 17 cases, the case workers did not act within the required time frame to provide crucial services to clients

findings.plain: In one case, a 68-year-old woman who said her foster son had struck her was not treated as high risk and was not contacted for 26 days, instead of within 24 hours as required for high-risk cases.
findings.quote: the provider did not designate this case as high risk and did not attempt to contact the client until 26 days later

findings.plain: The department did not ensure direct service staff got required training in detecting, reporting and counseling on elder abuse. Fifteen of 21 workers tested, or 71%, had not completed all required training, and some providers did not know the requirements existed.
findings.quote: Fifteen of the 21 workers tested (71%) did not complete all the required training.

findings.plain: The department did not enforce education and outreach requirements. It did not require providers to submit the annual outreach plans their contracts call for, and no provider submitted any during the audit period.
findings.quote: none of the providers submitted any annual plans to DFTA during the audit scope

findings.plain: Auditors also found broader oversight gaps, including a bill payer assistance program that was never evaluated, inconsistent performance metrics across records, unclear guidance to providers and unsupported expenses.
findings.quote: Significant deficiencies in DFTA’s oversight of the Elder Justice Program

numbers.label: Cost of elder abuse service contracts for 2023 through 2025
High-risk sampled cases where required deadlines were missed
Tested workers who had not completed all required training

recommendations: Strengthen oversight and monitoring of elder abuse cases so contracted providers deliver timely and appropriate services.
Take additional steps to make sure Elder Justice Program workers are properly trained.
Collect better documentation and step up monitoring to confirm providers hold the required number of educational presentations and outreach activities.
Enforce the requirement that providers submit annual plans and review those plans to see whether activities reach the intended people and communities with the right content.
For future programs, define what success looks like and set up monitoring and evaluation measures, including lessons learned, to guide decisions.

audits.title: The Remediation Action Plan
audits.plain_title: The Rikers remediation manager's first-year plan to fix the jails
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: The first annual Remediation Action Plan from Nicholas Deml, the court-appointed remediation manager in Nunez v. City of New York, laying out his assessment of the city jail system and the specific reforms he will direct the Department of Correction to carry out from July 14, 2026 through June 30, 2027.
audits.background: The federal court held New York City in civil contempt of eighteen provisions of four court orders meant to stem violence and excessive force in the jails, and appointed a remediation manager with broad authority over department operations. The court ordered him to produce yearly work plans, each building on the last, with this first plan prioritizing safety-related areas.

findings.plain: The remediation manager found the department struggles to perform even the most basic correctional functions such as staffing posts and securing housing units, and spent more than $370 million on overtime in the past fiscal year even as jail infrastructure crumbles.
findings.quote: spent more than $370 million on overtime this past fiscal year

findings.plain: In his team's first days he observed a housing unit filled with smoke from fires set by people in custody while an officer shrugged, and reviewed a large-scale fight involving nearly 30 people that started when an officer left a pantry door unsecured and abandoned his post.
findings.quote: A large-scale fight ensued, involving nearly 30 individuals

findings.plain: Such incidents are not outliers: from January to May 2026 people in custody set 130 fires and engaged in 2,978 fights, and the report notes the court has found violence in the jails is now worse than when the consent judgment took effect in 2015.
findings.quote: fires and engaged in 2,978 fights

findings.plain: The department operates inside an unusually dense network of oversight bodies in which each institution holds authority over part of jail operations but none is responsible for the whole system.
findings.quote: The environment is chaotic.

findings.plain: The remediation manager concluded that after more than a decade without meaningful improvement, incremental reform has itself become a form of failure, and said he will use his full court-granted authority to force change.
findings.quote: The system has reached the point where incrementalism is

findings.plain: He found the department's investigative and disciplinary units were disconnected and dispersed, weakening accountability, and in May 2026 began consolidating them into a single division under a new senior deputy commissioner who reports directly to his team.
findings.quote: DOC’s investigative and disciplinary units were disconnected and dispersed across the

findings.plain: Stakeholders broadly agree that programming for people in custody is insufficient in scale and diversity, and the plan calls for an estimated $50 million in annual funding for community-based programming.
findings.quote: existing programming is insufficient in

numbers.label: Department overtime spending in the past fiscal year
Fires set by people in custody, January through May 2026
Fights among people in custody, January through May 2026
Estimated annual funding sought for community-based programming
Court order provisions the city was held in contempt of

recommendations: Develop and begin executing a cohesive Security Plan: the department must submit a priority order for fixing lapses in core security practices by October 1, 2026, then create and carry out an approved practice-change plan for each item with monthly progress reports.
Validate and replace defective doors: document every defective door by September 1, 2026 and submit a procurement and replacement schedule by October 1, 2026, with the city funding the work.

Evaluate existing placement options and develop new ones for people who commit serious acts of violence, including a pilot housing program and data-driven strategies for managing persistently violent individuals.

Establish classification leadership by submitting a senior position description by September 1, 2026, recruiting a qualified official and having that official present a plan of action within 60 days of starting.

Establish a rapid executive reporting procedure requiring a standardized executive summary, presumptively within 24 hours, of serious security incidents, approved by October 15, 2026 and implemented by December 1, 2026.
Allocate dedicated annual funding, approximated at $50 million, for community-based programming, with a plan to administer the funding presented for approval by October 15, 2026.

Validate and assess staffing: the remediation manager will oversee an independent staffing analysis, with a completed assessment identifying deficiencies in posts, scheduling, deployment and supervision delivered by October 1, 2026.
Develop and execute a staffing plan that defines, prioritizes and assigns timelines to the tasks needed to maximize staff deployment, with monthly reporting on task completion.

Improve investigations staffing, structure and training: submit a redesigned Investigations, Intelligence, and Accountability Division proposal by September 1, 2026, a staffing plan and resources proposal by October 1, 2026 and a training plan by February 1, 2027.

Develop a strategic plan for the new investigations division by September 1, 2026 that streamlines operations and addresses the employee disciplinary framework and referral of apparently criminal conduct to prosecutors.

Develop a technology strategic plan: document gaps in data management systems by October 1, 2026 and submit an integrated technology plan by April 1, 2027, including fixing gaps in health data shared by Correctional Health Services.
Develop a business intelligence tool, such as a dashboard or daily executive briefing, proposed by October 1, 2026 and deployed for executive and facility leadership.
The remediation manager will design and launch a remediation compliance tool by October 15, 2026 for real-time tracking of the city's, department's, his own and the monitoring team's activities.
Develop new support for facility leaders: propose a new approach to coaching facility leadership by January 1, 2027 and maintain a log of corrective actions.
Adopt a dignity-based departmental values statement, drafted by April 1, 2027 and distributed to staff and people in custody after approval.
Assess compliance-focused resource use within 30 days of the plan's approval and every three months after, with the city directed to provide approved additional resources.
Enhance staff communication by proposing a new way to reach all staff across all posts by August 31, 2026 and putting it into operation by October 30, 2026.
audits.agency_response: The remediation manager reports that the new city administration and department leadership, including Commissioner Stanley Richards, appointed January 31, 2026 as the first formerly incarcerated person to lead the department, expressly support remediation and are actively engaged in the reform effort.
audits.compliance_note: The remediation manager describes a system in crisis where unconstitutional conditions persist despite a decade of court oversight, and warns that if the plan's aggressive timelines are not met his intervention will deepen.

audits.title: New York City Housing Authority Monitorship: Monitors' Report (Eighth Report)
audits.plain_title: Mold repairs speed up while heat and elevators slip
audits.agency: New York City Housing Authority
audits.what_they_audited: The federal monitors' eighth quarterly report on whether the New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) is meeting the housing conditions it promised under its 2019 agreement with the federal government, covering heat, elevators, pests and waste, mold and leaks, lead paint and inspections, plus organizational change and capital spending. It reports data for February 1, 2026 to April 30, 2026.
audits.background: On January 31, 2019 NYCHA agreed with the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York (SDNY), the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and the City of New York to fix housing conditions, and a monitor was appointed to evaluate compliance. Neil Barofsky and Matthew Cipolla of Jenner & Block LLP began a five-year term as co-monitors on February 28, 2024.

findings.plain: Mold repairs got much faster. NYCHA met the agreement's mold timeframes 42% of the time in the first quarter of Year 8, up from 20% in the same period of Year 7, including removing mold within five business days 36% of the time compared with 16%. The monitors still call NYCHA substantially out of compliance with the 95% standard.
findings.quote: dramatically improved its response rates to mold

findings.plain: The mold that residents report is still overwhelmingly severe. In the first quarter of Year 8, 86% of verified mold complaints involved visible mold covering ten square feet or more, against an agreement limit of 15%.
findings.quote: 86% of verified mold complaints

findings.plain: Heat came back faster but went out more often. NYCHA restored heat after in-apartment heating failures in an average of 13 hours, down from 14.6 hours at the same point last season, yet the share of occupied apartments hit by more than three heating service interruptions rose from 28% to 36% and unplanned heating outages climbed from 358 to 472.
findings.quote: heat in an average of 13 hours, down from an average

findings.plain: Elevator service slipped even though NYCHA beat one target. It resolved 89% of unplanned elevator car outages within ten hours, above the 85% requirement, but the average length of an unplanned outage grew 27% from 4.9 hours to 6.2 hours.
findings.quote: from 4.9 hours during the ﬁrst quarter of last year to 6.2

findings.plain: Pest results were mixed. NYCHA answered 98% of rat complaints within two business days against a 90% target and cut its estimated mouse population by 23% and bed bugs by 11.5%, but its estimated rat population rose 46% from the same period last year.
findings.quote: NYCHA’s rat population estimate in the ﬁrst quarter of

findings.plain: Lead work stayed on schedule. NYCHA has finished X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF) testing in about 94% of apartments presumed to have lead-based paint and has removed lead paint from 19,416 apartments, roughly 31.2% of those known to contain it, keeping it on track to abate half by 2029. Two children under six were reported with elevated blood lead levels in the quarter, down from 10 and 8 in the same period of the two prior years.
findings.quote: testing initiative. NYCHA has abated 19,416 apartments

findings.plain: The repair backlog remains enormous. NYCHA has roughly 62,000 open mold and leak work orders. Its Mold and Leak Restore and Renew program, which sends dedicated crews to the highest-need developments, has closed 1,981 work orders open for more than 100 days across four developments since August 2025, but a growing share of those closures involve no physical repair.
findings.quote: NYCHA has approximately 62,000 open mold and leak work

numbers.label: Mold work orders done on time, first quarter of Year 8
Verified mold complaints covering ten square feet or more
Average time to restore heat after an in-apartment failure
Rise in average length of an unplanned elevator outage
Apartments with lead paint removed as of April 30, 2026
Rise in the estimated rat population from a year earlier
Open mold and leak work orders
Total city capital funding under the agreement

recommendations: Secure enough money for both operating costs and capital repairs, which the monitors say NYCHA needs to fully comply with the agreement, especially given possible federal budget cuts.
Keep up the work on the mold and leak crew program, the new contract management group and the improved tracking of supervisory inspections.
Tailor efforts to get into apartments so crews reach residents who will grant access without repeatedly spending time on those who will not.
Use the dedicated mold and leak crews for the hands-on repair work the program was created to do, rather than closing work orders administratively.
Finish defining contract management roles with input from the staff most involved, including neighborhood contract managers, then communicate those roles to relevant staff.

Centralize management of the Transformation Plan initiatives and resources, standardize performance indicators across departments and build a framework for measuring whether the initiatives actually improve service.
audits.agency_response: The monitors describe NYCHA's leaders and staff as taking a constructive and collaborative approach. NYCHA launched its Contract Management Initiative in December 2025, delivered upgrades to its Maximo work order system a month ahead of schedule and expects a system for tracking supervisory inspections of maintenance workers by August 2026, months earlier than planned.
audits.compliance_note: The monitors say NYCHA has continued to build on earlier progress and should be commended, while several important areas still need work and NYCHA remains substantially out of compliance with the agreement's mold requirements. Under Paragraph 28 of the agreement, NYCHA does not yet meet the criteria for ending the monitorship.

audits.title: Thirtieth Report of the Independent Monitor: Compliance Snapshot of NYPD’s Stop, Frisk, and Search Practices
audits.plain_title: Stop and frisk compliance snapshot for summer 2025
audits.agency: New York City Police Department
audits.what_they_audited: A quarterly visual "compliance snapshot" updating the monitor's Twenty-Ninth Report on the New York City Police Department's (NYPD) compliance with the federal court's requirements in Floyd v. City of New York and Davis v. City of New York, covering the third quarter (July to September) of 2025.
audits.background: The report covers the third quarter of 2025 and in several slides compares it to the third quarter of 2024. It draws on the monitor team's audits of 100 stop reports per month and quarterly body-worn camera video audits, plus audits by the NYPD Quality Assurance Section, command self-inspections and first-line supervisor reviews; the quarter's sample includes 22 Community Response Team stops.

findings.plain: In the third quarter of 2025, the monitor's audits found 94% of reported stops, 81% of frisks and 74% of searches lawful, minimal improvement over the same quarter of 2024, with search compliance still far below acceptable levels.
findings.quote: compliance rates were 94% for stops, 81% for frisks, and...

findings.plain: Self-initiated stop compliance has improved over time, reaching a department-wide rate of 87% for the quarter, though frisks and searches during self-initiated stops were lawful only 68% and 66% of the time.
findings.quote: Self-initiated stop compliance rates have improved over time, with a Department-wide...

findings.plain: While assembling the data, the monitor discovered that the department's Quality Assurance Section never audited any stops by the Citywide Community Response Team from March 2023 to March 2026. The monitor requested and assessed a sample of 100 of those stops and included the results in the snapshot.
findings.quote: QAS never audited stops by this command

findings.plain: Supervisor review remained poor. The monitor found 6% of stops, 18% of frisks and 27% of searches unlawful, while reviewing supervisors flagged only 1% of stops, 4% of frisks and 7% of searches.
findings.quote: supervisors found that only 1% of stops, 4% of frisks, and 7% of searches

findings.plain: Officers failed to complete stop reports for 29% of stops identified in the monitor's audit (10 of 35), down from 47% in the third quarter of 2024, though the monitor said underreporting continues at an unacceptable rate and likely affects the accuracy of compliance figures.
findings.quote: For 29% of stops identified in the Monitor's audit for underreporting in the third

findings.plain: Officers recorded 96% of stops in their entirety on body-worn camera, up from 90% a year earlier.
findings.quote: for 96% of stops identified in the Monitor's audit

findings.plain: Housing Bureau compliance was low, especially for searches: 82% of stops, 75% of frisks and only 43% of searches were lawful, a sharp decline in search lawfulness from the previous quarter. Trespass arrest compliance was 96% on both the reason to approach and probable cause.
findings.quote: decline in the percentage of searches found lawful from the second quarter of 2025 to the third quarter of 2025.

audits.auditor: New York City Board of Correction
audits.title: Suicide Prevention in City Jails: March 2026 Observation Aide Assessment
audits.plain_title: Suicide watch aides missing from about a third of special units
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: Staff of the New York City Board of Correction (BOC), the city's jail oversight board, ran two structured audits in March and early April 2026 of the New York City Department of Correction's (DOC) Observation Aide program, which uses trained people in custody to watch over units where individuals may be at risk of suicide. Auditors visited housing areas, reviewed logbooks and interviewed aides and correction officers.
audits.background: New York City Charter section 626(e) charges the Board with setting minimum standards for the care and supervision of people held by DOC, and city rules require DOC to run an Observation Aide program to monitor individuals at risk of suicide. Under DOC's directive, aides must tour designated housing areas every 10 minutes, and if no aide is assigned uniformed staff must tour every 15 minutes.

findings.plain: In the March baseline survey, 41 of the 62 housing units visited had an observation aide assigned and present. About one in three units had no aide at the time of inspection.
findings.quote: about one in three units lacked coverage

findings.plain: Officer paperwork was almost always incomplete. In only 4 of the 41 staffed units did the control room officer record the aide's name and identifying number in the logbook as DOC's directive requires.
findings.quote: only 4 (9.8%) had proper “A” post officer

findings.plain: Where no aide was assigned, the backup safeguard often did not happen. Only 7 of 21 unstaffed units met the 15-minute tour requirement, and staff in one restrictive housing area said they skipped the tours when nobody was on suicide watch.
findings.quote: if there is no suicide watch on the tier, we do not make

findings.plain: Aides frequently lacked the gear they need. Only 11 of the 41 staffed units had all required equipment, with flashlights, logbooks and working clocks the most common items missing, and some aides used tablets or televisions to time their rounds.
findings.quote: Only 11 of 41 staffed units (26.8%) had all required equipment.

findings.plain: The follow-up audit three weeks later found real gains. Aide coverage, aide logbook use and equipment availability all rose.
findings.quote: Observation aide coverage improved (66.1% to 82.8%)

findings.plain: Two measures stayed weak or got worse. Officer documentation moved only from 9.8 percent to 12.5 percent, and 15-minute tour compliance in units without an aide fell from 33.3 percent to 20 percent.
findings.quote: remained low (9.8% to 12.5%)

findings.plain: One unit was outside the program entirely. Officers do not let people housed in the Rose M. Singer Enhanced Supervision Housing (RESH) serve as observation aides, citing security risk, and staff there log tours every 30 minutes rather than the 15 minutes the policy requires when no aide is present.
findings.quote: allow individuals in RESH to participate in the Observation Aide program

Units with correct officer logbook entries at follow-up

recommendations: Policy 1: Area supervisors must make sure "B" post officers conduct 15-minute tours in specialized units that have no observation aide, as Directive #4017R-D requires.
Policy 2: RESH should start using observation aides on a modified alternating schedule tied to tier lockdowns, per Directive #4009-R on lock-in and lockout.
Review 1: Correctional staff should ask observation aides and housing area staff for feedback to identify barriers and improve operations.
Coordination 1: Facility programs or job assignment staff should send out updated observation aide rosters every week so everyone knows who is covering which unit.
Coordination 2: The Eric M. Taylor Center should train and assign qualified city sentenced candidates as observation aides to offset high turnover in intake areas.
Reporting 1: "A" post officers must write the name of the observation aide on duty in the "A" post logbook.
Reporting 2: Leadership should set up a centralized inventory system with routine audits so aides have required equipment such as flashlights, logbooks, vests and clocks.

audits.title: 2025 Annual Anti-Corruption Report
audits.plain_title: Half of city agencies have no internal audit plan
audits.agency: New York City agencies (citywide)
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) surveyed city agencies about their internal auditing capacity: who performs audits, whether agencies can hire and keep auditors, what kinds of audits they run, whether they have an audit plan and whether they buy outside audit services. The report covers October 1, 2024, through September 30, 2025, and draws on responses from 50 agencies.
audits.background: Mayoral Executive Order No. 105 makes the DOI commissioner the city's independent inspector general and requires this annual report. City Charter section 389(a) requires agency heads to maintain an internal control system that reduces the agency's vulnerability to fraud, waste, abuse, error, conflict of interest and corruption. Like DOI's other annual anti-corruption reports, this one summarizes what agencies report about themselves rather than DOI's own investigative findings.

findings.plain: Seventy percent of responding agencies have staff who perform internal audit functions, and 30 percent have no such staff at all.
findings.quote:
A majority of agencies (70%) reported having staff who perform internal audit 
functions, while 30% reported that they do not  have such staff.

findings.plain: Agencies split evenly on whether they have an internal audit plan, which sets out the audit work expected over a given period. DOI notes that having one is best practice.
findings.quote:
Internal audit plans enhance the ability of agencies to achieve their 
objectives, and it is best practice to have one.

findings.plain: Seventeen agencies had fewer auditors actually working than their budget allowed. Nine agencies whose budgeted audit headcount fell between January 2022 and September 2025 blamed attrition, vacancy reductions or extended vacancies and citywide budget cuts.
findings.quote:
they cited attrition, vacancy reductions or extended vacancies, and Citywide budget 
reductions, among other rea sons.

findings.plain: Sixteen of the 50 agencies reported trouble recruiting or keeping auditors, pointing to funding, salary levels and difficulty finding qualified candidates, along with hiring freezes and long hiring approvals.
findings.quote:
numerous 
agencies cited issues of funding, salary and financial compensation, and identifying 
qualified candidates.

findings.plain: Most agencies said their auditors issue written reports and make recommendations for improvement, and several described tracking corrective action through follow-up audits, management reviews and tools for open action plans.
findings.quote:
the majority of agencies also reported that their auditors 
make recommendations for improvement.

findings.plain: Seven agencies said their auditing staff reported findings from completed audits to DOI during the year.
findings.quote:
Seven agencies also reported that in the last year, the ir respective  auditing 
staff/departments had made a report to DOI regarding findings from performed or 
completed audits.

findings.plain: Twenty-one of the 50 agencies had hired outside auditors in the past five years. Agencies without internal auditors were not more likely to buy external audits: of the 15 agencies with no internal audit staff, only one had procured an external audit in that period.
findings.quote:
agencies without inte rnal auditors were not more likely to hire external 
auditors.

numbers.label: Agencies with staff performing internal audit functions
Agencies with fewer active auditors than budgeted
Agencies reporting auditor recruitment or retention problems
Agencies whose auditors make recommendations
Agencies that hired outside auditors in five years
Agencies that referred audit findings to DOI

recommendations: City agencies should conduct audits on a consistent basis.
Agencies that do not have an internal audit plan should consider putting one together.
Agencies should review their existing auditing frameworks with the aim of maximizing audit capacity in a way that still fits the agency's overall capacity and specific mission.
audits.agency_response: The report is based on the agencies' own questionnaire responses. The commissioner thanked the responding agencies for assessing their audit functions and answering DOI's questionnaire.

audits.title: Twenty-First Report for the Monitoring Period July 1, 2025 to December 31, 2025
audits.plain_title: New leaders at Rikers, but no material change in risk of harm
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: The court-appointed independent monitor's 21st compliance assessment of the Department of Correction under the Nunez court orders, covering July through December 2025, with narrative updates on leadership, use of force, security practices, staff misconduct and deaths in custody plus compliance ratings for 45 court order provisions.
audits.background: Since the monitor's previous report, a new commissioner took office on February 16, 2026 and the court-appointed remediation manager began work on February 23, 2026. Much of the report covers a period under the prior city administration and before the remediation manager's appointment.

findings.plain: Despite the new leadership structure, the monitor found no material change in reducing the risk of harm in the jails as of the report's filing, with the reform effort still moving at a glacial pace.
findings.quote: no material change in ameliorating the risk of harm in the jails

findings.plain: The monitor's long list of problem centers, including normalized violence and poor security practices, no coherent operational plan, a revolving door of leadership and a perpetual state of crisis, remains essentially unchanged.
findings.quote: ...remain present with little to no change observed as of the filing of this Report.

findings.plain: The small group of persistently violent individuals responsible for most jail violence is dispersed across the jails with no dedicated management structure, and the monitor strongly urged the commissioner and remediation manager to take immediate action on classification and security deficits.
findings.quote: ...throughout the jails with no dedicated management structure in place to abate their patterns

findings.plain: Basic security failures persist, including failures to secure doors, remain on post, conduct meaningful tours, control housing areas, search and escort safely, de-escalate and activate body-worn cameras, all of which raise the risk of violence and preventable harm.
findings.quote: These deficiencies include failures to secure doors, remain on post, conduct meaningful

audits.title: Review of the City’s Animal Population Control Efforts
audits.plain_title: City spay and neuter program is underfunded and little known
audits.agency: Department of Health and Mental Hygiene
audits.what_they_audited: This was a review rather than a standard audit. The team evaluated how effectively the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene runs the city's Animal Population Control Program, which subsidizes free or low-cost spay and neuter surgeries for eligible pet owners, and looked at approaches other cities use.
audits.background: City law requires the health department to run a program that reduces the stray dog and cat population by offering no- or low-cost sterilization, funded by a surcharge on licenses for unsterilized dogs. To deliver the services the department contracted with the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA) for up to $3 million, covering as many as 24,000 surgeries at $125 each through 2028.

findings.plain: The health department set up the required low-cost spay and neuter program but has not been proactive about animal population control overall, relying on a single funding source and not seeking other public or private money it is allowed to pursue.
findings.quote: DOHMH has not been proactive in pursuing animal population control overall

findings.plain: The program's sole funding source, a surcharge on licenses for unsterilized dogs, brought in $950,819 over fiscal years 2022 to 2024, well short of the $1.5 million anticipated. As a result the ASPCA performed 6,733 sterilization surgeries, 37% fewer than its 10,660-surgery target.
findings.quote: The ASPCA performed a total of 6,733 sterilizations during FYs 2023 to 2025, 3,927 (37%) less than the 10,660 sterilizations anticipated under the contract.

findings.plain: Dog licensing outreach was heavily concentrated: five zip codes, about 3% of the city's more than 170, hosted 73% of the 192 licensing events held. Only about 70,000 dogs are licensed out of an estimated 500,000 pet dogs.
findings.quote: DOHMH concentrated its outreach and education efforts in only five (3%) of the City’s more than 170 zip codes

findings.plain: Oversight of the ASPCA contract is thin. The department reviews invoices but has no performance metrics, no way to verify the ASPCA's reported outreach and no record that required reports explaining the surgery shortfall were ever filed.
findings.quote: DOHMH provided no mechanism for verifying the reported outreach figures, stating instead that they rely on trust.

findings.plain: The department does not publicly report any data on the program's activities or outcomes, such as how many surgeries were performed or where the recipients live.
findings.quote: DOHMH does not publicly report any data regarding the activities and outcomes relating to the Program

findings.plain: In a survey conducted by the review team, 70% of respondents did not know the free or low-cost spay and neuter program exists and 61% did not know dog licenses are mandatory.
findings.quote: 74 (70%) stated that they were not aware that qualifying residents of the City could have their pet cats or dogs spayed or neutered free of charge or at low-cost through the Program

findings.plain: The city spends almost $54 million a year sheltering animals while the program meant to address a root cause of shelter crowding received an average of about $316,000 a year. Other cities use multiple funding streams and city-backed trap-neuter-return programs, which New York City does not support.
findings.quote: received an average of only $316,000 in each of the last three fiscal years reviewed

numbers.label: Dog license surcharge revenue collected over three years
Sterilization surgeries performed against a 10,660 target
Approximate yearly city spending on animal shelters
Average yearly funding for the sterilization program

recommendations: Lead a re-evaluation of the city's overall approach to animal population control and develop a new strategy for reducing all major drivers of shelter intake, including what resources would cut dependence on shelter spending.
Require the shelter operator, Animal Care and Control, to track why owners give up their pets and develop strategies to reduce those surrenders.
Work on reducing community cat populations by considering new options, including a formal assessment of city-funded trap-neuter-return programs with appropriate oversight.
Improve public awareness and enforcement of the rule that free-roaming cats be sterilized, formally track enforcement activity and create a dedicated 311 complaint category for free-roaming cats.
Develop a strategic plan so dog licensing outreach and education events are spread across all five boroughs to raise awareness and licensing rates.
Explore additional funding sources for the program, including asking the City Council to add mandatory revenue streams to the Animal Population Control Fund.
Develop, formalize and carry out a monitoring plan for the ASPCA contract with clear, measurable and publicly reported performance indicators.
Make sure the ASPCA submits the required reports when it performs fewer sterilization surgeries than expected.
Consider surveying residents periodically to gauge the program's effectiveness and identify areas for improvement.
audits.agency_response: The health department generally agreed with two of the nine recommendations, partially agreed with one and disagreed with or called unnecessary the other six. Its written response included new information it had not shared during the review, which the team said it could not validate.

audits.title: Access Denied: Challenges to DOI's Oversight of the City's Child Welfare System
audits.plain_title: State law blocks watchdog scrutiny of child welfare cases
audits.agency: New York City Administration for Children's Services
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) examined how New York State Social Services Law and the state Office of Children and Family Services (OCFS) restrict DOI's access to Administration for Children's Services (ACS) records, hindering its City Charter-mandated oversight of the child welfare system.
audits.background: ACS investigates reports of child abuse and maltreatment, while OCFS, a state agency, regulates many of ACS's policies and maintains the statewide child abuse hotline register. DOI is the city's inspector general and investigates systemic failures, criminality, corruption and inefficiencies at city agencies.

findings.plain: Five provisions of the state Social Services Law significantly restrict DOI's access to ACS records essential for rigorous oversight, including investigations of systemic failures, criminality and corruption.
findings.quote:
five provisions in the law  significantly restrict DOI’s access to records of the City Administration for Children’s 
Services (ACS) that are essential for rigorous oversight

findings.plain: Three provisions require OCFS authorization before DOI can access almost any records about children who had contact with ACS, and OCFS often exercises that discretion in ways DOI found more restrictive than the law requires, delaying investigations for months.
findings.quote:
OCFS’s responses 
to DOI record requests are often more restrictive than what the applicable laws intend or require

findings.plain: Two other provisions bar DOI entirely from records of abuse reports ACS deemed unfounded and reports diverted to the CARES alternative-to-investigation program, so DOI cannot investigate, for example, whether an employee failed to investigate abuse because of a bribe.
findings.quote:
Two other provisions of State law prohibit DOI from accessing certain categories of ACS records 
altogether

findings.plain: In 2025 DOI was notified of 18 child fatalities where ACS had prior involvement with the family in the past decade, but state law barred access to the full ACS history in 17 of them. The numbers were 13 of 16 in 2024 and 19 of 25 in 2023.
findings.quote: current state law bars DOI from accessing the full ACS history in 17 of those matters

findings.plain: Unfounded and diverted reports are precisely where lapses in ACS supervision or decision-making would likely appear, and the restrictions also prevent DOI from reviewing alleged systemic unfairness such as racial disparities.
findings.quote:
unfounded reports , and reports diverted to 
CARES, are exactly where one c ould expect to find lapses in ACS supervision or decision- making.

findings.plain: Years of negotiations with OCFS have produced no tangible improvements; the authorization process has grown more burdensome over time, even when ACS itself referred the allegations to DOI and is cooperating.
findings.quote:
the authorization process has become more burdensome over time, even in cases 
where ACS itself referred the initial allegations to DOI and is cooperating with the investigation.

recommendations: The state Social Services Law provisions restricting DOI's access to ACS records should be amended so DOI can carry out its City Charter-mandated oversight of ACS; DOI supports pending state legislation by Senator Jabari Brisport and Assemblymember Andrew Hevesi that would provide that access.
audits.agency_response: A draft of the report was provided to ACS and OCFS for comment, and DOI considered their comments in finalizing it. OCFS has repeatedly said it follows its legal obligations and does not wish to obstruct or delay DOI's work.

audits.auditor: New York City Board of Correction
audits.title: Third Report and Recommendations on 2025 Deaths in New York City Department of Correction Custody
audits.plain_title: Missed tours and abandoned posts before three jail deaths
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: The New York City Board of Correction (BOC), the city's jail oversight board, investigated the deaths of Edwin Ramos, Aramis Furse and Kyron Randall, three people who died in November and December 2025 in the custody of the New York City Department of Correction (DOC). Board staff reviewed DOC, medical, medical examiner, emergency medical and hospital records, surveillance and body-worn camera video, and interviewed staff and people in custody.
audits.background: The New York City Charter and city rules require the Board to investigate deaths in DOC custody and to recommend measures to DOC and NYC Health + Hospitals/Correctional Health Services (CHS) that could prevent the circumstances that contributed to a death. The Board says these investigations look for systemic flaws and policy failures rather than criminality, and this is its third report on the 15 people who died in custody in 2025.

findings.plain: Officers left their assigned housing area posts repeatedly during the tours in which Mr. Furse and Mr. Randall died, without logging that they had told a supervisor. In one case the officer was away from the post for nearly three hours.

findings.plain: The officer assigned to Mr. Randall's housing area did not tour as DOC policy requires, which calls for a visual check for signs of life in every person in a cell area twice an hour.
findings.quote: conduct visual observations at 30-minute intervals

findings.plain: Logbook entries in Mr. Randall's unit recorded 30-minute tours that video shows did not happen, because the officer was not on the post at the times logged.
findings.quote: logbook entry, the “B” oﬃcer was oﬀ post

findings.plain: When Mr. Randall was found in medical distress, the housing officer left him alone in his cell for 24 minutes, contrary to DOC rules requiring staff to stay close to a person needing medical attention.
findings.quote: unsupervised, for 24 minutes while he experienced a medical emergency

findings.plain: CHS emergency responders also stepped away from Mr. Randall twice while he was in distress, which CHS policy on emergency response does not allow.
findings.quote: CHS emergency response staﬀ left Mr. Randall unattended while in distress

findings.plain: Supervision lapses let people in Mr. Furse's unit stay out of their cells after the 9:00 pm mandatory lock-in, gather in single cells assigned to someone else, cover fixed cameras with tissues and pass items that looked like rolled cigarettes. Video in Mr. Ramos' unit also showed apparent drug paraphernalia in use.
findings.quote: individuals in Mr. Furse’s housing area were out of their cells, roaming

findings.plain: Cell windows in Mr. Furse's housing area were blocked, obstructing officers' view into the cells, which DOC's own rule book prohibits.
findings.quote: Multiple individuals in Mr. Furse’s housing area partially or completely covered their
