recommendations: To CHS 1: CHS should reinforce and retrain staff on the requirement to continuously monitor people in custody who are in medical distress, as set out in CHS Medical Policies Section 10 on emergency response.
To DOC 1: Reinforce and retrain staff on basic supervision, touring and logbook practices, including staying on post, staying alert and accurately documenting breaks, meals, tours and incidents.

To DOC 2: Facility leadership must assign supervisors to periodically review surveillance video to spot officers who tour and document poorly, require those officers to meet with leadership before returning to post and schedule refresher training when needed.

To DOC 3: Housing area staff must immediately notify a supervisor when they see contraband and step in to confiscate it, and DOC must then arrange an unscheduled search of the unit and drug test the people housed there.

To DOC 4: DOC must address the findings of the 2023 cell door audit cited by the Nunez federal monitor, conduct an updated audit if needed and develop an action plan for securing cell doors and promptly reporting broken ones, to be shared with the Board at least 30 days before it is put in place.

To DOC 5: Staff must tell people in custody to remove cell window coverings, notify a supervisor and log the encounter if that does not work, have a supervisor physically remove the coverings, and have supervisors regularly monitor housing areas and audit logbooks.
To DOC 6: Post and distribute notices telling people in custody to comply with the security bulletin on cell window obstruction or risk losing the items used to block the view.
To DOC 7: Use the Video Monitoring Unit as intended to help facilities spot security problems including drug and tobacco use, and improve records tracking people found with prohibited items.
To DOC 8: Enforce the Board's Minimum Standard barring more than one person from occupying a single cell.

To DOC 9: Report refusals to lock in at 9:00 pm to the Central Operations Desk and respond as the lock-in and lockout directive requires, which may include calling in other DOC units, and improve reporting to track housing areas where people refuse to lock in.
To DOC 10: Send out teletypes restating that officers may not leave their assignment without a supervisor's approval or being relieved.
To DOC 11: Retrain staff who do not follow the rule requiring them to stay close to a person needing medical attention so the person stays under close observation until medical responders arrive.
To DOC 12: Stay alert on post as the rules require and report anyone seen tampering with DOC equipment.
audits.agency_response: In a letter appended to the report, CHS accepted the single recommendation directed to it and said it will continue to reinforce with clinical staff the need to continuously monitor patients in medical distress. The report does not include a DOC response.

audits.title: Privacy and Security of Student Data
audits.plain_title: How well the school system protects student data
audits.agency: New York City Public Schools
audits.what_they_audited: Whether New York City Public Schools consistently followed all laws and regulations on the privacy and security of student data. The audit covered March 2020 through September 2025.
audits.background: New York City Public Schools, the largest school district in the country with about 1,600 schools and over 900,000 students, holds students' personally identifiable information and must follow federal and state privacy rules, including a state requirement to adopt a data security policy aligned with the National Institute of Standards and Technology Cybersecurity Framework.

findings.plain: The school system's data security and privacy policy does not fully align with the national cybersecurity framework, and it lacks written policies in some fundamental areas.
findings.quote: NYCPS does not have written policies covering the areas of data classification, risk assessment, and backup and recovery

findings.plain: The school system did not always report data breaches or notify affected people on time. Of 141 breaches reviewed from January 2023 through February 2025, reporting to the State Education Department was late for 48% and notification to affected individuals and families was late for 11%.
findings.quote: NYCPS delayed reporting 48% (67 of 141) of breaches to SED and delayed notifying affected individuals and families about 11% (16 of 141) of breaches

findings.plain: There is no documented data classification policy, only an informal practice, which could slow the school system's ability to figure out what sensitive data was involved in a security incident.
findings.quote: NYCPS does not have a documented data classification policy.

findings.plain: The school system does not keep a comprehensive list of the applications each school uses. Of 524 schools that answered a survey, 42% said they used at least 70 different student information system applications beyond the central systems.
findings.quote: Of the 524 responding schools, 218 (42%) stated they used at least 70 different SIS applications

findings.plain: Only 73% of employees completed required annual data privacy and security training in 2024, and the school system does not check that everyone with access to personally identifiable information has completed it.
findings.quote: in 2024, only 73% (117,763 of 161,337) of employees completed the training

findings.plain: Auditors identified weaknesses in technical controls over selected information systems, detailed in a confidential draft report.
findings.quote: We identified weaknesses in technical controls that need to be corrected

findings.plain: The audit team had trouble getting information and meetings from the school system, with some document requests taking over five months and meeting requests taking two months.
findings.quote: some documentation requests taking over 5 months to fulfill, and meeting requests taking 2 months to be scheduled

numbers.label: Students in New York City Public Schools, over
Breaches or unauthorized data releases reviewed
Share of breaches reported late to the state
Employees who completed required privacy training in 2024

recommendations: Use the applicable national cybersecurity framework to identify gaps and improvements to the overall security posture.
Build a mechanism to ensure notifications of breaches or unauthorized releases of personal information always go out within required time frames.
Complete a written data and asset classification policy covering all systems and data, and classify all of the school system's data.
Develop a way to account for every student information system used at schools.
Put in place monitoring to ensure all employees with access to personally identifiable information complete privacy and security training every year.
Implement the technical control fixes detailed in the confidential draft report.
Cooperate more promptly with authorized state oversight inquiries.

audits.title: Status Report on Local Law 42
audits.plain_title: New jail leaders and pilot projects reshape the solitary law fight
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: A status report from the court-appointed independent monitor in Nunez v. City of New York updating the court on the evaluation of Local Law 42, a city law changing jail practices on restraints, escorts, de-escalation, lock-ins, out of cell time and restricted housing, and on new pilot projects meant to advance the law's goals.
audits.background: Local Law 42's requirements overlap with the Nunez court orders on security and operations, and several policy areas require the monitor's consultation or approval. Since the monitor's January 14, 2026 report, the mayor appointed a new correction commissioner who took office February 16, 2026 and a new corporation counsel, and the court-appointed remediation manager began work on February 23, 2026.

findings.plain: After evaluating the law, the monitoring team raised concerns that some of Local Law 42's requirements may not be safe to put into practice and could make conditions in the jails worse.
findings.quote: some of the requirements of LL42 may not be safe to implement and could

findings.plain: The monitor is encouraged by the city's newly installed jail leadership but remains gravely concerned about dangerous conditions that continue to put people in custody and staff at risk of harm.
findings.quote: remains gravely concerned about the dangerous conditions in the jails

findings.plain: The monitoring team provided confidential draft findings to the parties identifying where Local Law 42 conflicts with the Nunez court orders and explaining its safety concerns, but says more work is needed before it can make final decisions on what it will approve.
findings.quote:
Additional work remains before the Monitor can 
render final determinations on what may be approved

findings.plain: Two pilot projects are being developed to test whether parts of the law can work safely: one to improve the department's restricted housing program and one to add due process protections, including legal representation, for people referred to restricted housing.
findings.quote:
one focused 
on an improved restricted housing model and the other focused on enhancing due process 
protections for people in custody who are referred to restricted housing

findings.plain: The monitor cautioned that the department's history is full of pilot projects that failed, citing a recent door security pilot that collapsed despite strong leadership attention, and said the new pilots must be designed differently to be scalable and sustainable.
findings.quote:
The record in this case is rife with examples of 
pilot projects that were ineffective, not scalable, not sustainable or were simply abandoned

findings.plain: The department is closing the North Infirmary Command jail, which the monitor says resolves long-running concerns about its cell-within-a-cell housing layout that was not conducive to programming and contributed to prolonged isolation.
findings.quote:
The closure of NIC resolves the 
concerns about the physical plant

numbers.label: Date the court-appointed remediation manager began work
Meet and confer sessions convened with the Local Law 42 parties

recommendations: Develop and refine the two restricted housing pilot projects, culminating in a work plan with benchmarks and timelines, to be discussed in the monitor's June 2026 report.
The monitoring team and remediation manager team should determine when a detailed joint position on the stayed Local Law 42 provisions can be completed and provided to the parties and the court.

The department, remediation manager team and monitoring team should continue engaging the Local Law 42 parties, including at least one meet and confer session and a confidential written submission to the City Council intervenors.
The city should deploy additional resources and staff, including skilled project management support, to advance both the Nunez court orders and Local Law 42 obligations.
audits.agency_response: The report describes the department's new leadership as working collaboratively with the monitor and remediation manager, including initiating coordination with defender organizations on the due process pilot and closing the North Infirmary Command.
audits.compliance_note: The monitor reports concrete positive steps toward a pathway on Local Law 42 under new city leadership but says dangerous conditions persist and final determinations on which provisions can be approved remain pending.

audits.title: Implementation of Selected Aspects of the Climate Mobilization Act
audits.plain_title: Enforcing the city's building emissions law
audits.agency: New York City Department of Buildings
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Department of Buildings has taken steps to ensure private building owners comply with selected parts of the Climate Mobilization Act by the mandated deadlines. The audit covered November 2019 to June 2025.
audits.background: The Climate Mobilization Act, enacted in 2019, aims to cut greenhouse gas emissions from the city's largest buildings 40% by 2030 and reach net zero by 2050. Its centerpiece, Local Law 97, sets emissions limits for large private buildings starting in 2024, and the Department of Buildings oversees implementation and enforcement.

findings.plain: While the department has made outreach efforts, including hiring third parties, it has not closely monitored either that outreach or building owners' compliance, so there is no assurance owners will meet the law's deadlines.
findings.quote: it has taken a hands-off approach to monitoring its outreach efforts and the building owners’ compliance with the requirements

findings.plain: The department could not substantiate its own outreach letters until after the audit's closing conference, and only a quarter of the addresses it supplied were on the list of buildings actually required to comply.
findings.quote: only 150 of the 602 addresses (25%) were on the CBL

findings.plain: A 2024 phone initiative to advise owners ahead of the first reporting deadline reached only 8% of the buildings required to comply.
findings.quote: DOB contacted only 1,118 of 13,269 (8%) of those required to comply.

findings.plain: In a survey auditors sent to 151 building owners, several respondents said they were unaware of the law or had never been contacted, and 20 of the letters came back undeliverable.
findings.quote: five respondents stated they were unaware of the CMA, seven said they were never contacted by DOB

findings.plain: The department refers owners to a service provider for help but does not follow up on referrals and has no documentation of what assistance the provider gave.
findings.quote: they do not follow up on the referrals

findings.plain: Auditors visited 55 buildings and found 24% had not posted the required energy efficiency label, while 31% of those that did post labels put them where the public could not see them, including one label inside a desk drawer. The department does not inspect for the labels.
findings.quote: found 13 (24%) did not have their energy efficiency labels posted as required

numbers.label: Covered buildings reached by the 2024 phone push
Outreach letter addresses actually on the covered list
Visited buildings missing the required energy label

recommendations: Contact building owners, especially those at risk of missing emissions requirements, and document that contact.
Reassess the resources assigned to contacting building owners about compliance.
Create a system to track referrals to the service provider, record what assistance was given and follow up on buildings at risk of missing emissions requirements.
Educate building owners on where energy efficiency labels must be posted.
Inspect buildings to verify a label is posted near each public entrance where the public can see it.

audits.title: Review of Schools’ Food Donation and Composting Efforts
audits.plain_title: How schools handle donating leftover food and composting waste
audits.agency: New York City Public Schools (Department of Education)
audits.what_they_audited: This was a review, not a full audit. The comptroller's office examined whether New York City Public Schools tracks data on its food donation and composting programs, how it promotes those programs and what school administrators say about participating in them.
audits.background: New York City Public Schools, the nation's largest school system, serves about 940,000 free meals a day and spent $600 million on food in fiscal year 2025, 12% of its operations budget. Two units, the Office of Food and Nutrition Services and the Office of Energy and Sustainability, are responsible for preventing food waste.

findings.plain: The school system does not centrally track how many meals are prepared and discarded, so it cannot measure whether its food waste prevention efforts are working.
findings.quote: NYCPS has no idea how successful its overall efforts to prevent food waste are

findings.plain: Only 67 of 1,319 school buildings, or 4%, donated food to outside organizations in fiscal year 2025, and central management does not compile records of which organizations receive donations.
findings.quote: in FY2025 only 67 (4%) of NYCPS’ 1,319 school buildings donated food to outside organizations

findings.plain: Composting has grown dramatically. Participating schools went from 725 in fiscal year 2017 to all 1,715 in fiscal year 2024, and compostable material collected nearly quadrupled over that period.
findings.quote: from 6,278 tons collected in FY2017 to 24,477 tons in FY2024

findings.plain: Most school food waste still is not composted. A Department of Sanitation study found only about 37% of food waste generated at schools was captured for composting, and 28% of what was collected was contaminated, versus a 4% contamination rate citywide.
findings.quote: The study found that 28% of the organics collected from schools were contaminated, well above the citywide organics contamination rate of 4%.

findings.plain: The school system's own sustainability survey showed low engagement. Of 1,182 schools surveyed, 15% engaged in none of six food waste prevention activities and 87% engaged in no more than three.
findings.quote: 15% of all schools engaged in none of the six activities, and most schools—87% in total—engaged in no more than three of the six activities

findings.plain: In the review team's own survey of school administrators, only 33% said their schools donate uneaten leftovers and 59% said they have a food sharing table. Schools cited lack of funding and staffing as the main barriers.
findings.quote: Only 33% of respondents who answered the question stated that their schools donated unused food to school families, staff, or outside organizations.

numbers.label: Spent on food by the school system in fiscal year 2025
Share of school buildings that donated food in fiscal 2025
Compostable material collected from schools in fiscal 2024
Contamination rate of school compost, versus 4% citywide

recommendations: Set system-wide targets for participation in composting, food donation and other food waste reduction programs.
Compile system-wide data to measure progress against those targets.
Conduct and publish a centralized assessment of progress by school and by program, identify barriers and develop strategies for improvement.
Develop system-wide training and outreach to increase participation, encourage idea sharing among sustainability coordinators, capture more food waste as compost and reduce contamination.
Visit schools to verify that recycling and composting bins are properly placed in cafeterias and classrooms.
Identify schools without appointed sustainability coordinators, fill those positions and support the new coordinators.
audits.agency_response: In its March 26, 2026 written response, New York City Public Schools agreed with the recommendation on sustainability coordinators, partially agreed with the recommendation on training and outreach and disagreed with the recommendations on targets, system-wide data and a centralized assessment.

audits.title: OIG-NYPD Twelfth Annual Report
audits.plain_title: Police watchdog tallies 275 recommendations, most adopted
audits.agency: New York City Police Department
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation's (DOI) Office of the Inspector General for the New York City Police Department (OIG-NYPD) issued its annual report, required by Local Law 70, discussing the 25 public reports and one statement of findings it issued between 2015 and December 31, 2025 and the status of 275 recommendations to the New York City Police Department (NYPD).
audits.background: Local Law 70 established OIG-NYPD within DOI to oversee the NYPD. The annual report catalogues the office's investigations and tracks how NYPD and the Civilian Complaint Review Board (CCRB) have responded to its recommendations; some recommendations made in late 2025 are not assessed.

findings.plain: NYPD has fully implemented 159 of the 275 recommendations, about 57.82 percent, partially implemented or accepted in principle 53, rejected 47 and is still considering seven. Nine are no longer applicable because of technology or procedure changes, and two CCRB recommendations were implemented.
findings.quote:
NYPD has  fully implemented 159 recommendations, or approximately 57.82 
percent; partially implemented or accepted in principle 53 recommendations, or approximately 19.27 percent

findings.plain: More than 75 percent of OIG-NYPD's recommendations have been implemented, partially implemented or accepted in principle, which the acting commissioner attributed to the office's consistent follow-up.
findings.quote: more than 75 percent of the recommendations being implemented, partially implemented, or accepted in principle

findings.plain: On the January 2025 social media report, NYPD accepted all six recommendations on April 28, 2025 and has implemented five; the staff training recommendation remains partially implemented until OIG-NYPD confirms all staff with account access are trained.
findings.quote:
NYPD accepted the six recommendations on April 28, 2025, and OIG-NYPD 
determined that NYPD has implemented five of them.

findings.plain: On the October 2025 Criminal Group Database update, NYPD's 90-day response of January 13, 2026 accepted all 13 new recommendations, which are counted as accepted in principle until implementation can be assessed in the 2026 cycle.
findings.quote:
According to NYPD’s 
90-day response, issued on January 13, 2026, the Department accepted all 13 recommendations.

findings.plain: The office's 2025 outreach included regular attendance at NYPD CompStat meetings and quarterly presentations to newly assigned Internal Affairs staff at the Police Academy.
findings.quote:
regular attendance at  
NYPD CompStat and conducting quarterly presentations for newly assigned Internal Affairs staff

numbers.label: Recommendations issued to NYPD whose status is tracked
Recommendations fully implemented
Recommendations rejected by NYPD
Public reports issued by OIG-NYPD since 2015

recommendations: The report makes no new formal recommendations; it catalogues the office's prior reports and tracks the status of the 275 recommendations already issued to NYPD and two to the CCRB.
audits.agency_response: NYPD's responses are tracked throughout: it accepted all six social media recommendations and implemented five, and accepted all 13 new Criminal Group Database recommendations in its January 2026 response.
audits.implementation_note: Of 275 recommendations issued to NYPD through 2025, 159 were fully implemented (about 57.82%), 53 partially implemented or accepted in principle (about 19.27%), 47 rejected (about 17.09%), seven under consideration and nine no longer applicable; two CCRB recommendations were implemented.

audits.title: Facilitated Programs to Assist Small Businesses
audits.plain_title: Helping small businesses get financing
audits.agency: New York City Department of Small Business Services
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Department of Small Business Services provided the services available under its programs to help small businesses obtain funding to open, operate and expand. The audit covered July 2019 to November 2023.
audits.background: The department contracts with Industrial Business Service Providers and Business Solutions Centers to help businesses analyze finances, package loan applications and get training. During the four fiscal years from 2019 to 2022, the department reported the programs facilitated about $220 million in financing.

findings.plain: The department monitors its contractors' expenses and outputs but does not develop or review operational data that would show how the programs are helping small businesses reach their goals.
findings.quote: it does not include the development and review of operational data that would enable the agency to determine how its programs are helping small businesses reach their goals

findings.plain: The 76 businesses auditors reviewed obtained facilitated loans of $97,363,816, but the department collected no data on what the financing accomplished, such as new jobs or stronger operations.
findings.quote: SBS did not collect data on the beneficial effects of this financing, such as the creation of new jobs or strengthening of the businesses’ operations

findings.plain: Program results such as the number and amount of facilitated loans are self-reported by vendors and the department does not verify them.
findings.quote: the program results are self-reported by the vendors

findings.plain: Contractor files were incomplete. Fifteen sampled businesses received 24 loans worth $23,113,349 with no lender proof letter on file, and three others had loan amounts that did not match their proof letters.
findings.quote: did not have a proof letter from the lender in Dynamics

findings.plain: Some loans went to businesses that may not have qualified. Auditors found 158 facilitated loans worth $10,242,747 went to businesses outside New York City or lacking documentation of a city presence.
findings.quote: 158 of the 2,129 facilitated loans, valued at $10,242,747, were made to businesses located outside of New York City or there was no documentation to support a presence in New York City

findings.plain: Controls over training enrollment and attendance need improvement. Attendance records were missing for 13% of counted participants, 18% of attendees with records did not stay for at least half the session and before 2023 the department did not run post-course surveys.
findings.quote: we found that 173 attendees (18%) did not stay for at least half of the course/session

numbers.label: Reported financing facilitated, fiscal years 2019 to 2022
Facilitated loans obtained by the 76 reviewed businesses
Loans to businesses outside the city or undocumented

recommendations: Improve monitoring so the programs align with the department's mission, including possibly expanding required reporting in future contracts to capture program outcomes.
Improve oversight of provider data so records are complete and accurate and all required fields in the department's system are filled in.
Ensure all served businesses are located in New York City or have a formal city presence.
Require Business Solutions Centers to keep better attendance records for training webinars and workshops.
Set a minimum attendance time before a participant counts as having received a contracted service.
Revisit how post-training surveys are conducted, including whether the department should run them itself.

audits.title: New York City Housing Authority Monitorship: Monitors' Report (Second Annual Report, Seventh Overall)
audits.plain_title: Year seven: pests and mold improve, elevators and IT go backward
audits.agency: New York City Housing Authority
audits.what_they_audited: The federal monitors' annual review of the New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) for the seventh year of the monitorship, January 31, 2025 to January 31, 2026. It covers the six property areas of the 2019 agreement with the federal government, heat, elevators, pests and waste, mold and leaks, lead paint and inspections, plus the 47 initiatives in NYCHA's Transformation Plan, capital spending and the monitors' own budget.
audits.background: On January 31, 2019 NYCHA agreed with the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York (SDNY), the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and the City of New York to fix housing conditions, and a monitor was appointed. About two-thirds of NYCHA's funding comes from federal grants, and the monitors write that contemplated federal budget cuts could cost NYCHA as much as $100 million starting next year.

findings.plain: Pest response times improved sharply while pest populations went the other way. NYCHA answered 87% of mouse, cockroach and bed bug complaints within seven calendar days, a 22 percentage point jump, and kept meeting its rat targets at 98% within two business days. But its estimated populations rose 19% for rats, 39% for mice, 21% for bed bugs and 4% for cockroaches compared with Year 6, though all four remain far below where they stood at the start of the monitorship.
findings.quote: increased from Year 6, with a 19% increase for rats, 39% for

findings.plain: Mold work improved but stayed far short of the standard. NYCHA met the agreement's mold timeframes 29% of the time, up from 9% in Year 6 and well below the 95% requirement, and average remediation time fell from 120 days in Year 4 to 12 days. Severity remains a problem, with 85% of complaints involving mold covering ten square feet or more, and the combined mold and leak backlog is over 65,000 open work orders.
findings.quote: mold and leak backlog—over 65,000 open work orders—

findings.plain: NYCHA finished its boiler obligation a year early, replacing 198 boilers itself and transferring 698 to private partners who replaced 462, but heating outages rose. There were 307 unplanned central heating outages in the first half of the 2025-2026 season against 206 a year earlier, affecting 61% of occupied apartments compared with 54%.
findings.quote: there have been 307 unplanned central heating outages,

findings.plain: Elevator performance stalled or declined after three years of gains. NYCHA finally completed its obligation to replace or modernize 275 elevators, a year late, and restored service within ten hours for 89% of unplanned outages, but the average outage lasted 6.5 hours, 16% worse than the 5.6 hours of the prior year.
findings.quote: elevator outages in an average of 6.5 hours per outage,

findings.plain: HUD inspection results improved markedly. NYCHA passed 64 of 89 inspections in 2025, or 72%, compared with 46% of 138 inspections in 2024, and completed annual self-inspections in 95% of occupied apartments, up from 91%. The monitors found HUD had flagged problems NYCHA's own inspectors could have caught, such as missing smoke detectors and kitchen and bathroom outlets without ground-fault protection.
findings.quote: passed 64 of 89 inspections (72%), a signiﬁcant

findings.plain: A large lead paint remediation backlog remains open. Of 19,835 remediation work orders identified in December 2024, NYCHA completed 9,412 and cancelled 610, leaving 9,813 open, many unresolved because NYCHA cannot get into the apartment or more work is needed. Separately, NYCHA has completed X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF) testing in about 97% of units known or presumed to have lead paint.
findings.quote: remediation work orders. Of 19,835 remediation work

findings.plain: NYCHA's biggest technology project collapsed. The replacement of its Resident Case Management System, first due to go live in April 2025, has no launch date after NYCHA terminated the vendor's contract in 2025, and two other major systems also slipped. The monitors traced the failure to vendor selection, heavy customization and weak vendor management, and NYCHA paid $350,000 for a second outside technical assessment.
findings.quote: either select vendors with more public housing experience or take

numbers.label: Mouse, cockroach and bed bug complaints answered in 7 days
Mold work orders finished within required timeframes
Open mold and leak work orders
Unplanned heating outages, first half of the 2025-26 season
Average length of an unplanned elevator outage
HUD inspections passed in 2025
Possible loss of federal support starting next year
Budget for the monitorship's work

recommendations: Keep replacing boilers and invest in the heating distribution system, which NYCHA estimates would take $4 billion in additional funding to fully repair or replace.
Improve the quality of pest control treatments, not just their timeliness, so pest populations actually fall.
Strengthen annual self-inspections so health and safety problems are caught and fixed before HUD inspectors arrive.
Pick technology vendors with real public housing experience, or move faster to enforce contract terms requiring a vendor to bring in that expertise.
Minimize customization when buying the next resident case management system, taking account of HUD requirements that are common to public housing agencies.
Adopt vendor performance measures earlier in technology projects and enforce contract requirements more proactively.
Share the monitors' findings about the failed project with candidates for NYCHA's new technology leadership.

Simplify the employee performance evaluation process, add a second layer of review, tie evaluations to objective performance indicators and connect low ratings to corrective action including training.
audits.agency_response: NYCHA agreed to adopt several of the monitors' performance evaluation recommendations in the cycle that began in January 2026, including a four-point rating scale and review by next-level supervisors, and plans to use key performance indicators in evaluations in 2027. It declined to add training for low-rated employees, saying that kind of follow-up is already part of its traditional progressive management of staff. NYCHA also agreed to share the monitors' technology findings with candidates for new information technology leadership.
audits.compliance_note: The monitors found NYCHA built on earlier progress and should be commended, but that performance regressed in several areas and full compliance will require both continued cultural and organizational reform and enough money for operations and capital work. Under Paragraph 28 of the agreement, NYCHA does not yet meet the criteria for ending the monitorship.

audits.title: Review of the Small Business Forward Initiative and Its Impact on Violations Enforcement
audits.plain_title: Did small business fine reforms actually reach small businesses?
audits.agency: Mayor's Office, Department of Small Business Services and six enforcement agencies
audits.what_they_audited: This was a review, not a full audit. The comptroller's office checked the status of the 116 regulatory reforms recommended under the Small Business Forward initiative and, where possible, whether the projected savings for small businesses were actually realized.
audits.background: In January 2022 Mayor Eric Adams signed Executive Order 2, directing six city agencies to reform business regulations to reduce fines for small businesses; the agencies recommended changes to 116 of 232 regulations reviewed, with estimated savings of about $8.9 million a year. Many reforms were codified in Local Law 151 of 2023, and Mayor Mamdani extended the initiative in January 2026 with Executive Order 11.

findings.plain: The city never defined "small business" for the initiative, and the agencies carrying it out generally did not consider the impact on small businesses when choosing regulations to reform. No agency tracks violations by business size.
findings.quote: the agencies charged with implementing Small Business Forward generally did not consider the potential impact on small businesses when identifying regulations for potential reform

findings.plain: The claimed outreach behind the reforms, including a survey of nearly 1,000 small business owners, could not be verified. No agency produced the survey or any documentation of consultation.
findings.quote: none of the entities contacted during this review could substantiate that the survey or consultation with small businesses occurred

findings.plain: Most of the regulations picked for reform were rarely or never enforced. Only 36 of the 116 were regularly used as the basis for violations in calendar year 2021, and 59 produced no violations at all that year.
findings.quote: only 36 (31%) had related violations that were issued frequently during CY 2021

findings.plain: No one has measured the initiative's full financial impact because agencies did not collect the needed data. Using the data available, auditors estimated the reforms cut fines for all businesses of any size from $14.5 million to $12.1 million over 15 months, a 17% reduction.
findings.quote: went from $14.5 million (pre-adoption) to $12.1 million (post-adoption), a 17% reduction

findings.plain: Of the 30 regularly enforced regulations whose changes were implemented, 14 related to health and safety, such as hazardous materials and emergency exits. Auditors could not tell whether softer penalties slowed how quickly violations were fixed.
findings.quote: Of the 30, 14 (47%) related to health and safety issues.

findings.plain: No single agency was put in charge of the initiative, no performance indicators were set and no impact assessment was ever conducted, even as the program was rebooted in 2025 and extended in 2026.
findings.quote: There appears to be no single entity responsible for overseeing the SBF initiative

findings.plain: The administration's projection of roughly $8.9 million in annual savings for small businesses had no documented methodology and could not be substantiated.
findings.quote: the SBF report’s estimated annual savings of approximately $8.9 million cannot be verified or relied upon as accurate

numbers.label: Regulations recommended for reform under the initiative
Of those 116 regularly enforced in the year before reform
Estimated fine reduction, January 2024 through March 2025
Projected annual savings that could not be verified

recommendations: Formally designate a lead agency to oversee and coordinate the initiative, track savings and ensure it stays effective.
Publish regular public reports on the initiative's progress, realized savings for small businesses and compliance rates, with clearly defined indicators and methods.
Adopt a uniform definition of "small business" used by all participating agencies.
Have agencies prioritize violations and reforms based on their impact on businesses that fit that definition, not on businesses generally.
Develop a framework for monitoring both financial savings and non-financial impacts such as reduced administrative burden and time savings.
Have the six regulatory agencies consider adding a small business identifier to their systems to track violations, fine reductions, waivers and cure periods for small entities.
Create a formal, documented methodology for calculating projected and realized savings from the reforms.
Implement a formal protocol to monitor whether reduced penalties or extended cure periods affect how quickly health and safety violations are fixed.
Have the lead agency review the reforms already implemented to determine whether the financial savings actually benefited small businesses.
audits.agency_response: The Mayor's Office agreed with six of the nine recommendations, agreed in principle with two and did not address one, and the Department of Small Business Services deferred to the Mayor's Office. The Fire Department disagreed with the recommendation on prioritizing reforms by small business impact.

audits.title: Oversight of Language Access Services
audits.plain_title: Interpretation and translation at the health department
audits.agency: New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene adequately serves people with limited English proficiency, complies with state regulations and local laws and provides sufficient oversight of its language access services. The audit covered January 2019 through December 2024.
audits.background: An estimated 1.7 million New York City residents have limited English proficiency, and local law requires the health department to provide free language access services, including telephone interpretation in at least 100 languages and translated key documents in the top 10 citywide languages. The department's Language Services Unit creates and distributes these resources for all public-facing programs.

findings.plain: The department has no centralized system for recording and tracking the language services it provides, so requests may be underreported and the needs of clients with limited English proficiency may not be fully known.
findings.quote: DOHMH does not have a centralized system for recording and tracking LAS

findings.plain: Officials do not know how many calls are dropped or how often an interpreter cannot be found.
findings.quote: DOHMH officials are unaware of the number of dropped calls and instances where an interpreter could not be found.

findings.plain: Some bilingual staff provide clinical services in a non-English language without passing the department's required fluency assessment, and the department reports its assessment numbers inconsistently.
findings.quote: there are uncertified bilingual staff providing clinical services in a non-English language

findings.plain: In a survey of 50 restaurants and food establishments, many owners and workers did not know about available language services or the Business Owner's Bill of Rights, which covers the right to language help during inspections.
findings.quote: many owners and workers were unaware of available LAS resources or the Business Owner’s Bill of Rights

findings.plain: When multilingual state auditors called department facilities unannounced, they hit barriers including staff not trying to connect them to interpreters, hard-to-navigate automated systems, disconnected calls, long waits and missing website translations.
findings.quote: DOHMH staff not attempting to connect callers to an interpreter.

findings.plain: Visits to 10 public-facing facilities found inadequate or missing signage for giving feedback and complaints, plus delays, technical problems and apparent shortages of language access equipment at some sites.
findings.quote: Installation delays and technical issues with LAS equipment

numbers.label: Estimated city residents with limited English proficiency
Minimum languages required for telephone interpretation

recommendations: Develop a system-wide database to collect and track clients' language preferences across all facilities and work with vendors to gather data on service delivery and unfulfilled requests.

Make sure all communications aimed at people with limited English proficiency, including automated phone systems, signage, surveys and feedback boxes, are available in the appropriate languages and always accessible.
Ensure all bilingual staff who provide interpretation complete the department's fluency assessment.
Periodically assess each program and facility's language access equipment and connection needs.

audits.title: DOI's Investigation into the Reclamation of Vacant NYCHA Apartments
audits.plain_title: Vacant public housing units are a growing safety risk
audits.agency: New York City Housing Authority
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) examined the public safety risks posed by the growing number of vacant New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) apartments and how well NYCHA secures those units against illegal occupancy.
audits.background: Vacant NYCHA apartments rose from about 2,840 in January 2022 to 6,740 as of May 2025, with the average vacancy lasting about a year, while 165,000 applicants sit on the public housing waitlist. Lead and asbestos abatement requirements and funding constraints drive the lengthy turnover process.

findings.plain: Vacant apartments without adequate security create opportunities for illegal occupancy, and some unauthorized occupants use the units as a base for illegal activities.
findings.quote:
vacant apartments, without adequate security measures, create opportunities for illegal occupancy by 
unauthorized individuals, some of whom use the apartments as a base for illegal activities.

findings.plain: From January 2022 to May 2025, the New York City Police Department reclaimed 548 apartments from unauthorized occupants, 60 through joint efforts with DOI, and those joint efforts produced 81 arrests on charges including trespassing, drug possession and weapon possession.
findings.quote:
the NYPD reclaimed 548 apartments  from 
unauthorized occupants, 60 of which were reclaimed through joint efforts  by the NYPD and DOI.

findings.plain: NYCHA does not proactively inspect vacant apartments throughout the turnover cycle, which lets trespassing and other illegal activity go undetected and delays the discovery of unauthorized occupants.
findings.quote:
NYCHA does not proactively inspect vacant apartments to ensure that the unit is in fact vacant 
throughout the entirety of the apartment turnover cycle.

findings.plain: NYCHA procedure requires every vacant apartment in a development to use the same lockset and key, so anyone with the key can enter any vacant unit. Some employees instead use a generic "65 key" that also opens utility rooms and management offices authority-wide, adding to the risk.
findings.quote:
presenting the risk that individuals could, upon acquiring a key, access any vacant unit in the 
development.

findings.plain: Turning over an apartment costs about $52,000 on average, including roughly $17,000 for lead abatement, $25,000 for asbestos abatement and $10,000 for general renovations, and funding constraints make it hard for NYCHA to shorten the process.
findings.quote: The average cost to complete the turnover process is approximately $52,000

numbers.label: Vacant NYCHA apartments as of May 2025
Vacant apartments in January 2022
Apartments reclaimed from unauthorized occupants
Arrests from joint NYPD-DOI reclamation efforts
Applicants on the public housing waitlist
Average cost to turn over a vacant apartment

recommendations: NYCHA should revise its apartment turnover procedure to require monthly property management inspections of vacant apartments not yet ready for rental, secure windows and door locks during those inspections and report any unauthorized occupants to NYCHA's law department within 72 hours.

NYCHA should evaluate alternative locksets or security technologies such as electronic locks, and meanwhile require each development to rotate among at least two or three versions of move-out cylinders and keys, with no two developments sharing the same keys.

NYCHA should revise its Resident Watch guidelines to require volunteers to report suspected unauthorized inhabitants or illegal activity in vacant apartments to their supervisor, who should inform property management by the end of the shift and log the reports.
When property management receives such a report from a Resident Watch supervisor, it should immediately seek to confirm it and, if verified, report to NYCHA's law department within 72 hours.
If NYCHA receives additional refurbishment funding, it should deploy the money to shorten the time needed to complete apartment turnovers.
audits.agency_response: NYCHA accepted all five recommendations, noting it will need about a year to build automated work orders for the monthly inspections, six months to a year to update the Quality of Life form and that the funding recommendation is subject to available money.

audits.title: Twenty-Ninth Report of the Independent Monitor: Compliance Snapshot of NYPD’s Stop, Frisk, and Search Practices
audits.plain_title: Stop and frisk compliance snapshot for spring 2025
audits.agency: New York City Police Department
audits.what_they_audited: A quarterly visual "compliance snapshot" updating the monitor's Twenty-Eighth Report on the New York City Police Department's (NYPD) compliance with the federal court's requirements in Floyd v. City of New York, Ligon v. City of New York and Davis v. City of New York, covering the second quarter (April to June) of 2025.
audits.background: The report covers the second quarter of 2025 and in several slides compares it to the second quarter of 2024. It draws on the monitor team's audits of 100 stop reports per month and quarterly body-worn camera video audits, plus audits by the NYPD Quality Assurance Section, command self-inspections and first-line supervisor reviews.

findings.plain: In the second quarter of 2025, the monitor's audits found 91% of reported stops, 79% of frisks and 77% of searches lawful. The monitor said compliance had not changed substantially from previous quarters and that frisks and searches continued to have unacceptably low compliance rates.
findings.quote: 91% of stops, 79% of frisks, and 77% of searches were assessed as lawful

findings.plain: Self-initiated stops remained less lawful than stops from radio runs or witnesses: 85% of self-initiated stops were lawful, with frisks during them at 71% and searches at 60%.
findings.quote: Frisks during self-initiated stops were lawful 71% of the time

findings.quote: 87% of commands had a compliance rate for stops greater than 85%

findings.quote: For 27% of stops identified in the Monitor's audit for underreporting in

findings.quote: the NYPD properly recorded the stop in its entirety

findings.plain: Housing Bureau officers' compliance was 82% for stops, 84% for frisks and 80% for searches, with trespass arrests at 98% compliance on the reason to approach and 100% on probable cause.

audits.title: 2025 End of Year Monitor Update
audits.plain_title: After twelve years, NYPD still not in compliance on stop and frisk
audits.agency: New York City Police Department
audits.what_they_audited: The monitor's year-end summary of the New York City Police Department's (NYPD) 2025 efforts to comply with the federal court's 2013 order requiring constitutional policing in the Floyd, Ligon and Davis stop and frisk cases, covering accountability, self-initiated stops, underreporting, discipline, Fourteenth Amendment compliance and community engagement.
audits.background: A federal court ordered the NYPD in 2013 to bring its stop, question and frisk practices in line with the Constitution and appointed an independent monitor. The monitor writes that ongoing compliance problems fall into three main categories: lack of meaningful accountability, unlawfulness of self-initiated stops and persistent underreporting of Terry stops.

findings.plain: After twelve years of oversight, the department has yet to reach substantial compliance with the court's 2013 order. The monitor called the report a wake-up call and said there should not be a permanent monitor.
findings.quote: the NYPD has yet to reach substantial compliance

findings.plain: Supervisors still approved nearly everything. In the first half of 2025, reviewing supervisors found 99% of stops, 95% of frisks and 94% of searches compliant, while the monitor's audits found only 89% of stops, 73% of frisks and 73% of searches lawful.
findings.quote: 99% of all stops, 95% of frisks, and 94% of searches compliant

findings.plain: Discipline remained rare. In the first half of 2025, commands took no action in 97 of 305 cases where the Quality Assurance Section found a stop unlawful, issued command discipline in only 8 cases and in 29 cases rejected the audit finding outright, a practice the monitor said undermines compliance efforts.
findings.quote: command discipline (“CD”) issued in only 8 cases

findings.plain: Self-initiated stops, nearly half of all reported stops, were far less lawful (79.4% for stops, 64.0% for frisks and 53.3% for searches in the first half of 2025) than stops from radio runs or witnesses. Specialized units performed worst, with only 75% of Neighborhood Safety Team stops and 64% of Public Safety Team stops lawful, and the monitor's preliminary audits show the department is unlikely to meet the compliance targets of 85% by the third quarter of 2025 and 90% by year end. The department eliminated its Public Safety Teams on November 7, 2025.
findings.quote: self -initiated stops ( 79.4% stops, 64.0% frisks, 53.3% searches)

findings.plain: Underreporting improved but nearly one-third of stops still went undocumented: the monitor's 2025 audits found 71% of stops reviewed were properly documented, up from 61% in 2024.
findings.quote: The Monitor’s 2025 audits showed  that 71% of the...

findings.plain: Work on police discipline reform stalled. The Discipline Working Group of plaintiffs, the City and the monitor had to be paused after the City sought to revamp the process at the end of 2025 and said it could agree to only a few of the recommendations in Judge James Yates' September 2024 discipline report.
findings.quote: the DWG had to be paused because at the end of 2025, the City sent a letter

findings.plain: The department advanced a Fourteenth Amendment compliance plan, delivering a revised plan on December 31, 2025 that includes a Racial Disparities Review Committee, and hired academic advisors to analyze racial disparities in stops. Separately, in five bias cases where the Civilian Complaint Review Board sought charges, the police commissioner found the conduct improper but not racially motivated and declined to bring charges.
findings.quote: This plan includes a Racial Disparities Review...

numbers.label: Stops that reviewing supervisors called compliant, first half of 2025
Stops the monitor found unlawful, first half of 2025
Cases with command discipline out of 305 unlawful stops
Cases where commands rejected the audit's unlawfulness finding
Stops properly documented in 2025 audits, up from 61% in 2024
Self-initiated stops found lawful, first half of 2025

recommendations: Implement more robust corrective actions, including discipline, for supervisors and officers who repeatedly do not comply with legal requirements.
Have leadership demand accountability through ComplianceStat at the same level required under CompStat, so poor supervisor performance consistently results in discipline or reassignment.
Provide ongoing monitoring in the Early Intervention Program and have the Early Intervention Committee define and measure success for officers who come through the program.
audits.agency_response: The department continued ComplianceStat, revised the Early Intervention Program in May 2025 with the monitor's input and delivered a revised Fourteenth Amendment compliance plan on December 31, 2025. At the end of 2025 the City sought to revamp the discipline working group process and agreed to only a few of its recommendations, then withdrew the letter after discussions.
audits.compliance_note: The monitor concluded that after twelve years of oversight the NYPD has yet to reach substantial compliance with the court's 2013 order, citing little to no discipline for noncompliant stops, supervisors who deem nearly all encounters lawful, low compliance for self-initiated stops and specialized teams and underreporting of almost one-third of stops.

audits.auditor: New York City Board of Correction
audits.title: Injury Response in NYC Jails: Board of Correction Analysis of 2024 Data
audits.plain_title: Jail injury counts still do not match and reports run months late
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: The New York City Board of Correction (BOC) checked whether the New York City Department of Correction (DOC) and New York City Health + Hospitals/Correctional Health Services (CHS) followed the Board's minimum standard on injury response during calendar year 2024. The review combined analysis of administrative data, the agencies' monthly and annual reports and a random sample of 99 Injury-to-Inmate forms.
audits.background: The Board published a report on serious injuries in 2019 that found DOC underreported serious injuries and had no single reliable count, and it then adopted rules requiring the two agencies to build a shared electronic injury tracking system and file joint monthly injury reports. Those requirements were phased in through August 2022, making 2023 the first full year of data collection after implementation.

findings.plain: Both agencies have written injury policies, which technically satisfies the standard, but the Board found the policies do not set deadlines for closing investigations or explain how investigative findings feed into preventing future injuries.
findings.quote: The lack of a formal definition for “prompt” and “expeditious” in

findings.plain: Injury investigations closed in nine days on average, but the spread ran from same day to about three months, and one in ten sampled forms carried date problems: missing dates, a closure date before the injury date or dates from before 2000. The Board says bad dates undercut its ability to sequence events and follow up.
findings.quote: a mean closure time of nine days

findings.plain: Most narratives read as neutral, with 86 of 99 rated fully objective, but people in custody declined to take part in the investigation in 97 of the 99 sampled cases.
findings.quote: people in custody refused to participate in the investigation process

findings.plain: The shared electronic injury tracking system the rules require still does not exist. DOC and CHS keep separate systems, and for 2024 CHS counted 29,405 injuries against DOC's 28,273, a gap the agencies say cannot be reconciled month to month because each counts a different set of cases.
findings.quote: The agencies continue to maintain separate systems

findings.plain: Self-harm reporting runs through three separate unreconciled figures in the same joint monthly report, two from CHS and one from DOC, with no explanation of the differences. CHS shares self-injury data with DOC but not its mental health self-harm data, so some self-harm incidents are never investigated by DOC.
findings.quote: these numbers match, and the report does not include an explanation or footnote

findings.plain: Reporting to the Board was late and incomplete. DOC first supplied 23,664 of the 28,273 injury forms for 2024, or 84 percent, rising to 94 percent after it uploaded missing May 2024 forms in November 2025, and the joint monthly reports slipped from an average 17 days late in 2023 to 72 days late in 2024.
findings.quote: In 2023, the average delay was 17 days, increasing substantially to 72 days in 2024.

findings.plain: DOC's 2024 annual injury review attributed a 4 percent rise in injuries to a growing jail population, but the Board's own rate calculation shows injuries per 1,000 people in custody fell from 372 in 2023 to 365 in 2024. The review also identified no compliance problems and set out no corrective action plan.
findings.quote: did not articulate corrective action plans with defined steps or timelines

numbers.label: Injuries CHS reported for 2024
Injuries DOC reported for 2024
Injury-to-Inmate forms DOC first gave the Board
Average lateness of joint monthly injury reports in 2024
Average time to close an injury investigation
Sampled forms with missing or inconsistent dates
Sampled investigation narratives rated fully objective
Cases where the injured person declined to participate

recommendations: DOC and CHS should update their policies on addressing and preventing injuries so they line up with the investigation, coordination and reporting requirements of Minimum Standard 3-16.
DOC policies should spell out how investigative findings are used to inform injury prevention, tying investigation results to corrective action.

CHS policies should spell out expected timelines for injury response, documentation such as Injury-to-Inmate forms and reporting such as the joint monthly injury report and the monthly public self-harm report.
DOC should digitize the Injury-to-Inmate form with required fields, room for supporting evidence such as video and electronic signatures, to cut down on missing data and handwritten sign-offs.
DOC should set up internal monitoring of investigation timeliness, including clear deadlines for closing an investigation, to address the cases that run long.
Given how often people in custody decline to take part, DOC should look for ways to engage them during investigations while respecting their rights and the standards.
DOC and CHS should voluntarily give the Board detailed minutes or summaries of the quarterly meetings the rules require, showing the data review, trends identified and quality assurance work.
DOC and CHS must build and maintain the coordinated electronic injury tracking system the rules require, covering serious and non-serious injuries in one reconciled platform.
DOC and CHS should put internal controls in place to submit Injury-to-Inmate forms and joint monthly injury reports on time.
DOC and CHS should reconcile their differing injury and self-injurious behavior counts into a single joint monthly injury report with all required breakdowns.

DOC should make its required annual review of the joint monthly reports document compliance findings, systemic issues and corrective action plans with steps and timelines, and should publish the annual reports as well as send them to the Board.
CHS should make its monthly public self-harm reports consistently break the data out by seriousness, separating serious from non-serious injuries as the minimum standards require.
audits.agency_response: The report notes that DOC and CHS staff reviewed and commented on it. After reviewing an earlier draft, DOC uploaded the missing May 2024 Injury-to-Inmate forms in November 2025, raising the share of 2024 forms provided to the Board from 84 percent to 94 percent.

audits.title: Twenty-Eighth Report of the Independent Monitor: Compliance Snapshot of NYPD’s Stop, Frisk, and Search Practices
audits.plain_title: Stop and frisk compliance snapshot for early 2025
audits.agency: New York City Police Department
audits.what_they_audited: A quarterly visual "compliance snapshot" updating the monitor's Twenty-Seventh Report on the New York City Police Department's (NYPD) compliance with the federal court's requirements in Floyd v. City of New York, Ligon v. City of New York and Davis v. City of New York, covering the first quarter of 2025.
audits.background: The report covers the first quarter of 2025 and in several slides compares it to the first quarter of 2024. It draws on the monitor team's audits of 100 stop reports per month and quarterly body-worn camera video audits, plus audits by the NYPD Quality Assurance Section, command self-inspections and first-line supervisor reviews.

findings.plain: In the first quarter of 2025, the monitor's audits found 86% of reported stops, 69% of frisks and 68% of searches lawful, a slight increase for frisks and searches over a year earlier that the monitor cautioned may not reflect a permanent improvement.
findings.quote: 86% of stops, 69% of frisks, and 68% of searches were assessed as lawful

findings.quote: Frisks during self-initiated stops were lawful 58% of the time

findings.plain: By the department's own audits, 81% of commands had stop compliance above 85%, but only 51% cleared that bar for frisks and 41% for searches, an improvement over the first quarter of 2024.
findings.quote: 41% of commands had a compliance rate for searches greater than 85%

findings.plain: Supervision remained inadequate. The monitor found 14% of stops, 31% of frisks and 32% of searches unlawful, while reviewing supervisors flagged only 1% of stops, 6% of frisks and 8% of searches in the same encounters.
findings.quote: supervisors found that only 1% of stops, 6% of frisks, and 8% of searches

findings.plain: Officers failed to complete stop reports for 31% of stops identified in the monitor's audit (12 of 39), down from 44% in the first quarter of 2024, suggesting stop reporting may be improving.
findings.quote: 31% of the stops identified in the Monitor’s audit for underreporting

findings.plain: Body-worn camera recording improved substantially: 96% of stops identified in the audit were recorded in their entirety, up from 82% in the first quarter of 2024.
findings.quote: for 96% of stops identified in the Monitor's audit

findings.plain: Housing Bureau officers' compliance was 80% for stops, 66% for frisks and 77% for searches, while trespass arrests showed 100% compliance on both the reason to approach and probable cause.
findings.quote: 80% of stops, 66% of frisks, and 77% of...

Searches during self-initiated stops found lawful

recommendations: The report makes no new formal recommendations.
audits.compliance_note: The monitor found compliance rates of 86% for stops, 69% for frisks and 68% for searches in the first quarter of 2025, with self-initiated encounters and first-line supervision still falling well short: supervisors approved nearly all stops, frisks and searches including unlawful ones, suggesting continued inadequate supervision at the command level.

audits.title: Physical and Financial Conditions at Selected Mitchell-Lama Developments
audits.plain_title: Conditions and spending at three Mitchell-Lama developments
audits.agency: New York City Department of Housing Preservation and Development
audits.what_they_audited: Whether Mitchell-Lama developments supervised by the Department of Housing Preservation and Development are maintained in a way that protects residents' health and safety and whether their funds are used for intended purposes. The audit covered January 2019 through April 2025.
audits.background: The Mitchell-Lama program, created in 1955, provides affordable rental and co-op housing for middle-income families, and the department supervises 92 city developments with about 46,787 units. The audit sampled three developments: Clinton Towers in Manhattan, Evergreen Gardens in the Bronx and Tivoli Towers in Brooklyn.

findings.plain: The department needs to improve its oversight. Management at all three sampled developments failed to provide a safe and clean living environment and spent development funds on activities not directly related to operations.
findings.quote: Management at all three sampled developments failed to provide a safe and clean living environment

findings.plain: Auditors observed hazardous conditions across the three developments, including facade damage, fire doors that did not close, units with mold, water damage and peeling paint and a day care tenant with mouse droppings in classrooms.
findings.quote: façade damage; non-working self-closing/fire doors; units with mold, water damage, and peeling paint; and a commercial tenant (day care) with mouse droppings in classrooms

findings.plain: About $163,862 in transactions from 2019 through 2024 were unrelated to normal operations or inadequately supported, including $114,288 in non-mandated bonuses, holiday events and gratuities and $49,574 in expenses without invoices or canceled checks.
findings.quote: approximately $163,862 in transactions for the period from January 2019 through December 2024 that were either unrelated to normal operations or inadequately supported

findings.plain: Managing agents at Clinton and Tivoli Towers lost an estimated $327,514 in rent from units that sat vacant for more than 120 days.
findings.quote: managing agents were unable to collect $327,514 in unrealized rental income from units that remained vacant for more than 120 days

findings.plain: All three developments paid vendors more than $100,000 in aggregate without notifying the department as required, and Evergreen hired five such vendors with no department approval and no evidence of competitive bidding.
findings.quote: Evergreen contracted with five vendors with payments over $100,000 without receiving HPD approval and no evidence of competitive bidding.

numbers.label: Spending unrelated to operations or unsupported
Estimated rent lost to units vacant more than 120 days
Units in city-supervised Mitchell-Lama developments, about

recommendations: Improve monitoring of the three developments, verifying that managing agents conduct annual unit inspections, complete related reports, correct deficiencies and keep self-closing fire doors working.
Ensure immediate corrective action when hazardous conditions are identified.
Develop and implement policies and procedures on bonus and gratuity payments.
Ensure managing agents operate the developments in a fiscally sound way by adequately reviewing expenses and supporting documentation during annual reviews.
Promptly fill vacant units.
Periodically review expenses to identify vendor payments that reach $100,000 in a fiscal year and confirm the department approved them and contracts were competitively bid.

audits.title: Status Report on Local Law 42
audits.plain_title: Monitor says final rulings on the solitary limits law must wait
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: A status report from the court-appointed independent monitor in Nunez v. City of New York on the monitoring team's analysis of Local Law 42, a city law that would change how the jails use restraints, escorts, de-escalation confinement, emergency lock-ins and restricted housing, and how those requirements interact with the Nunez court orders.
audits.background: The City Council passed Local Law 42 on December 20, 2023 and enacted it over the mayor's veto on January 30, 2024. The mayor then suspended parts of the law by emergency order, a state court found that suspension improper in July 2025 and the federal Nunez court granted a temporary injunction of certain provisions on July 3, 2025 while the monitor analyzed conflicts with its orders.

findings.plain: The monitor concluded that certain provisions of Local Law 42 as written would work against the Nunez court orders' goal of a constitutionally sufficient level of safety and would impede the Department of Correction's ability to comply with those orders.
findings.quote: would undermine and are antithetical to the purpose of the Nunez Court Orders

findings.plain: The monitor said the department currently lacks the basic operational foundation needed to carry out the reforms the court has already ordered, let alone the changes the new law would add.
findings.quote: the Department lacks the foundation to support the basic reforms

findings.plain: The monitoring team's concerns focus on provisions that apply universally in situations that require staff discretion, or that set standards the team considers impractical or unsafe to put into operation in these jails.
findings.quote: concerns center around the universal application of certain requirements that

findings.plain: The monitor stated it will not approve or direct department practices that include the problematic components of Local Law 42 unless those requirements are modified.
findings.quote: ...approve or direct such practices absent modifications to those requirements.

findings.plain: The monitor said it would be premature to make final determinations on Local Law 42 now, given conditions in the jails, the newly created remediation manager position, the new mayor who took office January 1, 2026 and signs that the parties want to find a mutually agreeable path.
findings.quote: a report issued at this juncture would be both speculative and premature

numbers.label: Proposed deadline for the monitor's confidential draft findings
Date the monitor proposed for its next update to the court

recommendations: The monitor should confidentially provide the parties with its preliminary draft findings identifying specific conflicts between Local Law 42 provisions and the Nunez court orders, no later than January 29, 2026.

Meet and confer sessions should be sequenced and timed so that the remediation manager, once onboarded, and the new mayor's correction commissioner can meaningfully participate in discussions of complex operational matters.
The court should set a date certain for the monitor's next update on this work, which the monitor recommends be provided by March 26, 2026.
The court should suspend its December 19, 2025 order outlining next steps so the three recommendations above can be adopted.
audits.agency_response: The city defendants agreed with confidentially sharing the draft findings but disagreed with delaying substantive meet and confer sessions until a remediation manager is appointed, and proposed a court update by February 27, 2026 instead of March 26. The plaintiff class, federal prosecutors and the City Council intervenors also opposed delay.
audits.compliance_note: The monitor assessed that the department lacks the foundation to support the basic reforms required by the Nunez court orders and that certain Local Law 42 provisions, as designed, would impede compliance with those orders.

audits.title: Twentieth Report for the Monitoring Period January 1, 2025 to June 30, 2025
audits.plain_title: Monitor finds toxic culture and backsliding on candor at Rikers
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: The court-appointed independent monitor's 20th compliance assessment of the Department of Correction under the Nunez court orders, covering January through June 2025, including staff deployment, use of force and security practices, management of people in custody, in-custody deaths and compliance ratings for 40 court order provisions.
audits.background: The report was filed just over 10 years after the 2015 consent judgment, days after the court announced it was actively reviewing remediation manager applicants and before the new mayor had named a correction commissioner. Five commissioners have led the agency over the decade and the monitor describes 2021 to 2023 as a true crisis at all levels.

findings.plain: Two December 2025 use of force incidents captured on body-worn cameras, one in which an officer yelled 'Don't leave marks' before another apparently kicked a restrained man and one in which an officer appeared to secretly apply chemical spray to his boot and place it by a restrained man's face, illustrate what the monitor calls a toxic culture of coordinated deception.
findings.quote: including body-worn cameras and stationary cameras, is demonstrative of a toxic culture

findings.plain: The reform effort continues at a glacial pace, with the department still normalizing poor practices and high violence, lacking elementary skills at all levels, cycling through leadership and operating in a perpetual state of crisis.
findings.quote: The reform effort continues to progress at a glacial pace.

findings.plain: The risk of harm remains unreasonably high, and the circumstances of most of the 15 in-custody deaths in 2025 reflect dereliction of duty including staff off post, failures to supervise, unenforced lock-in procedures, dangerous contraband and lack of urgency in emergencies.
findings.quote: ...duty, including staff being off post, failure to supervise, failure to enforce basic lock-in

findings.plain: The monitor found that past patterns of limiting transparency, minimizing problems, shifting blame and using false or misleading information appear to have reemerged in some instances, including in the department's August 2025 Safety Plan and its consultants' recommendations.
findings.quote: previous patterns of attempting to limit transparency, minimize issues, divert

findings.plain: The monitor also documented real progress: violence indicators remain below the 2021 crisis peak, nearly 1,000 backlogged intake investigations were closed, the use of force disciplinary backlog is at an all-time low, body-worn camera use expanded and 270 new correction officers graduated from the academy.
findings.quote: The Trials Division’s use of force-related disciplinary backlog is at an all-time low

findings.plain: With 15 contempt provisions added to the existing 25 this period, the monitoring team now rates the department's compliance with 40 of the hundreds of provisions in the Nunez court orders.
findings.quote: ...assesses compliance with 40 of the hundreds of provisions contained in the Nunez Court Orders.

numbers.label: In-custody deaths in 2025 discussed in the report
Court order provisions now rated for compliance
Backlogged intake investigations closed
New correction officers who graduated from the academy

recommendations: Develop a strategic plan that clearly defines reform priorities and how leadership, staffing and resources will be allocated to address them.

Officers and captains must properly manage and supervise housing units to reduce violence and assaults, with supervisors adopting a skill-development focus and consideration given to a larger organizational management strategy with the remediation manager.
Basic and sound security practices must become embedded in staff's routine duties on housing units.
Staff absenteeism must continue to be curtailed and the number of staff deployed to posts engaging the incarcerated population must be maximized.
Tour commanders and control room captains must ensure sufficient staff are assigned to housing unit and ancillary posts so services are provided consistently and reliably.

Unnecessary and excessive force must be reduced, especially high impact force such as head strikes, with consistent implementation of the use of force directive and greater staff understanding of proportionality.
Facility leadership must be more directly involved in identifying and remediating poor staff practice, with an infusion of correctional expertise reaching more deeply into daily practice.
The department must continue reducing investigative caseloads by allocating resources according to incident severity, expanding the triage pilot as appropriate.
Accountability for staff misconduct must be imposed closer in time to the incidents in which it occurred.
The department must engage the remediation manager and the monitoring team transparently and collaboratively, without which the synergy required to advance reform will remain elusive.
audits.agency_response: The department produced an August 2025 Safety Plan and worked with retained consultants on recommendations for achieving compliance, but the monitor found this work premised in part on false and misleading information, mischaracterizations of the record and arguments the court has already repudiated.
audits.compliance_note: The monitor concludes the department's entrenched culture of dysfunction persists, the risk of harm to people in custody and staff remains unreasonably high and there has not been sufficient forward momentum to counteract the pull of dysfunctional practices, despite pockets of progress since the 2021 crisis.

audits.title: Administration of the CityFHEPS Program for Department of Social Services Homebase Clients
audits.plain_title: Running the CityFHEPS rent subsidy for Homebase clients
audits.agency: New York City Department of Social Services
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Department of Social Services administers the City Fighting Homelessness and Eviction Prevention Supplement (CityFHEPS) program according to the rules, helping residents served by Homebase providers secure permanent housing. The audit covered July 2021 through July 2025.
audits.background: CityFHEPS, launched in 2018, is a rental assistance program for New Yorkers in shelters or at risk of homelessness. Officials say it has helped 123,762 people secure permanent housing through March 2025, with costs rising from $176 million in fiscal year 2019 to $834 million in fiscal year 2024 and projected at $1.2 billion for fiscal year 2025.

findings.plain: Consistent with a prior audit, the department lacks adequate oversight and monitoring of CityFHEPS for people served by Homebase providers, leaving applicants exposed to hazardous apartments and eligibility and payments insufficiently supported.
findings.quote: program applicants were exposed to apartment units with immediately hazardous violations despite preclearance and inspection requirements

findings.plain: In five of 45 sampled cases the department approved units with open hazardous housing violations, including rat and roach infestations. It approved clients for buildings owned by one landlord whose properties had 110 open violations, and it has no landlord disqualification list.
