findings.quote: DSS approved CityFHEPS clients to move into three other properties owned by the same landlord with similar issues

findings.plain: Thirty of 75 sampled case records had no evidence that income was verified, so there is no assurance only eligible applicants got the subsidy.
findings.quote: Thirty of 75 CityFHEPS case records sampled showed no evidence that income was verified

findings.plain: The department does not sufficiently verify landlord-broker relationships. In one case it paid $6,800 in broker's fees before finding the landlord and broker shared the same parent company.
findings.quote: DSS paid $6,800 in broker’s fees before later finding that the landlord and broker were both owned by the same parent company

findings.plain: The department could not show it tested whether rents were reasonable in any of 30 sampled Statewide CityFHEPS cases. In 11 of them the approved rent exceeded comparable units, by $525 on average and by as much as $1,647 a month.
findings.quote: DSS officials could not provide evidence that a rent reasonableness test was completed for any of the 30 sampled Statewide CityFHEPS cases

findings.plain: Because of insufficient monitoring of landlord payments and inaccurate tax forms sent to landlords, there is less assurance that accurate rent payments are reported to the Internal Revenue Service.
findings.quote: DSS issuing inaccurate Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Form 1099s to landlords

numbers.label: Projected CityFHEPS costs for fiscal year 2025
People the program has helped secure permanent housing
Average excess of approved rents over comparable units

recommendations: Establish policies and procedures to check for all housing violations during preclearance and expand preclearance checks to all CityFHEPS cases.
Create a landlord disqualification list with written procedures for adding and removing landlords, and monitor for compliance.
Follow eligibility verification policies, including income checks for all household members 18 and older, and keep all eligibility documents.
Develop written procedures, and monitor compliance, to confirm no substantiated relationship exists between landlords, brokers and managing members and that rent payments go to the correct parties.

audits.title: Audit of the New York City Board of Correction’s Governance Structure and Accessibility of Public Meetings and Website
audits.plain_title: How the jail oversight board runs its meetings and website
audits.agency: New York City Board of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Board of Correction, the independent agency that oversees the city's jails, has an adequate governance structure and follows the laws and rules that govern its proceedings and the accessibility of its meetings, website and communications.
audits.background: The Board of Correction oversees the Department of Correction and sets minimum standards for the care, custody and treatment of everyone in the department's jails. The board is supposed to have nine members serving six-year terms, with three appointed by the mayor, three by the City Council and three by the mayor on the joint nomination of state appellate judges.

findings.plain: The board's committees, which examine critical issues in the city's jails, met behind closed doors. None of the committee meetings were open to the public and minutes, recordings and meeting materials were not posted online as the state Open Meetings Law requires.
findings.quote: BOC does not make any of its committee meetings open to the public or post meeting minutes, recordings, or materials discussed at meetings on its website, as required by the Open Meetings Law.

findings.plain: No formal rules spell out what each committee is authorized to do, what members' roles are, how often committees should meet or what records they must keep, so committee operations were inconsistent.
findings.quote: there are no formal rules or regulations that govern BOC committees or detail their scope of authority, roles and responsibilities of committee Chairs and members, how often they should meet, and requirements for meeting agendas, notice, and minutes.

findings.plain: Rule changes approved in late 2024 concentrated power over committees in the hands of the board chair, who now controls which committees are created and who serves on and leads them.
findings.quote: the new rules gave the Board Chair more control over the establishment and composition of Board committees.

findings.plain: One board member may have been improperly removed by the mayor. She had two appointment letters with different term end dates, and after appellate judges nominated her for reappointment she instead received a letter from the mayor ending her tenure with no explanation.
findings.quote: it is unclear whether the Board member was removed by the Mayor prior to the expiration of her term, and, if so, whether this was done without cause.

findings.plain: The board has not consistently had its full slate of nine members. Seats sat vacant for roughly six to 11 months because appointing authorities did not promptly fill them, leaving the City Council and the judiciary underrepresented.
findings.quote: from September 2024 through November 13, 2025, the Board had seven to eight members. When Board members resigned, appointing authorities did not promptly fill vacancies, and Board member seats were vacant for approximately six to 11 months.

findings.plain: The board falls short of federal, state and city accessibility requirements. An August 2025 test found 656 accessibility errors on its website, it never made a planned switch to a more accessible virtual meeting platform and its meeting notices omit required information for people with disabilities.
findings.quote: based on the audit team’s review in August 2025, the BOC website had 656 accessibility errors.

numbers.label: Accessibility errors found on the board's website
Accessibility errors on the website's own feedback form
How long board seats sat vacant
Use-of-force incidents in city jails in fiscal year 2025

recommendations: Hold board committee meetings in compliance with the state Open Meetings Law, including opening them to the public, giving advance notice and posting minutes or recordings on time.
Write formal rules for each standing and ad hoc committee covering its authority, members' roles, meeting frequency and requirements for agendas, notices and minutes.
Revisit the rules for creating committees and appointing their members and officers, and consider restoring collective decision-making by the full board.
Work with the appointing authorities to fill board vacancies promptly so each authority is equally represented.
Review digital content and coordinate with the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities and the city's technology office to fix accessibility errors.
Immediately switch to an accessible virtual meeting platform.
Update the board's digital accessibility policy and make sure meeting notices include all legally required accessibility information, with accurate details about meeting locations.
Train staff and officials to handle calls made through Telecommunications Relay Service and periodically reassess the need for assistive listening devices.
The Mayor's Office of Appointments should share vetting results with board nominees and give them a chance to respond.
audits.agency_response: The board agreed with two recommendations, partially agreed with two, neither agreed nor disagreed with two and disagreed with two, arguing among other things that its committees are advisory and that appointments are outside its control. The Mayor's Office of Appointments did not respond to the recommendation directed at it.

audits.title: Audit of the Financial and Operating Practices of the Joint Health Insurance Stabilization Fund
audits.plain_title: The fund meant to stabilize city health costs is insolvent
audits.agency: New York City Office of Labor Relations
audits.what_they_audited: The financial condition of the Health Insurance Stabilization Fund (HISF), a reserve fund for city employee health insurance jointly managed by the Office of Labor Relations (OLR) and the Municipal Labor Committee (MLC), and whether the fund's money was used for its intended purposes.
audits.background: HISF was created in 1985 to help support the cost of health insurance coverage for city employees, retirees and their dependents, mainly by covering the cost difference between the city's two no-cost health plans. It is jointly administered by OLR, representing the city, and the MLC, representing municipal labor unions.

findings.plain: The fund is insolvent. Its reported year-end cash balance fell from nearly $1.6 billion in fiscal year 2019 to $843 million in fiscal year 2024, and once required reserves are set aside only about $3.1 million was actually available.
findings.quote: The audit found that HISF is insolvent , and the Office of Labor Relations (OLR) and the Municipal Labor Committee (MLC) did not take adequate steps to improve the Fund’s position.

findings.plain: Since 2001, OLR and the MLC authorized at least $4.3 billion in lump sum payments and recurring transfers from the fund that were not consistent with its stated purpose, including $2.8 billion to the city and $1.5 billion to union-administered welfare funds to cover raises, deferred layoffs and other costs.
findings.quote: these lump sum payments and recurring transfers have resulted in at least $4.3 billion being transferred from HISF to the City ($2.8 billion) and welfare funds ($1.5 billion), as detailed in Tables IV and V below.

findings.plain: Healthcare savings agreements in 2014 and 2018 let the MLC count reductions in the city's payments into the fund as "savings." These offsets reduced the fund's balance by $3.3 billion and ultimately led to its insolvency in fiscal year 2022.
findings.quote: These offsets reduced the Fund’s balance year over year, which ultimately led to its insolvency in FY2022.

findings.plain: OLR and the MLC knew as early as 2018 that the fund would be insolvent by fiscal year 2021 unless significant action was taken, but did not act in time. A committee created to recommend fixes never issued formal findings, the planned Medicare Advantage switch was dropped and a new health plan procurement did not start until 2022, after the fund was already insolvent.
findings.quote: OLR and the MLC knew as early as 2018 that the Fund would be insolvent by FY2021 unless significant action was taken, but did not take timely or effective action

findings.plain: The fund has accrued about $3.1 billion in liabilities it cannot pay, mostly equalization payments owed to the city, and these liabilities were never reported on the fund's annual certifications, materially underreporting its deficits since fiscal year 2022.
findings.quote: OLR and the MLC have been materially underreporting the Fund’s deficits since FY2022. This underreporting of deficits totals approximately $3.1 billion as of April 2025.

findings.plain: The fund kept paying for additional benefits such as the Psychotropic, Injectable, Chemotherapy and Asthma (PICA) drug program even when money was not available. These recurring benefit expenses grew from $83.2 million in fiscal year 2020 to $166.5 million in fiscal year 2024.
findings.quote: These benefit expenses are paid on a monthly or quarterly basis and have increased significantly from $83.2 million in FY2020 to $166.5 million in FY2024

findings.plain: The fund lacks transparency and adequate governance. The joint committee that discusses it has no governing documents, keeps no meeting minutes and its monthly reports leave out the fund's large unreported liabilities.
findings.quote: The audit also found that HISF lacks transparency and has inadequate governance and decision-making capacity.

numbers.label: Fund liabilities it is unable to pay, as of April 2025
Transfers unrelated to the fund's stated purpose since 2001
Offsets to equalization payments that eroded the fund
Reported fiscal year 2024 year-end cash balance
Cash left in fiscal year 2024 after required reserves
Fiscal year 2024 spending on additional benefits

recommendations: Work with the Municipal Labor Committee to dissolve the fund and transfer carrier reserves and remaining balances to the city.
Create a new restricted account for health insurance carrier reserves.
Budget appropriately for the healthcare costs and benefits the city agrees to fund in collective bargaining.
audits.agency_response: OLR and the MLC disagreed with the findings, arguing the fund could be used for any mutually agreed purpose. OLR agreed with one recommendation, did not expressly agree or disagree with another and said the remaining recommendation will no longer be applicable.

audits.title: Audit of the Monitoring of the City’s Trade Waste Carting Industry by the Business Integrity Commission
audits.plain_title: How the city polices its private trash hauling industry
audits.agency: New York City Business Integrity Commission
audits.what_they_audited: How effectively the Business Integrity Commission monitors the city's private trash hauling industry, focusing on its inspection program, the violations it issues and how it investigates complaints.
audits.background: The commission was created after state and federal investigations exposed pervasive corruption, organized crime influence and price-fixing in the private carting industry, and it licenses and regulates the companies that haul commercial waste. As of September 2025 it oversaw 1,850 active carting companies, and a 2019 local law added promoting safety to its mandate.

findings.plain: The commission has no written standards saying when a troubled company should be audited, assigned an independent monitor or pushed toward losing its license, and it has not created internal policies to fill that gap.
findings.quote: the rules do not offer guidance on when BIC should refer a company for audit or when it should consider imposing a monitor or escalate toward revocation.

findings.plain: Nearly half of the 7,641 charges the commission issued between January 2021 and December 2024 were concentrated among just 140 companies, yet almost all of those chronic violators faced nothing beyond fines. Only five got any additional oversight and only one lost its license.
findings.quote: Nearly half of the charges issued by BIC were concentrated among 140 companies; however, other than the issuance of fines, 96% of the companies faced no additional enforcement actions of any kind.

findings.plain: Enforcement did not match risk. Companies with extensive crash histories and serious safety violations kept operating with no extra scrutiny while others with fewer, less severe infractions were audited or assigned monitors.
findings.quote: Companies posing the highest potential danger to workers and the public continued to operate with little additional scrutiny, while others with primarily administrative deficiencies were placed under enhanced oversight.

findings.plain: Even when the commission did impose independent monitors, the fix did not stick. Companies kept racking up violations after their monitorships ended.
findings.quote: Three of the four companies with repeat violations continued to incur violations even after the monitorships ended

findings.plain: The commission's audit function barely operates. There is no audit manual, selection of companies is not based on risk and coverage is minimal, with zero audits conducted in 2023.
findings.quote: The unit completed only 11 audits over five years, covering less than 4% of licensees.

findings.plain: On the positive side, the commission cleared its backlog and got much faster at processing violations and complaints, cutting average violation issuance time from 148 workdays in 2021 to 20 in 2024.
findings.quote: there was an 86% reduction in the average issuance time, from 148 workdays in 2021 to just 20 workdays in 2024.

numbers.label: Charges issued to carting companies from 2021 through 2024
Companies that accounted for nearly half of all charges
Audits of carting companies completed over five years
Drop in average time to issue a violation since 2021

recommendations: Develop standard operating procedures that define when and how to escalate enforcement, with clear criteria and benchmarks, such as numbers of crashes or repeated inspection failures, that trigger review for audits, monitorships or license revocation.
Adopt formal, risk-based criteria for choosing which companies to audit and write an audit procedures manual to standardize audit steps and ensure consistent quality.
Set annual audit targets focused on high-risk companies and repeat offenders, and seek enough staff and resources to expand coverage and finish audits faster.
audits.agency_response: The commission partially agreed with three recommendations and disagreed with the rest, arguing that formal enforcement thresholds would be incompatible with its case-by-case, quasi-judicial decision-making and that the audit's conclusions rested on incorrect assumptions. The auditors disagreed and stood by the findings.

audits.title: Audit of the New York City Department of Environmental Protection’s Leak Detection Program
audits.plain_title: Does the city's water leak detection program actually find leaks?
audits.agency: New York City Department of Environmental Protection
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Department of Environmental Protection's Leak Detection Program, which sends crews with acoustic listening equipment to find underground water main leaks before they become breaks, effectively identifies and repairs leaks through proactive surveys and adequate tracking systems.
audits.background: The department manages the city's water supply, delivering more than one billion gallons of drinking water a day, and launched the Leak Detection Program in July 2022 to catch small leaks before they escalate into water main breaks. The city is divided into survey grids, with a goal of covering roughly a third of grids a year in most of the city and all of lower Manhattan's grids annually.

findings.plain: The program covered only a small fraction of the city. Over three years the department surveyed just 27% of the 401 grids it was supposed to cover in the outer boroughs and upper Manhattan, often revisiting the same locations, and Staten Island got no surveys at all.
findings.quote: DEP surveyed only 108 of the 401 grids, leaving 293 grids (73%) uninspected during the three-year cycle.

findings.plain: Leak detection still depends almost entirely on the public. Of 1,314 water main breaks repaired over three fiscal years, only 42 were found through the program's surveys; the rest surfaced through 311 complaints, emergencies or other work.
findings.quote: only 42 repairs (3%) originated from proactive detection efforts, while 1,272 repairs (97%) were initiated in response to public complaints, emergency conditions, or while other work was conducted.

findings.plain: The program has not reduced breaks. Water main breaks rose 54% in fiscal year 2025 compared with the prior year, hitting their highest level in five years.
findings.quote: The number of water main breaks peaked in FY25 with 552 in total.

findings.plain: There is no structured, risk-based process for deciding which grids to survey. Crews are sent based on staff judgment and institutional knowledge rather than measurable indicators like pipe age, leak history or proximity to critical infrastructure.
findings.quote: DEP has not established written criteria for selecting grids based on documented risk factors

findings.plain: Staffing is far too thin to meet the department's own goals. During the audit period the entire city was covered by a single survey crew and a single scan crew.
findings.quote: This explanation is consistent with the Program’s limited staffing: one survey crew and one scan crew.

findings.plain: A computer system from the 1990s makes it hard to tell whether leaks found in surveys ever get repaired, leaving management without visibility into whether the program works.
findings.quote: the agency’s work-order management platform—IPS—was implemented in the 1990s and is now considered outdated.

numbers.label: Share of planned survey grids covered in three years
Share of water main break repairs found through surveys
Rise in water main breaks in fiscal year 2025
Water main breaks in fiscal year 2025, a five-year peak

recommendations: Develop a structured, risk-based survey planning process with written procedures for selecting grids using measurable risk indicators like the age, size and material of water mains, leak history, recent construction and proximity to critical infrastructure.

Regularly measure and report progress toward the department's goals of surveying 30% of each borough's grids annually and full coverage within three years, using quarterly performance reviews to catch shortfalls.
Create a formal process for scheduling and tracking survey coverage so work is spread across all grids, avoids unnecessary repeats and ensures every grid is inspected on schedule.
Periodically review proactive detection rates, repair times and water main break trends to assess the program's effectiveness.
Reevaluate whether current survey goals are feasible with existing staff, and consider reallocating personnel, adding training or shifts, and seeking additional funding to expand the program.

Make sure the department's computer system, whether updated or new, can trace a leak from survey to scan to repair and includes performance dashboards and reporting tools for program-level monitoring.
audits.agency_response: The department did not respond to each recommendation individually, stating generally that it agrees with many of the report's recommendations.

audits.title: Audit on the Timeliness of Civilian Complaint Review Board’s Investigations and New York City Police Department’s Implementation of the Board’s Recommendations
audits.plain_title: How long police misconduct cases take and what discipline follows
audits.agency: New York City Civilian Complaint Review Board and New York City Police Department
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Civilian Complaint Review Board, the independent agency that investigates complaints of police misconduct, completes its investigations on time, and how often the New York City Police Department actually implements the board's discipline recommendations.
audits.background: The Civilian Complaint Review Board investigates misconduct complaints against uniformed police officers and recommends discipline, but the police commissioner has final say and can accept, reject or modify any recommendation. State law generally requires disciplinary action to begin within 18 months of the misconduct.

findings.plain: The board met its average targets for finishing investigations, but more than half of individual cases blew past them. Over half of full investigations took more than 14 months and 62% of substantiated cases took more than the 480-day target.
findings.quote: it took CCRB more than 420 days (more than 14 months) to complete and close 54.9% of fully investigated civilian complaints.

findings.plain: Because cases arrived so close to the legal deadline for discipline, the police department closed more than half of all substantiated cases during the audit period without reviewing them and without any disciplinary action.
findings.quote: resulted in NYPD closing 51.5% of the substantiated cases without any review and without disciplinary action.

findings.plain: Delays had several causes: complaints jumped 67.6% from fiscal year 2021 to 2025 while staffing lagged, cases waited an average of 5.1 months just to be assigned to a board review panel and it took an average of 185 days to request and collect evidence from the police department. Budget constraints even forced the board to stop investigating certain types of complaints.
findings.quote: The number of complaints received by CCRB significantly increased from 3,326 in Fiscal Year 2021 to 5,575 in FY2025, an increase of 2,249 (67.6%)

findings.plain: The appointing authorities left board seats empty, which slowed case reviews. The board is supposed to have 15 members but operated short-handed, one City Council seat sat vacant for over two years and the board has had no permanent chair since 2022.
findings.quote: CCRB operated with 11 to 14 members due to unfilled vacancies.

findings.plain: How often the police department accepted the board's discipline recommendations depended heavily on who was police commissioner. Commissioner Jessica Tisch accepted the recommended discipline in 77.8% of substantiated cases while Commissioner Edward Caban did so in only 22.9%.
findings.quote: Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch accepted and imposed the same level of discipline recommended by the board in 77.8% of substantiated cases, while Police Commissioner Edward Caban...

findings.plain: Overall the police department did not implement the board's discipline recommendations in 53.9% of substantiated non-charges cases, though it did serve charges in 86.3% of the most serious misconduct cases.
findings.quote: NYPD accepted CCRB’s recommendations in 541 (86.3%) of 627 cases involving the most serious charges.

findings.plain: The police department did not consistently tell the board what discipline it actually imposed, which keeps the board from notifying victims of case outcomes as required.
findings.quote: NYPD did not report disciplinary actions or penalties imposed against MOS in 289 (14.5%) of 2,000 substantiated non-charges cases submitted to NYPD between January 2, 2024 and May 29, 2025.

numbers.label: Substantiated cases the police closed without any review
Discipline acceptance rate under Commissioner Tisch
Discipline acceptance rate under Commissioner Caban
Complaints the board received in fiscal year 2025
Cases awaiting board review as of December 2, 2025

recommendations: The police department and the board should jointly enter a formal agreement setting timeframes for requesting and producing evidence other than body-worn camera footage.
The two agencies should jointly agree on deadlines for the board to submit cases to the police department.
The two agencies should jointly enter a formal agreement setting standardized protocols for reporting the police commissioner's final decisions on board cases.
The two agencies should jointly work on integrating a system for tracking what happens to cases the board sends to the police department.
The police department should write internal policies with timeframe guidelines for cases approaching the statute of limitations.
The police department should set formal internal deadlines for answering the board's requests for evidence.
The police department should step up recruiting for its Department Advocate's Office legal staff and seek funding to keep it adequately staffed.
The police department should make sure penalties match discipline determinations under its disciplinary matrix.
The police department should adopt policies requiring it to follow the City Charter and city rules and report specific officer penalties to the board.
The police department should build recordkeeping system controls that allow automated, streamlined reporting on board cases, including the commissioner's final decision.
The police department should make sure its recordkeeping system tracks compliance with city rules and the Charter when sharing case information with the board.
The board should set formal timeframes for requesting evidence from the police department to fix the bottlenecks the auditors identified.
The board should keep seeking additional funding so it can investigate every complaint in its jurisdiction and give the police time to act within the statute of limitations.
The board should adopt internal policies on how to handle cases where the police never reported final dispositions and penalties.
The appointing authorities should fill existing board vacancies and fill future ones within 60 days so the maximum number of review panels can meet each month.
The appointing authorities should fill the board chair vacancy as the Charter requires to keep operations moving and protect the board's independence.
The city should consider increasing the number of board members so more panels can meet and investigations finish faster.
The city should comply with Charter-mandated funding levels for the board given rising complaints and its expanded responsibilities.
audits.agency_response: Neither agency explicitly agreed or disagreed with most recommendations; both said they would work collaboratively to review timelines and practices, and the board agreed with the recommendation to keep seeking funding. The Mayor's Office did not respond to the recommendations directed at the appointing authorities or the city.

audits.title: Audit Report on the New York City Office of Technology and Innovation’s MyCity System
audits.plain_title: What the city got for $100 million spent on the MyCity portal
audits.agency: New York City Office of Technology and Innovation
audits.what_they_audited: Whether MyCity, the online portal the Office of Technology and Innovation built to be a one-stop shop for city services and benefits, actually streamlines the delivery of services and lets the city track agency performance in real time.
audits.background: Mayor Adams announced MyCity in January 2022 as a single platform where New Yorkers could search and apply for city services and benefits, with a universal application, proactive benefit recommendations and a digital wallet. It was meant especially to help low-income New Yorkers who qualify for benefits but do not receive them because applications are complicated and time-consuming.

findings.plain: After more than four years and over $100 million, the promised one-stop shop does not exist. Users still cannot apply for city benefits through a single form or receive benefits through a digital wallet, and the office wants $81 million more.
findings.quote: the agency has very little else to show after spending more than four years and $100 million on the program.

findings.plain: The office lacked a clear vision and detailed development plan. It paid a consultant $2.5 million for project plans, a roadmap and cost estimates but could not show auditors any evidence those deliverables were ever produced.
findings.quote: OTI has failed to produce any evidence that IBC delivered to the City a roadmap document, detailed project plans, or associated cost estimates.

findings.plain: Most of MyCity's portals are old city websites with new paint. The benefits portal simply sends users to the preexisting ACCESS NYC site, and the jobs and business portals mainly rebrand pages that already existed.
findings.quote: it largely redirects users to pre-existing City websites that have been rebranded and redesigned as MyCity applications.

findings.plain: The childcare portal, the program's most developed piece, lacks basic eligibility checks based on a child's age and household income. Nearly half of all applications submitted through it were found ineligible.
findings.quote: 140,760 applications were submitted through MyCity since inception, of which 65,369 (46%) were ineligible (as of October 2025).

findings.plain: Project management and contract oversight were poor. The office spread the work across roughly 50 vendors and more than 120 agreements without documented build-versus-buy analysis or adequate records showing it oversaw deliverables.
findings.quote: OTI spent approximately $100 million through more than 120 agreements (including contracts, purchase orders, and delivery orders) to plan, design, develop, and implement MyCity.

findings.plain: The portal performs badly for users, with slow page loads and response times. Scans gave the childcare voucher mobile site a score of 7 out of 100.
findings.quote: The new mobile site for the childcare voucher scored 7 out of 100, while the desktop version scored 9 out of 100.

findings.plain: The MyCity artificial intelligence chatbot gives inaccurate and inconsistent answers, sometimes responding differently to the identical question, and most users who left feedback were dissatisfied. The portal also does not track city agency performance as promised.
findings.quote: 50 out of 70 respondents (71.4%) submitted negative feedback, indicating their dissatisfaction with the Chatbot’s answers.

numbers.label: Spent on MyCity over more than four years
Additional funding requested in the 2026 budget
Childcare applications through the portal found ineligible
Chatbot feedback that was negative

recommendations: Conduct a comprehensive review of the project's technical, economic, legal and operational feasibility to decide whether to continue, change scope or terminate it to minimize wasted resources.
Develop a clear, detailed project plan for MyCity's end state, with detailed functional requirements and time and cost benchmarks.
Establish a dedicated project management team responsible for meeting short and long-term goals on time and within budget.
Hold vendors accountable for expected deliverables, timelines, budgets and standards.
Build eligibility criteria into the childcare application to alert users to, or prevent submission of, applications that would be ineligible.
Make sure MyCity meets the minimum standards in the city's own policy for performance testing of public-facing applications.
Run structured testing exercises known as artificial intelligence red-teaming to find chatbot flaws such as inaccurate or inconsistent responses and improve data quality.
audits.agency_response: The office disagreed with all seven recommendations and with the findings on project management and contract oversight, arguing the report misstates MyCity's intent and that the platform was never meant to replace individual agency websites. It nonetheless said it welcomes a level-setting program review.

audits.title: Final Audit Letter Report on the Office of Administrative Tax Appeals’ Equitable Handling of Appeals of Real Property Assessment
audits.plain_title: Property tax appeals take longer in Queens and Staten Island
audits.agency: New York City Office of Administrative Tax Appeals
audits.what_they_audited: This audit letter report looked at how the Office of Administrative Tax Appeals (OATA) handles property owners' appeals of their real property assessments, and whether it processes and reviews those appeals fairly and equitably.
audits.background: Real property tax is the city's largest source of tax revenue. Owners who disagree with the Department of Finance's assessment of their property value can appeal to OATA, an independent agency created by Local Law 59 of 2007; about 57,000 appeal applications were filed annually in tax years 2023-24 and 2024-25.

findings.plain: Once hearings are scheduled, OATA treats all applications fairly and equitably, and it conducts internal supervisory reviews to help keep decisions consistent and accurate.
findings.quote: The audit found that OATA treats all applications fairly and equitably once appeal hearings are scheduled.

findings.plain: Property owners in Queens and Staten Island waited longer than owners in other boroughs. In tax year 2023-24 their appeals took an average of 198 days to process, 37 days longer than Manhattan and the Bronx, and the pattern continued in 2024-25.
findings.quote: property owners in Queens and Staten Island on average experienced longer wait times to receive hearings and determinations for their appeals compared to other boroughs.

findings.plain: Because OATA schedules high-value properties first, owners of lower-value properties get hearings later in the year. In tax year 2023-24, 45% of Staten Island applicants and 42% of Queens applicants had hearings in the last quarter of the year, compared with just 18% in Manhattan.
findings.quote: This prioritization results in property owners in certain boroughs waiting longer for hearings, and ultimately the final determination of their applications.

findings.plain: OATA did not keep formal workpapers documenting supervisory reviews of hearing officers' decisions. Supervisors sometimes recorded notes on informal paper slips such as Post-it Notes, so auditors could not verify the required checks happened.
findings.quote: OATA did not maintain formal workpapers to document the supervisory reviews conducted by supervising hearing officers

findings.plain: The audit identified a loophole: many owners of Class 1 homes file an appeal, then ask OATA for "no further review" before a decision and instead take their case to the state's Small Claims Assessment Review (SCAR), where they win far more often. Of 768 applicants who went to SCAR over two tax years, 93.4% got a reduction, versus 10.3% of Class 1 applicants who completed OATA's process.
findings.quote: The data suggests that property owners are using this loophole to forum shop in an effort to increase the likelihood of obtaining a reduction.

numbers.label: Average appeal wait in Queens and Staten Island, 2023-24
Approximate annual appeal applications filed
Share of state small claims filers who won a reduction
Share of Class 1 applicants offered a reduction by OATA

recommendations: Consider modifying how hearings are scheduled so processing times are not delayed based on the applicant's borough.
Document supervisory reviews using standardized workpapers or templates, stored securely in a physical file or electronic system.

Consult with the Department of Finance, the Office of Management and Budget and others on whether state small claims and OATA apply consistent property tax principles, and whether to close the "no further review" loophole.
audits.agency_response: OATA agreed with two of the three recommendations. It neither agreed nor disagreed with the third, saying it has no control over the state's small claims hearing process.

audits.title: Audit Report of the Department of Design and Construction’s Mitigation of Delays and Cost Overruns on Capital Construction Projects
audits.plain_title: Most city construction projects run years behind schedule
audits.agency: New York City Department of Design and Construction
audits.what_they_audited: How well the Department of Design and Construction (DDC), the city's lead capital construction agency, manages construction projects and whether its practices are effective in limiting time and cost overruns.
audits.background: DDC began operations in 1996 to centralize the construction of the city's capital projects. In partnership with over 20 city agencies, it manages the design and construction of civic facilities and maintains the city's streets, sidewalks, water mains and sewers.

findings.plain: 80% of DDC-managed projects that reached or were projected to reach substantial completion after fiscal year 2018 were behind their original schedule, by an average of 3.5 years. At least half were behind by 2.5 years or more.
findings.quote: 877 projects (80%) were behind the original schedule at project initiation with an average delay of 1,265 days (3.5 years) since project initiation

findings.plain: A random sample of 18 large-scale projects ($100 million or more) grew from $4.14 billion at construction start to $4.51 billion, a 9.1% increase. Extrapolated across all 49 large-scale projects, that would mean roughly $870 million in added costs to date.
findings.quote: the total cost to the City for these projects would be $10.4 billion to date, an increase of approximately $870 million or 9.1%.

findings.plain: DDC has no system that tracks project costs from initiation to completion. It replaces the original cost estimate with updated ones as projects proceed, so it cannot readily say what share of its projects run over budget.
findings.quote: DDC does not have a system capable of tracking real-time project costs from initiation to completion, or for forecasting future costs across its project portfolio.

findings.plain: DDC's public reporting understates delays. Because it rebases schedules and excludes delays it deems outside its control, the Mayor's Management Report underreported design delays by between 12% and 87% and construction delays by between 32% and 66% from fiscal years 2018 through 2024.
findings.quote: the MMR under-reported design delays by between 12% and 87% and construction delays by between 32% and 66% over this six-year period.

findings.plain: DDC stopped reporting project cost against original budget in the Mayor's Management Report from fiscal year 2021 through fiscal year 2024, and the auditors found the 0.66% cost variance it reported for fiscal year 2025 not credible.
findings.quote: DDC did not report performance against original budgets in the MMR for FY2021 through FY2024, and only recently provided figures for FY2025.

findings.plain: Deep dives into three delayed projects for the sanitation, environmental protection and transportation departments found delays driven by incomplete designs, poor coordination and bad information about underground utilities. A Staten Island sanitation garage ran 790 days late, with 695 of those days attributable to design errors and omissions.
findings.quote: The primary causes were inadequate design coordination, insufficient pre-construction utility investigations (resulting in dependence on outdated utility information), and inaccurate cost and quantity estimates.

findings.plain: A program meant to help agencies plan complex projects up front is underutilized. The city set a goal of 20 Capital Project Scope Development studies per year, but only 11 were ordered in fiscal year 2025. The city's public capital project dashboard also had not been updated in over six months.
findings.quote: In FY2025, there were four Master Agreements valued at $60 million with task orders issued for only 11 CPSD projects, nine short of the goal.

numbers.label: DDC projects behind their original schedule
Average delay from original completion date
Aggregate cost increase in 18 sampled large projects
Estimated cost growth across all 49 large-scale projects
Delay on the Staten Island sanitation garage project
DDC-managed projects assessed

recommendations: Create a dedicated project cost management team to track and report cost overruns in the aggregate while planning system upgrades for full cost management.
Report the full extent of cost and time overruns from the first baseline in the Mayor's Management Report and categorize the causes, per project and in aggregate.
Improve the construction schedule set at project initiation, or consider not providing a completion date until the design phase ends.
Work with City Hall to get private utility companies to better document and engineer their systems during design, and support extending the Joint Bidding Law.
Launch a virtual design and construction practice, including updated building information modeling standards.
Establish record-keeping requirements for project documentation in the Benchmark system.
Continue implementing front-end planning, report its impact and compare it to non-front-end-planning project performance.
City agencies should use the funding earmarked for pre-construction planning by increasing the number of scope development studies.
City agencies should discuss using capital funds versus expense funding with the Office of Management and Budget and the incoming administration.
The Mayor's Office of Operations should comply with Local Law 37 by updating the capital project dashboard on time with all needed information.
audits.agency_response: DDC agreed with nine recommendations and disagreed with one, on discussing capital versus expense funding. The Mayor's Office did not respond to the recommendation directed to it.

audits.title: Audit Report on the NYC Department of Veterans’ Services’ Coordination of Housing Assistance
audits.plain_title: Veterans agency housed 153 people but tracked its work poorly
audits.agency: New York City Department of Veterans' Services
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Department of Veterans' Services (DVS) is efficiently and effectively helping veterans find housing and avoid homelessness, focusing on its housing assistance services in fiscal year 2025.
audits.background: New York City is home to more than 129,000 veterans. DVS was created in 2016 to connect veterans with city services including housing, and the city has cut its homeless veteran population by nearly 90%, from 4,677 in 2011 to 624 in 2024.

findings.plain: DVS effectively helped 153 veterans secure permanent housing in fiscal year 2025, a 21% increase over the prior year, and provided required aftercare services to veterans housed through Collaborative Case Management vouchers.
findings.quote: the agency effectively helped 153 veterans secure housing in FY2025.

findings.plain: More than a quarter (27%) of veterans' housing assistance requests were not answered within the agency's five-business-day target, and 52 requests took at least 21 business days to get a first contact attempt.
findings.quote: DVS failed to respond to more than a quarter (27%) of veterans’ housing assistance requests within its five-business-day target.

findings.plain: DVS lacked written standard operating procedures and formal training for its housing work, and its housing guide was outdated, referring to subsidies that have not existed since 2019. It provided a new policy manual only after the exit conference.
findings.quote: DVS has not developed written standard operating procedures governing its operations, including the Veteran Peer Coordinator Program and Aftercare Assistance

findings.plain: Tracking errors meant DVS overstated its work. Its tracker listed 1,582 housing assistance requests but 41 were duplicates, so it actually received 1,541. In a sample of 60 clients, 25 were recorded as still housed but case notes supported only 11.
findings.quote: although 1,582 housing assistance requests were listed in the tracker, DVS in fact received only 1,541 requests in FY2025.

findings.plain: DVS reported in the Mayor's Management Report that it provided 509 veterans with homelessness prevention and aftercare assistance, but after removing duplicates the real number was 447. The agency acknowledged the error and asked City Hall to correct it.
findings.quote: After subtracting these 62 discrepancies, the actual number of veterans assisted appears to be 447.

findings.plain: DVS gave auditors four different answers over four months about how often staff were supposed to make aftercare check-in calls, showing its internal guidance was unclear.
findings.quote: DVS also offered inconsistent information regarding the frequency with which staff were to make aftercare service calls.

findings.plain: As of December 1, 2025, DVS had not filed its legally mandated annual report to the City Council since 2023 or its three most recent semiannual reports on veteran resource centers. It submitted all outstanding reports on December 15, 2025 after receiving the draft audit.
findings.quote: On December 15, 2025, following the issuance of the Draft Report to the agency, DVS submitted all outstanding required reports and published them on its website.

numbers.label: Veterans DVS helped secure housing in fiscal year 2025
Housing requests not answered within five business days
Actual housing assistance requests received
Veterans actually given prevention and aftercare help
Homeless veterans in New York City in 2024

recommendations: Train all current and new staff on the newly created written policies and standard operating procedures, including intake, request tracking, move-out tracking, aftercare tracking and documentation protocols.
Completely and accurately transfer fiscal year 2025 data from the Master Tracker to the new VetConnectNYC system, removing duplicates and recording all dates.
Completely and accurately transfer fiscal year 2025 Aftercare Tracker data to VetConnectNYC so housing outcomes are correctly recorded.
Implement a mechanism to ensure housing assistance requests are tracked and processed within five business days.
Accurately track and report the number of veterans given homelessness prevention and aftercare help in the Mayor's Management Report, or relabel the indicator as counting requests.
Submit the annual services report and biannual veteran resource center reports on time as required by Local Laws 44 of 2019 and 215 of 2018.
audits.agency_response: DVS agreed with all six of the audit's recommendations.

audits.title: New York City Bike Share Program – Oversight of Revenue Collection and Monitoring
audits.plain_title: Whether the city collects and checks its Citi Bike money
audits.agency: New York City Department of Transportation
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the New York City Department of Transportation collects the revenues it is owed from the Citi Bike bike share program under its agreement with the vendor and whether it monitors the vendor's compliance with the contract. The audit covered July 2019 to October 2024.
audits.background: The city launched the bike share program in 2013 as a public-private partnership: a vendor operates the system while the department handles planning, outreach and oversight. The program generates revenue from rides, sponsorship and advertising, liquidated damages and a fixed $1 million a year to replace lost parking meter revenue.

findings.plain: The department monitors Citi Bike passively. It does not run scheduled monitoring of its own, conduct program reviews or audits, or do its own calculations to check the accuracy of what the vendor reports.
findings.quote: DOT takes a passive approach to monitoring the Citi Bike program.

findings.plain: Department officials responsible for monitoring were not familiar with the vendor's reports and, despite real-time access to program information, could not explain key elements of them.
findings.quote: Despite having real-time access to program information, DOT officials were not able to explain key elements of the reports.

findings.plain: Errors went unnoticed until the audit. Faulty database queries wrongly excluded 900,829 trips from the ridership count used to figure the department's share of revenue, and on all 203 days of data reviewed the daily data feed did not match the vendor's reported figures.
findings.quote: Errors in the queries (questions used to retrieve and analyze data from databases or information systems) resulted in the erroneous exclusion of 900,829 trips from the ridership count

findings.plain: The contract called for the main sponsor to pay $54.9 million in sponsorship revenue, but auditors found evidence that only $33.6 million was received, a $21.3 million gap.
findings.quote: we only found evidence that $33.6 million in sponsorship revenue was received—a difference of $21.3 million.

findings.plain: The department could not show it counted $26.7 million in accelerated fees the vendor paid to extend the contract, and it had no evidence that the $1 million annual deposit of lost parking meter revenue was made for 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2024, a total of $4 million.
findings.quote: DOT did not provide evidence that the annual deposit of $1 million in lost parking meter revenue was deposited into the City’s bank account for 2019, 2020, 2021, and 2024—totaling $4 million.

findings.plain: For the one year with records, the department treated the $1 million parking meter payment as a bookkeeping credit rather than a bank deposit, which could leave funds unavailable for program improvements and operating costs.
findings.quote: believes that creating a liability in its general ledger satisfies the requirement for the annual deposit

numbers.label: Trips wrongly excluded from the ridership count
Gap between sponsorship revenue owed and evidence of receipt
Accelerated fees with no proof they were counted
Lost parking meter deposits with no evidence for four years

recommendations: Verify Citi Bike data by inspecting stations and bicycles and reviewing the data received for accuracy and completeness.
Make sure payments are received according to the terms of the agreement.
Set up a process to track revenues from each source and ensure all money due to the city is deposited into the right accounts and transferred to the city's general fund as the agreement requires.

audits.title: New York City Housing Authority Monitorship: Monitors' Report (Sixth Report)
audits.plain_title: Heating outages spike and a chimney falls as mold work improves
audits.agency: New York City Housing Authority
audits.what_they_audited: The federal monitors' sixth quarterly report on the New York City Housing Authority's (NYCHA) compliance with its 2019 agreement with the federal government, covering heat, elevators, pests and waste, mold and leaks, lead paint and inspections, plus organizational change and capital spending. It reports data for August 1, 2025 to October 31, 2025.
audits.background: On January 31, 2019 NYCHA agreed with the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York (SDNY), the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and the City of New York to improve housing conditions, and a monitor was appointed to evaluate compliance. Neil Barofsky and Matthew Cipolla of Jenner & Block LLP began a five-year term as co-monitors on February 28, 2024.

findings.plain: The heating season opened badly. There were 30 unplanned central heating outages in October 2025 compared with four in October 2024, affecting 13% of occupied apartments rather than 2%, though NYCHA still resolved them in an average of 7.3 hours. October 2025 was colder, with 198 heating degree days against 128 a year earlier.
findings.quote: season, there have been 30 unplanned central heating

findings.plain: A 20-story exterior chimney serving the boiler room at Mitchel Houses in the Bronx collapsed on October 1, 2025. No one was hurt, but 38 apartments were evacuated, about 88 residents went to hotels and gas service to the whole development was shut off. The Fire Department, the Department of Buildings and the Department of Investigation are all investigating.
findings.quote: approximately 88 residents were temporarily relocated to hotels

findings.plain: Mold response kept improving from a very low base. NYCHA removed mold within five business days 24% of the time in the third quarter of Year 7, up from 7% a year earlier, and met the agreement's combined mold timeframes 28% of the time across three quarters versus 8%. The requirement is 95%.
findings.quote: days 24% of the time, compared to 7% of the time

findings.plain: The mold and leak backlog stayed far too high, with 61,675 work orders pending for 16 days or more. A new Mold and Leaks Restore and Renew program at Sotomayor Houses had closed roughly 65% of targeted work orders by November 17, 2025, including repairs that had gone unaddressed for more than 1,000 days.
findings.quote: high, with 61,675 work orders that have been pending

findings.plain: Pest response times improved but populations did not. NYCHA answered 86% of mouse, cockroach and bed bug complaints within seven calendar days, 27 percentage points better than a year earlier, yet its estimated rat population rose about 33% and the cumulative rat reduction stood at 48%, short of the 75% target.
findings.quote: to 86% of these pest complaints within seven calendar

findings.plain: Elevator performance slipped modestly across nearly every requirement, and NYCHA still had not finished replacing 275 elevators, an obligation due December 31, 2024. It had completed 258 replacements as of October 31, 2025. Low voltage conditions, including Con Edison voltage reductions during summer heat waves, contributed to outages.
findings.quote: met this obligation, completing 258 total elevator replacements as of

findings.plain: HUD inspection scores improved overall but a group of developments got much worse. NYCHA passed 63% of 87 inspections in 2025 compared with 46% of 138 in 2024, and 42 developments gained ten points or more, but 14 developments lost ten points or more and Farragut Houses drew a preliminary score of nine. Annual self-inspections reached 91% of occupied apartments, up from 82%.
findings.quote: improved its overall NSPIRE pass rate to 63% in 2025 as

numbers.label: Occupied apartments hit by an unplanned outage in October
Moved to hotels after the Mitchel Houses chimney collapse
Mold and leak work orders pending 16 days or more
Cumulative rat reduction, against a 75% target
Elevators replaced of the 275 due by the end of 2024
HUD inspections passed in 2025, up from 46% in 2024
Occupied apartments self-inspected as of October 31, 2025
Apartments where lead paint has been removed

recommendations: Improve the quality of pest control treatments so that pest populations actually decline, not just the speed of the response.
Find additional funding to install automatic voltage regulators on more elevators, since only a small fraction will get them under projected funding.

Formalize the process for third and later attempts to enter an apartment for annual inspections and record those attempts in the work order system so residents get notice and NYCHA can enforce access.
Investigate and fix the root causes at the 14 developments whose HUD inspection scores fell ten points or more.
Strengthen self-inspections so health and safety problems such as missing smoke detectors and outlets without ground-fault protection are found and fixed before HUD inspects.
audits.agency_response: NYCHA says it is cooperating fully with the investigations into the Mitchel Houses collapse. It installed mobile boilers within a week, later added a third, gave residents electric hot plates while cooking gas was out and is appealing numerous failing HUD inspection scores, having already persuaded HUD to change ten scores from failing to passing.
audits.compliance_note: The monitors say NYCHA has continued to build on earlier progress and should be commended, while heat, elevators, mold and inspections all need continued focus. Under Paragraph 28 of the agreement, NYCHA does not yet meet the criteria for ending the monitorship.

audits.title: Report on the New York City Conflicts of Interest Board's Advisory Opinion and Moonlighting Waiver Practices
audits.plain_title: Ethics board quietly cleared a top official's second job
audits.agency: New York City Conflicts of Interest Board
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) examined how the New York City Conflicts of Interest Board (COIB) interprets the city Conflicts of Interest Law's "moonlighting restrictions" and whether COIB makes its advisory opinions public as the law requires.
audits.background: The city's Conflicts of Interest Law, known as Chapter 68, generally prohibits full-time city employees from holding second jobs with firms that do business with the city. DOI looked into the issue after learning COIB issued an advisory opinion letting First Deputy Mayor Randy Mastro continue serving as an outside attorney for the Madison Square Garden Group (MSG) in a lawsuit against a former New York Knicks player.

findings.plain: DOI found no legal authority supporting COIB's apparent position that the moonlighting restrictions do not apply to city-employed attorneys acting as outside counsel to entities with city business, and concluded COIB overlooked those restrictions in the Mastro opinion.
findings.quote:
DOI is unaware of any legal authority supporting COIB’s view and found that COIB overlooked the 
law’s “moonlighting restrictions” in its advisory opinion issued to First Deputy Mayor Mastro.

findings.plain: DOI's position, based on the plain language of Chapter 68, is that COIB could only have permitted the arrangement through a public waiver, which would have disclosed both the attorney-client relationship and COIB's permission. Instead COIB issued what it considered a confidential advice letter.
findings.quote:
it is DOI’s position, supported by the plain language of Chapter 68,  that the law requires 
COIB to do so via public waiver.

findings.plain: COIB does not comply with Chapter 68's requirement to publish advisory opinions in redacted form and has not published one since 2018 despite issuing hundreds of written opinions since then.
findings.quote: has not done so since 2018 despite having issued hundreds of written advisory opinions since then.

findings.plain: The fact that COIB cleared the first deputy mayor to represent a powerful local business became public only through the press and litigation, which DOI said points to COIB operating less transparently than the law envisions.
findings.quote:
COIB is operating in a less transparent manner 
than Chapter 68 envisions.

findings.plain: DOI did not investigate Mastro himself, noting he continued the representation only after obtaining COIB's permission and was entitled to rely on the board's advice even though DOI believes that advice was legally flawed.
findings.quote:
Mastro was entitled to rely on the advice he received from COIB, even though 
DOI believes that the advice was legally flawed.

numbers.label: Last year COIB published a redacted advisory opinion
Recommendations DOI issued to COIB

recommendations: COIB should review the advice it gave First Deputy Mayor Mastro on his MSG representation to ensure it is consistent with the moonlighting restrictions, and amend the advice and issue a waiver if appropriate.

COIB should review its previously issued advisory opinions to determine whether it has permitted other city-employed attorneys to represent private firms with city business, and where that conduct is ongoing, reconsider and amend the advice and issue waivers if appropriate.
Alternatively, if COIB maintains that the moonlighting restrictions apply only to in-house attorneys of firms with city business, it should issue a formal rule saying so.
COIB should publish waivers on its website in a searchable format so the public does not need to file Freedom of Information Law requests to see them.

COIB should comply with the City Charter's requirement to publish its advisory opinions, including the March 2025 Mastro opinion, either with redactions or as summaries omitting the parties' identities.
audits.agency_response: DOI noted that the board has already implemented some changes in response to its review, particularly changes to COIB's website concerning its advice practices. COIB takes the position that its advisory opinions are confidential and would not produce them to DOI.

audits.title: Audit Report of the New York City Department of Education’s Oversight of Its Contracted Bus Services
audits.plain_title: Schools barely police the companies running their buses
audits.agency: New York City Department of Education
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Department of Education (DOE) has proper operational controls over its contracted school bus vendors to ensure that bus service is adequately provided to New York City schoolchildren and complies with laws, regulations and contract requirements.
audits.background: DOE's Office of Pupil Transportation coordinates busing for public, charter and nonpublic schools. In school year 2023-24 it bused about 68,742 students on stop-to-school routes and about 56,446 students on curb-to-school routes for students with disabilities, with $1.7 billion of DOE's budget dedicated to transportation.

findings.plain: DOE does not adequately oversee its school bus vendors or hold them accountable for poor performance. Despite having global positioning system (GPS) and complaint data, it does not proactively use it to enforce contract terms, spot problem vendors or routes or improve service.
findings.quote: DOE does not proactively or systematically use readily available global positioning system (GPS) or complaint data to oversee school bus vendors, enforce contract terms, identify trends and problematic vendors or routes, or improve performance.

findings.plain: Complaints to the Office of Pupil Transportation rose nearly 82% in three years, from 84,849 in school year 2021-22 to 154,376 in 2023-24, yet DOE did not analyze the data or require any vendor to adopt a corrective action plan.
findings.quote: The number of complaints reported to OPT increased by nearly 82% over the three-year period between 2021 and 2024.

findings.plain: Special education students were disproportionately hurt. Curb-to-school routes serving students with individualized education programs averaged 11.5 delays per route versus 5.6 for general education routes, accounted for 99% of "problem run" delays and had far more delays over an hour.
findings.quote: students with IEPs were disproportionately impacted by unreliable bus service.

findings.plain: On the 10 routes with the most no-show and late-service complaints, all serving students with disabilities, DOE staff generally closed complaints after talking to vendors instead of checking GPS data, and route changes did not fix the problems. After modifications, buses still ran four minutes to 2 hours and 20 minutes late.
findings.quote: After modifications, delays ranged from four minutes to 2 hours and 20 minutes.

findings.plain: DOE did not ensure practice "dry runs" happened before the first day of school. Nineteen vendors failed to comply, one skipped dry runs on all 24 of its routes, and DOE waived at least an estimated $268,691 in liquidated damages it could have assessed.
findings.quote: For SY2023–24, the audit team estimated that, at minimum, DOE failed to assess liquidated damages of $268,691.

findings.plain: Drivers often failed to log in so parents could track buses, and DOE collected penalties in only 5.5% of 200,556 violations, leaving almost $42.6 million in damages unassessed. Roughly 11,209 pre-K students rode buses without real-time tracking devices.
findings.quote: This means that DOE was entitled to assess almost $42.6 million in damages but failed to do so.

findings.plain: DOE did not hold Via Transportation, whose contracts total $51.7 million, accountable for delivering route optimization and student boarding-tracking technology that was due in December 2021 and still has not been implemented. DOE meanwhile creates special education routes with an unsupported legacy system built in 1994.
findings.quote: This technology was expected to be implemented in December 2021 but to date, this has not happened.

numbers.label: Bus service complaints in school year 2023-24
Three-year rise in complaints to pupil transportation office
Average delays per special education route, versus 5.6
Driver log-in penalties DOE could have assessed but did not
Combined value of Via Transportation's technology contracts
DOE transportation budget in school year 2023-24

recommendations: Assign contract managers to vendor contracts to routinely review complaint and delay data, identify problem routes and vendors, require corrective action plans and assess damages when vendors do not improve.
Review and use prior complaints as part of investigations to identify trends in vendors' poor performance.
Consistently maintain the vehicle numbers serving each route and use them to run a GPS review for every no-show or late-service complaint.
Routinely compare planned route start and end times to actual times to check compliance with contracts and individualized education programs, issuing violations and penalties as appropriate.

Consider enhanced minimum performance standards in new bus contracts, including monthly metrics for on-time performance and ride times, a tiered penalty scale, GPS-based liquidated damages and taking routes away from the poorest performers.
Collect curb-to-school route information, including pick-up and drop-off times, from vendors at the start of each school year rather than relying on vendors to keep it.
Fully enforce bus contracts and assess penalties when GPS devices are not operational while buses are in service.
Ensure DOE recovers any money paid to Via Transportation for required work that was not performed.
Establish comprehensive policies and procedures for reviewing complaints, including required supervisory review before complaints are resolved.
Provide vendors with reports comparing planned and actual route times, discuss them and document the discussions.
Formally document and keep records of all performance discussions with vendors.
Formally document amendments to Via Transportation's delivery dates and work plan and submit the amendment for registration.
audits.agency_response: DOE agreed with eight recommendations and partially agreed with two. It did not explicitly agree or disagree with the remaining two, saying it would take them under advisement. DOE said improving bus service is a top priority and it is shifting from a reactive to a proactive approach.

audits.title: Audit on the Department of Investigation’s Background Investigations for City Employees
audits.plain_title: City background checks lagged years behind hiring
audits.agency: New York City Department of Investigation
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Department of Investigation, the city's watchdog agency, conducts background investigations of high-level and sensitive city hires well enough to identify adverse information in a timely way. The audit covered July 1, 2022 through December 31, 2024.
audits.background: Mayoral executive orders require the Department of Investigation to run background checks on city employees appointed to positions of responsibility, such as those earning more than $125,000 or with authority over contracts, but agencies generally hire candidates before the check is finished. By July 1, 2019 the department had accumulated a backlog of 6,479 pending investigations.

findings.plain: Backlogged cases took years to resolve. Backlogged investigations closed during the audit period had been pending an average of 5.7 years, with delays ranging from three to eight years.
findings.quote: backlogged investigations closed during the audit scope period were pending for an average of 5.7 years, with delays ranging from three to eight years

findings.plain: Two in five backlogged cases were closed without a completed investigation because the person had already retired or otherwise left city government.
findings.quote: 40% of all cases closed during this period were administratively closed because the subject of the investigation had already left City service or retired

findings.plain: People with criminal histories or other red flags served in positions of trust while their checks sat pending. Auditors found evidence of criminal history in 27 of 30 sampled backlogged files, and those cases were pending almost six years on average.
findings.quote: auditors found evidence of criminal history in 27 of 30 sampled files, including petty larceny, driving while intoxicated, attempted criminal possession of a controlled substance, and aggravated unlicensed operation of a motor vehicle

findings.plain: The department does not advise agencies on whether a candidate is suitable and does not track what agencies do when a check turns up adverse information, which the audit calls a gap in oversight.
findings.quote: DOI does not track whether candidates with adverse information are retained by agencies.

findings.plain: Case files were incomplete. Of 50 sampled files with completed investigations, 30 were missing required documents or evidence that steps such as tax checks or education verification were taken.
findings.quote: Of the remaining 50 sampled files, 30 (60%) were missing required documents or evidence that certain investigation steps were performed.

findings.plain: Fingerprint records that must be destroyed within three months of closing a case were still in 31 of 75 sampled files, an issue a state review also flagged in 2021.
findings.quote: Fingerprint results were found in 31 (41%) of 75 sampled files.

findings.plain: New investigations are on track. The department has prevented a new backlog from forming since July 1, 2019 and completed 99% of routine checks in under 180 days.
findings.quote: DOI completed 99% of the routine background investigations it received in under 180 days.

numbers.label: Backlogged investigations pending as of July 1, 2019
Average pendency of backlogged cases closed in the period
Backlogged cases closed because the person had left
Sampled case files missing documents or evidence of steps
Routine checks completed in under 180 days
Backlog cases remaining as of October 16, 2025

recommendations: Assign administrative staff to check the city's Payroll Management System for remaining backlog cases and administratively close cases where the person is no longer employed.
Consider making recommendations or otherwise giving agencies guidance on how certain kinds of adverse information should affect the suitability of appointments.
Consider tracking whether candidates are retained or terminated when investigations identify adverse information.
Require the use of checklists and review forms so every applicable investigation step is conducted and documented.
Establish written timeframes for completing expedited, priority and backlog investigations.
Report separately in the Mayor's Management Report on completion timelines for routine, expedited, priority and backlog investigations.
Consider creating additional closing categories, or severity levels within the catch-all "Other" category.
Ensure fingerprints and results are removed from files within required timeframes and monitor compliance on a periodic sample basis.
Conduct periodic reviews to make sure agencies are submitting all required candidates for background investigations.
Consider tracking appointment dates to determine whether agencies submit applications within required timeframes.
Issue updated memos or guidance to city agencies at least every two years on their responsibilities for submitting background investigation packages.
Ensure Kaseware, the department's new case system, has adequate documentation, including a data dictionary.
audits.agency_response: The Department of Investigation agreed with four of the 12 recommendations and disagreed with the other eight, objecting in particular to the ideas that it should advise agencies on hiring suitability or track hiring outcomes.

audits.title: Letter to Vice Chair Master Re: Final Letter Report on the Processing of Permit Applications by the Landmarks Preservation Commission
audits.plain_title: Landmark work permits sped up after a digital portal
audits.agency: New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission
audits.what_they_audited: A letter report assessing how the Landmarks Preservation Commission processes applications for permits to do work on landmarked properties, covering July 1, 2022 through June 30, 2025.
audits.background: The commission regulates changes to more than 38,000 landmarked properties and reported receiving 12,211 permit applications in fiscal year 2023 alone. In March 2024 it launched Portico, a web portal that lets owners of landmarked buildings apply for permits and track their applications electronically.

findings.plain: The commission generally followed its own procedures. Of 50 sampled applications, 47 resulted in permits, and the three that did not had open violations, were withdrawn or lacked required documents.
findings.quote: auditors concluded that LPC satisfactorily complied with its protocols when processing permit applications and issuing permits

findings.plain: Processing got faster after the Portico portal launched. Average processing time for certificates of no effect dropped 33% and the share of permits issued on time rose for all four permit types reviewed.
findings.quote: Since the implementation of Portico, the percentage of permits issued within established timeframes for the four permit types reviewed has increased

findings.plain: Some targets were missed. 98% of expedited certificates of no effect were issued within two business days against a 100% target, and only 55% of certificates of appropriateness were issued within 10 business days.
findings.quote: Although LPC came close, it did not meet its target for issuing 100% of XCNEs within two business days.

findings.plain: Two of the 47 sampled applications that received permits were missing the commission's required approval stamp.
findings.quote: all but two of the 47 sampled applications that were issued permits had LPC’s Approval Stamp

numbers.label: Landmarked properties under the commission's oversight
Permit applications received in fiscal year 2023
Drop in processing time for certificates of no effect
Certificates of appropriateness issued within 10 days

recommendations: Ensure every permit carries the commission's approval stamp before it is issued.
Make efforts to issue certificates of appropriateness within 10 business days.
Consider setting percentage goals for issuing permits for minor work within established timeframes.
audits.agency_response: The commission agreed with the audit findings and all three recommendations.

audits.title: Audit Report on the Office of City Clerk’s Enforcement of the Lobbying Law
audits.plain_title: Weak spots in how the city polices lobbying
audits.agency: New York City Office of the City Clerk
audits.what_they_audited: How the Office of the City Clerk administers and enforces the city's Lobbying Law, including lobbyist registration, audits of filings and investigations of unregistered lobbying. The audit covered January 1, 2022 through June 30, 2025.
audits.background: The office's Lobbying Bureau registers lobbyists, audits their filings and investigates unreported lobbying activity. According to the office's annual report, entities spent $138.4 million on outside lobbying in New York City in 2024, an all-time high.

findings.plain: The office generally meets the law's core requirements, auditing registered lobbyists each year and publishing the required annual report.
findings.quote: the Office of the City Clerk (OCC) generally complies with the requirements of the Lobbying Law by conducting audits of registered lobbyists and by publishing the required annual report

findings.plain: The burden of catching unregistered lobbying falls on the office because the law does not require city officials or employees to report contacts that may be lobbying. The office has discussed amendments with the City Council.
findings.quote: Instead, the burden to detect unregistered lobbying falls on OCC.

findings.plain: Searches for unregistered lobbyists skip high-risk areas such as land use applications and non-competitive contracts. Auditors found 11 of 45 private land use applicants in 2024 were not registered, and the office's follow-up has already produced $120,480 in accumulated late filing penalties for two entities.
findings.quote: The audit team found that 11 (24%) of the 45 ULURP applicants during CY2024 had not registered with the Lobbying Bureau

findings.plain: Outreach emails to 1,863 recipients of City Council discretionary funds drew only 58 responses and produced no new registrations, and the office does not ask recipients to state whether they lobby.
findings.quote: OCC sent emails to 1,863 such recipients and received only 58 (3%) responses. These efforts did not result in the registration of any new lobbyists.

findings.plain: Investigations of unreported lobbying are limited in scope. All nine closed cases auditors reviewed ended with findings of no probable cause, and files showed no evidence that staff contacted the officials who were allegedly lobbied.
findings.quote: the files contained no evidence that staff attempted to reach out to the City agencies or officials that were allegedly the subject of lobbying
