findings.plain: The Lobbying Bureau lacks detailed written policies for staff and is short-staffed, with five people, three vacancies and a budget the office says does not allow new hires.
findings.quote: OCC has not developed written policies and procedures outlining OCC’s key requirements and responsibilities as they pertain to the Lobbying Law.

numbers.label: Spent on outside lobbying in New York City in 2024
Registered lobbyists on average, 2022 through 2024
Of 45 private land use applicants not registered in 2024
Late filing penalties imposed after auditors flagged filers
Discretionary fund recipients emailed about registering

recommendations: Keep petitioning the City Council to amend the Lobbying Law to require training of city agencies and require agencies to report contacts with known or potential lobbyists, including names, meeting dates, locations and subjects discussed.
Regularly review land use applicants and vendors awarded non-competitive contracts to determine whether they lobbied, registered as lobbyists and accurately recorded their lobbying activity.

Require entities under review for possible unreported lobbying to respond to inquiries and explicitly state their lobbying or political fundraising activities, whether they met with city agencies and the purpose of those meetings.

Formally establish the steps staff must follow when investigating alleged unreported lobbying, including contacting both the subjects of complaints and the alleged lobbying targets, and document all steps, evidence and conclusions.
Establish written policies and procedures with detailed guidance for staff on carrying out their duties, including investigation steps.
Continue advocating to the Office of Management and Budget for the funding needed to hire staff to carry out its mandated duties.
audits.agency_response: The office agreed with all six recommendations, though the auditors noted its response appeared to narrow the scope of the written policies it committed to and urged a comprehensive policy framework.

audits.title: DOI Investigation into the NYPD's Compliance with Local Laws Restricting City Assistance with Immigration Enforcement
audits.plain_title: One of five incidents broke immigration cooperation limits
audits.agency: New York City Police Department
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) examined the New York City Police Department's (NYPD) compliance with local laws and executive orders restricting assistance with federal civil immigration enforcement, investigating five specific incidents and the department's related policies.
audits.background: The investigation was prompted by a June 2025 referral from City Council Speaker Adrienne Adams and Oversight and Investigations Committee Chair Gale Brewer after media reports raised questions about NYPD involvement in civil immigration enforcement. City laws limit such assistance while permitting cooperation with federal criminal investigations.

findings.plain: DOI concluded that NYPD's current policies, particularly as strengthened by reforms in 2025, comply with city law, but identified one incident of five in which an officer violated local law by assisting federal civil immigration enforcement.
findings.quote:
DOI identified one incident in which an officer violated local law  by providing assistance to federal 
authorities in connection with enforcement of the federal civil immigration law

findings.plain: In November 2024, an NYPD officer on a Homeland Security Investigations task force placed alerts on a list of people subject to potential civil immigration enforcement so he would be emailed if they interacted with the NYPD, violating policy and local law. The officer was removed from the task force and discipline is ongoing.
findings.quote:
The officer honored that request in 
violation of NYPD policy and local law.

findings.plain: In three other incidents, including the transfer of Merwil Gutiérrez Flores to Federal Bureau of Investigation custody and the disclosure of Leqaa Kordia's sealed arrest records, DOI found no violation of the sanctuary laws, though the Kordia records should not have been shared because they were sealed.
findings.quote:
the prior arrest information should not have been disclosed to HSI because the arrest records were 
sealed.

findings.plain: NYPD does not comply with Local Law 228, which requires documenting each request for assistance with civil immigration enforcement: its documentation is underinclusive and it does not send all required information to the Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs for quarterly reports.
findings.quote:
the NYPD does not comply with this law, because its documentation of requests is 
underinclusive and does not contain the level of detail required by local law and other City policies.

findings.plain: NYPD has not adopted a policy limiting non-local law enforcement agents' access to city property as Local Law 246 of 2017 requires, though it began drafting one when DOI raised the issue. It does comply with Local Law 59's annual detainer reporting requirement.
findings.quote:
DOI found that the NYPD has not 
adopted such a policy, apart from general policy statements prohibiting the use of City property to 
assist in immigration enforcement

findings.plain: Gaps in NYPD's policies, including detainer rules that cover only formal paperwork from civil immigration agents and four inconsistent policy documents, raise the risk of improper information sharing or assistance.
findings.quote:
found gaps in the NYPD’s current policies and practices that raise the risk of  
improper information sharing or assistance to federal authorities for purposes of civil immigration enforcement

numbers.label: Incidents DOI investigated
Incident where an officer violated local law
Recommendations issued, all accepted by NYPD

recommendations: Amend NYPD policies to require enhanced review of all custody transfers to federal agents, not only transfers to federal civil immigration agents presenting formal detainer paperwork.

Adopt a standalone policy on custodial transfer requests from federal agents covering which requests are subject to the policy, what documentation to collect, which NYPD division handles them and the standards for deciding whether to honor them.

Improve policies for processing federal assistance requests with guidance on assessing whether a request is for civil immigration enforcement and routing requests about unknown subjects, and require task force officers to document their verification steps.
Provide officers further training on when and how to report and document requests for assistance from federal law enforcement.

Improve recordkeeping and reporting under Local Law 228, including recording the nature of each request, the requesting agency and the NYPD's response, and reporting non-detainer requests to the Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs.
Conduct an email audit of NYPD members assigned to federal task forces to ensure their compliance with local law.
Adopt guidelines implementing Local Law 246 of 2017, which requires restricting non-local law enforcement officers' access to city property.
audits.agency_response: NYPD accepted all seven recommendations. It had already tightened scrutiny of federal justifications after the Kordia incident, removed the task force officer who placed the alerts and began drafting a Local Law 246 policy when DOI flagged the gap.

audits.title: Enforcement of Local Law 144 – Automated Employment Decision Tools
audits.plain_title: How the city enforces its law on automated hiring tools
audits.agency: New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection has designed and put in place an effective system to enforce Local Law 144, the city law governing automated employment decision tools. The audit covered July 2023 through June 2025.
audits.background: Local Law 144 of 2021 requires employers and employment agencies that use automated employment decision tools to conduct a bias audit within a year before using a tool, post a summary of the results on their website and notify candidates that a tool will be used. The department enforces the law with civil penalties of $500 to $1,500 per day and has an agreement with the city Office of Technology and Innovation for technical help.

findings.plain: The department's complaint process does not ensure that complaints about violations reach it, and after its initial stakeholder education it has done no further outreach. That approach will not catch employers that simply skip the law's requirements, such as posting bias audits.
findings.quote: DCWP’s AEDT complaint process is ineffective in ensuring that all complaints related to non-compliance with LL144 are routed to DCWP.

findings.plain: The department received only two complaints about automated employment decision tools during the audit period but did not look into whether its complaint intake process was working.
findings.quote: DCWP did not investigate whether the complaint intake process worked.

findings.plain: When the department surveyed the websites and bias audits of 32 companies it found a single compliance issue. Auditors reviewed the same companies and found at least 17 instances of potential non-compliance. The department's review skipped the formal procedures its technology partner created and did not cover all of the law's requirements.
findings.quote: We reviewed the same companies and identified at least 17 instances of potential non-compliance under LL144.

findings.plain: Department officials lack the technical expertise to evaluate how these tools are used, yet they did not consult the Office of Technology and Innovation when making determinations about them.
findings.quote: DCWP officials did not consult with OTI when making determinations about AEDTs.

numbers.label: Complaints about automated hiring tools in two years
Companies whose websites and bias audits the department surveyed
Potential violations auditors found at those same companies
Top daily civil penalty for violating the law

recommendations: Implement processes to make sure complaints about automated employment decision tools are properly handled and routed.
Implement mechanisms to make sure such complaints received by 311 are properly routed to the department.
Research and test why so few complaints about the tools come in and take steps to address those factors.
Make sure the department's bias audit reviews address all potential non-compliance, including by using existing Office of Technology and Innovation resources such as the Enforcement Workbook.
Create and implement a process to improve enforcement by identifying potential violations through research and other leads, not just complaints.
Use the Office of Technology and Innovation's expertise to evaluate the technical workings of suspected automated tools in support of enforcement.

audits.title: Oversight of Housing Discrimination Complaints
audits.plain_title: How the human rights agency handles housing bias complaints
audits.agency: New York City Commission on Human Rights
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the New York City Commission on Human Rights reviewed and addressed housing discrimination complaints on time and in line with its own policies and the law. The audit covered July 2019 through March 2025.
audits.background: The commission enforces the New York City Human Rights Law, which bans housing discrimination based on race, source of income, disability and other protected classes. From July 2019 through July 2024 it received 51,702 housing discrimination inquiries, of which 474 had been filed as formal complaints as of July 31, 2024.

findings.plain: The commission does not adequately monitor how housing discrimination inquiries and complaints are handled and has no benchmarks for timeliness. In a sample of 29 cases, determinations came more than 2 years on average after complaints were filed, and where submission dates were documented, decisions took over 3 years on average, with one case lingering more than 7 years.
findings.quote: for the 18 inquiries where the submission date was documented, decisions took over 3 years on average—including one that lingered for more than 7 years.

findings.plain: Staff often failed to respond to people alleging discrimination within the expected 14 days. In 12 of 25 sampled inquiries with dates recorded, the first contact attempt came about 39 days after the commission was contacted, and in one case not until 165 days later.
findings.quote: they did not contact the inquirer until approximately 39 days after CCHR was contacted.

findings.plain: The commission has no policy requiring timely intake appointments. Where appointment dates were documented, intake took almost 3 months on average from submission, and in one instance almost 9 months.
findings.quote: LEB staff did not conduct an intake appointment for these inquiries until, on average, almost 3 months (84 days) from the day the inquiries were submitted.

findings.plain: Guidelines say attorneys should draft a complaint within 14 days of the intake appointment, but officials did not monitor this. For the six sampled cases with dates recorded, drafts took nearly 4 months on average, and one attorney took more than 11 months.
findings.quote: on average, attorneys took nearly 4 months (115 days) to submit a draft complaint to their supervisor.

findings.plain: When an assigned attorney left or was removed from a case, the commission was slow to assign a new one, taking over 11 months on average for five of 36 sampled complaints and over 2 years in one case.
findings.quote: it took CCHR over 11 months (348 days) to reassign a new attorney to five of 36 sampled complaints.

findings.plain: The commission did not ensure staff documented and kept evidence that sampled housing discrimination cases were being supervised.
findings.quote: CCHR did not ensure its staff documented and maintained evidence of case supervision for sampled housing discrimination complaints.

numbers.label: Housing discrimination inquiries received over five years
Inquiries filed as formal complaints as of July 31, 2024
Longest wait to reassign an attorney to an open case

recommendations: Develop policies and procedures to reduce delays in processing housing discrimination complaints, including setting time frames for each step of intake, filing and investigation, monitoring dates in the case management system, analyzing its data and assessing resources to find bottlenecks, and strengthening policies and monitoring compliance.
Establish a procedure that prioritizes attorney reassignments to minimize disruption to investigations.

Make sure staff use available tools for thorough case management, including documenting evidence of case supervision and recording all intake and investigation activities and essential documents in the case management system.

audits.title: Oversight of the Practice of Funeral Directing
audits.plain_title: State and city oversight of funeral directors
audits.agency: New York State Department of Health and New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the state Department of Health effectively oversees the practice of funeral directing under state law and whether the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene effectively oversees selected aspects of the practice. The audit covered April 2019 through November 2023.
audits.background: Under the Public Health Law, only licensed and registered funeral directors working at registered firms may handle the care, preparation and burial or cremation of the dead. Deaths outside New York City are registered in the state's Electronic Death Registration System and deaths in the city in the city's eVital system; together the systems recorded 801,421 deaths statewide during the audit period.

findings.plain: Some funeral directors interviewed said they do not use the tests prescribed by regulation to verify that death has occurred, and some said they do not always label or otherwise identify the bodies in their care, raising the risk of misidentification.
findings.quote: some said they don’t always label or otherwise identify the bodies in their care, increasing the risk that bodies may be misidentified.

findings.plain: The state health department has reduced or no assurance that some funeral firms met, or still meet, the required standards for their preparation rooms.
findings.quote: DOH has reduced or no assurance that some firms initially met or continue to meet standards for their preparation rooms.

findings.plain: In more than 2,500 cases, deaths were registered after the bodies had already been buried or cremated, according to the two vital records systems.
findings.quote: There were more than 2,500 cases in which deaths were registered after the disposition of bodies

findings.plain: Auditors found two instances where a firm may have been practicing at an unknown or unregistered location and over 23,000 death certificates issued in the state and city systems by unregistered or unknown funeral directors or firms.
findings.quote: over 23,000 death certificates that were issued in both DOH and DOHMH’s systems by unregistered or unknown funeral directors and/or firms.

findings.plain: Auditors identified 7,484 death certificates with duplicated or missing Social Security numbers, which undermines the certificates' accuracy and their usefulness in post-death arrangements.
findings.quote: We identified 7,484 death certificates (2,785 EDRS, 4,699 eVital) with duplicated or no SSNs

findings.plain: The state's practices for learning about and following up on funeral firm closures give it little assurance that it has the information needed to investigate risks.
findings.quote: DOH’s practices for learning about and following up on firm closures provide little assurance that it has the information it needs to investigate any risks identified.

numbers.label: Deaths recorded statewide during the audit period
Death certificates issued by unregistered or unknown directors or firms
Death certificates with duplicated or missing Social Security numbers
Deaths registered only after burial or cremation

recommendations: To the state Department of Health: take steps to better ensure funeral directors and firms know about and comply with required death tests and minimize the risk of misidentifying human remains.
To the state Department of Health: take action to gain greater assurance that firms meet requirements for their preparation rooms.
To the state Department of Health: work with the city health department on an approach to identify and follow up on the risk that bodies are buried or cremated before the death is registered.

To the state Department of Health: strengthen methods to identify and address unauthorized funeral directing by unregistered directors or firms or at unregistered locations, which might include better internal communication between its funeral directing and vital records bureaus.
To the state Department of Health: evaluate the benefit of inspecting funeral firms based on identified risks and document the results.
To the state Department of Health: take steps to improve assurance that closing or closed firms have actually stopped operating.
To both departments: improve interagency communication, which could include analyzing registration data and sharing results, to better identify and address unauthorized funeral directing activity.
To both departments: improve the completeness and accuracy of Social Security number information on death certificates in their respective systems.

audits.title: Oversight of Language Access Services
audits.plain_title: How well city hospitals serve patients with limited English
audits.agency: New York City Health and Hospitals Corporation
audits.what_they_audited: Whether New York City Health + Hospitals, the city's public hospital system, adequately serves patients with limited English proficiency, complies with state regulations and local laws and provides enough oversight of its language access services. The audit covered January 2019 through December 2024.
audits.background: Health + Hospitals, the nation's largest municipal public health care system, serves about 1 million New Yorkers a year, and the Census Bureau estimates over 1.7 million city residents have limited English proficiency. In fiscal year 2024 the system answered 2.6 million requests for language services with 35.6 million minutes of interpretation in 255 languages and dialects at a cost of $24.1 million.

findings.plain: The system did not adequately oversee its language services data. Records had missing or mislabeled information, the system could not confirm that interpretation in rarer languages was actually provided and it did not reconcile the data against vendor invoices.
findings.quote: H+H did not reconcile LAS data with billed invoices, and there are no standard review procedures for invoices.

findings.plain: The system has not fully met state regulatory requirements. It failed to perform required annual assessments of limited English proficiency needs for 2019 through 2023, workers at Bellevue Hospital missed 4,061 required annual training sessions and no training records were provided for Woodhull and Harlem hospitals.
findings.quote: H+H failed to perform required annual LEP needs assessments for years 2019–2023

findings.plain: There is no centralized list of qualified in-house interpreters and bilingual staff, and lists at individual facilities were missing or outdated. Some bilingual staff interpretation was never reported in the data.
findings.quote: H+H lacks a centralized list of qualified in-house interpreters and bilingual staff.

findings.plain: Twenty-nine facilities or programs had no language access policies at all, and at the 21 that did, policies did not always match systemwide guidelines or actual practice.
findings.quote: We found 29 facilities/programs had no LAS policies.

findings.plain: Auditors found no assurance that translations of medical records, after-visit summaries and discharge papers are managed and tracked for accuracy, and the system could not confirm that patient calls lasting 2 hours were reviewed.
findings.quote: We have no assurance that H+H manages and tracks translations of patient medical records, after-visit summaries, and discharge papers into different languages

findings.plain: Bilingual state auditors made anonymous, unannounced calls and visits and hit barriers: staff who did not try to connect them to an interpreter, hard-to-navigate automated phone systems and no language access through the system's street outreach mobile units.
findings.quote: Instances where H+H staff did not attempt to connect callers to an interpreter or to provide information.

findings.plain: Contract payments were poorly managed. The system overpaid language vendors $215,879 between January 2022 and June 2024, including phone interpretation billed at higher video rates, and would have saved $8,247,840 over two fiscal years by negotiating or using vendors with lower per-minute rates.
findings.quote: H+H made $215,879 in overpayments to vendors for LAS.

numbers.label: Cost of interpretation services in fiscal year 2024
Languages and dialects in which interpretation was provided
Overpayments to language service vendors
Potential two-year savings from lower vendor rates
Required training sessions missed at Bellevue Hospital

recommendations: Develop procedures to ensure information for all language service requests is reported, and periodically review the data for completeness, accuracy and proof that services were delivered.
Comply with the state hospital regulation, including conducting annual assessments of limited English proficiency needs and ensuring staff complete all annual trainings.
Prepare and maintain centralized and facility-level lists of in-house interpreters and bilingual staff.
Make sure every facility and program develops language access policies or updates existing ones to match systemwide guidelines.
Ensure information in patient records is accurately translated into various languages.
Review and keep documentation for patient calls lasting over 2 hours.

Establish procedures to improve patients' experience accessing and navigating language service phone lines and mobile health units, for example through bilingual staff or phone and video interpretation.
Review records and recoup outstanding overpayments made to vendors as appropriate.
Establish procedures to select the most cost-effective language service vendors, based on negotiation or lower per-minute contract rates.

audits.title: Letter to Commissioner Rehman Re: Audit Report on the New York City Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings’ Provision of Language Access Services
audits.plain_title: Hearings office meets its language access obligations
audits.agency: New York City Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings
audits.what_they_audited: A letter report on whether the Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings, the city's central administrative law court, provides the interpretation and translation services required by city and state language access laws. The scope ran from January 1, 2018 through October 30, 2025.
audits.background: Nearly one-half of all New Yorkers speak a language other than English at home and almost 25% are not proficient in English. Local Law 30 of 2017 requires city agencies that serve the public to provide language services in 10 designated citywide languages and to adopt a language access implementation plan.

findings.plain: The agency complies with the website translation, document translation and interpretation standards set by the relevant laws and guidelines.
findings.quote: OATH complies with the website translation, document translation, and in-person and telephonic interpretation standards prescribed by relevant laws, standards, and guidelines

findings.plain: Services generally meet the needs of residents who prefer languages other than English, who have the same access to the agency's services as English speakers.
findings.quote: the NELP population has the same access to government services as the English-speaking population

findings.plain: Its language access plan contains every key element required by Local Law 30, including a designated coordinator, telephone interpretation in over 100 languages, translated documents, staff training and complaint monitoring.
findings.quote: The LAIP contained all key aspects required by Local Law 30

findings.plain: Contracted vendors cover the required languages. The interpretation vendor offers over 250 languages and the translation vendors over 160, including the designated citywide and temporary languages.
findings.quote: Language Line can provide interpretation in over 250 languages including the designated citywide languages

findings.plain: The agency tells the public that free language services are available through signs in its offices, notices on its website and messages on its help line, and its website translates into the required languages.
findings.quote: OATH informs the public of the availability of free language access services by posting signs in conspicuous locations

numbers.label: Foreign-born New York City residents
City residents not proficient in English
Designated citywide languages agencies must serve
Languages available through the interpretation vendor

recommendations: The report makes no formal recommendations.
audits.agency_response: In a written response dated November 6, 2025, the Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings agreed with the audit's findings.

audits.title: New York City Department of Homeless Services – Oversight of Contract Expenditures of Institute for Community Living, Inc. (Follow-Up)
audits.plain_title: Checkup on oversight of a women's shelter contractor's spending
audits.agency: New York City Department of Social Services
audits.what_they_audited: How far the New York City Department of Homeless Services has gone in carrying out the nine recommendations from a 2022 state audit of its oversight of contract spending by the Institute for Community Living, Inc.
audits.background: The department contracted with the nonprofit Institute for Community Living in 2014 to run the 200-bed Tillary Street Women's Shelter for women with mental illness and substance abuse disorders, a contract with an aggregate cost of about $50.8 million. The initial audit found the department was not effectively monitoring the contract and identified $2,376,462, or 9.7% of reported costs, that did not comply with fiscal requirements.

findings.plain: The department has made some progress since the initial audit but more work remains. Of the nine original recommendations, one was implemented, five were partially implemented and three were not implemented.
findings.quote: Of the initial report’s nine audit recommendations, one was implemented, five were partially implemented, and three were not implemented.

numbers.label: Noncompliant costs found by the initial audit
Approximate aggregate cost of the shelter contract
Meals the initial audit estimated the contractor discarded

recommendations: Officials are asked, though not required, to report within 30 days on any actions planned to address the unresolved issues.
audits.implementation_note: Of the nine recommendations in the 2022 audit, the follow-up found one implemented, five partially implemented and three not implemented.

audits.title: Review of the New York City Police Department’s Body-Worn Camera Program
audits.plain_title: Police body camera footage is slow to reach the public
audits.agency: New York City Police Department
audits.what_they_audited: A review, rather than a full audit, of the police department's body-worn camera program: how the department handles public records requests for footage, whether officers activate cameras as required and how the program is overseen. The scope ran from January 1, 2020 through May 21, 2025.
audits.background: The 2013 federal court settlement in Floyd v. City of New York required the police department to adopt body-worn cameras to record stops and other encounters, with a federal monitor overseeing the reforms. The camera program began in April 2017 and most officers had cameras by August 2019.

findings.plain: Footage requests moved slowly. The department took an average of 133 business days to grant or deny Freedom of Information Law requests for camera footage, missed its own 95-day goal more than half the time and took as long as four years in one case.
findings.quote: On average, NYPD took 133 business days to grant or deny FOIL requests during the review period.

findings.plain: Denials rarely held up. 97% of appeals of denied footage requests were granted, and 12 of 13 decided court challenges ended with the department providing footage or being ordered to provide it.
findings.quote: NYPD’s FOIL appeal process resulted in production of BWC footage 97% of the time, and footage was provided after being challenged in court 92% of the time.

findings.plain: Footage was often missing or incomplete. In the department's own reviews of dispatched 911 calls, 36% of review determinations had no video on file, and where video existed, cameras were activated late or shut off early 18% of the time.
findings.quote: 4,319 (36%) of 12,116 review determinations had no corresponding video on file

findings.plain: Required internal checks were skipped. Precincts could not produce monthly self-inspections of camera activation for more than half of the months sampled, and nobody independently reviews the inspections that are done.
findings.quote: NYPD was unable to provide Self-Inspections for 87—more than half—of the requested months.

findings.plain: Department supervisors and the federal monitor reach very different conclusions about stops. Internal reviews found officers applied the law appropriately over 98% of the time, while the monitor found 11% to 14% of reviewed stops unconstitutional in 2020 through 2023.
findings.quote: NYPD supervisors do not assess stops correctly

findings.plain: Use-of-force paperwork is not ensured. In a sample of 25 substantiated excessive force complaints, the department acknowledged a Threat, Resistance, or Injury Report was required in 17 cases, but four of those had none.
findings.quote: for four (24%) of the 17 incidents, a TRI Report was not prepared

findings.plain: The department does not aggregate camera data or analyze trends, even though precincts with poor camera compliance overlapped with precincts with above-average substantiated excessive force allegations.
findings.quote: NYPD does not aggregate data or perform trend analyses of its Self-Inspections and ICAD reviews

numbers.label: Average time to grant or deny a footage request
Denied footage requests granted on appeal
Dispatch review determinations with no video on file
Videos activated late or deactivated early
Sampled months missing self-inspection records
Longest time to decide a footage request

recommendations: Increase Legal Bureau staffing and make additional efforts to answer records requests on time.
Promptly notify requesters when a required 160.50 waiver form is missing.
Take steps to ensure all officers on patrol duty are immediately given cameras.
Formalize a policy for dispatch call audits, including the number, frequency and sampling plan, and exclude interactions that did not require recording.
Investigate why activation rates are lower in certain boroughs and precincts and keep improving them citywide.
Conduct an overall assessment of whether the camera program has improved compliance with policies, regulations and laws, including respectful interaction with the public.
Aggregate the results of the department's various camera reviews to identify anomalies or trends and address them.
Ensure monthly self-inspections of camera activation are completed as required.
Have the Professional Standards Division independently review self-inspections.
Ensure monthly stop report worksheets are completed as required.
Take additional steps to identify improper stops and ensure compliance with stop and frisk policy.
Review a sample of footage from investigative encounters to identify force that was used and check whether the required report was completed.
Ensure Threat, Resistance, or Injury Reports are completed for every use-of-force incident.
audits.agency_response: The police department agreed with nine recommendations, said three others reflect its current practice and said it would consider one more, while also questioning the review team's methodology and conclusions.

audits.title: Twenty-Seventh Report of the Independent Monitor (Corrected): Compliance Snapshot of NYPD’s Stop, Frisk, and Search Practices
audits.plain_title: Stop and frisk compliance snapshot for late 2024
audits.agency: New York City Police Department
audits.what_they_audited: A visual "compliance snapshot" updating the monitor's Twenty-Fourth Report on the New York City Police Department's (NYPD) compliance with the federal court's requirements in Floyd v. City of New York, Ligon v. City of New York and Davis v. City of New York, covering the fourth quarter of 2024. This summary uses the corrected version of the report, filed November 19, 2025.
audits.background: The report covers the fourth quarter of 2024 and in several places compares that quarter to the fourth quarter of 2023. It draws on the monitor team's audits of 100 stop reports per month and 225 body-worn camera videos per quarter, plus the NYPD Quality Assurance Section's own audits.

findings.plain: In the fourth quarter of 2024, the monitor's audits found 89% of reported stops, 71% of frisks and 73% of searches lawful, with little if any improvement compared to a year earlier.
findings.quote: In the fourth quarter of 2024, 89% of stops, 71% of frisks, and 73% of searches were assessed as lawful.

findings.plain: Self-initiated activity remained the weak spot. While 96% of radio run stops and 100% of stops based on complainant information were lawful, only 81% of self-initiated stops were, along with just 58% of frisks and 60% of searches during self-initiated stops.
findings.quote: 81% of self-initiated stops were lawful, showing no change from the fourth quarter of 2023.

findings.plain: Most commands fell short of an 85% compliance rate: the department's own audits found 61% of the NYPD's 98 commands below that bar for frisks and 69% below it for searches.
findings.quote: 61% of NYPD’s 98 commands

findings.plain: Supervisors still approved nearly everything. The monitor found 11% of stops, 29% of frisks and 27% of searches unlawful in the quarter, while reviewing supervisors flagged only 1% of stops, 1% of frisks and 3% of searches.
findings.quote: approved close to 100% of all stops, frisks, and searches and barely identified any as unlawful.

findings.plain: Underreporting improved slightly but persisted: officers failed to complete stop reports for 28% of stops identified in the monitor's audit, down from 37% in the fourth quarter of 2023.
findings.quote: 28% of stops identified in the audit.

findings.plain: Housing Bureau officers improved markedly: 90% of their stops, 81% of frisks and 79% of searches were lawful in the quarter, and trespass arrests showed 96% compliance on the reason to approach and 100% on probable cause.
findings.quote: 90% of stops, 81% of frisks, and 79% of searches were assessed as lawful

numbers.label: Reported stops found lawful, fourth quarter of 2024
Frisks found lawful, fourth quarter of 2024
Searches found lawful, fourth quarter of 2024
Stops missing a stop report in the monitor's audit
Commands with frisk compliance above 85%

recommendations: The report makes no new formal recommendations.
audits.compliance_note: The monitor found little improvement in overall compliance compared to the fourth quarter of 2023: most commands did not have compliance rates above 85% for frisks and searches, underreporting remained a problem and reviewing supervisors rarely identified any stop, frisk or search as unlawful.

audits.title: Audit on the Effectiveness of the Mayor’s Office of Housing Recovery Operations’ Build It Back Program
audits.plain_title: How well Build It Back rebuilt homes after Hurricane Sandy
audits.agency: Mayor's Office of Housing Recovery Operations
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Build It Back program run by the Mayor's Office of Housing Recovery Operations (HRO) achieved its goal of helping property owners affected by Hurricane Sandy repair, rebuild or relocate, and whether it made Sandy-affected New Yorkers and communities safer and more resilient.
audits.background: Hurricane Sandy damaged or destroyed over 17,000 homes in New York City in October 2012, and the city created HRO to coordinate recovery. HRO launched Build It Back in June 2013, with $2.3 billion in federal Community Development Block Grant Disaster Recovery funding allocated for the single-family program and a stated goal of finishing construction by the end of 2016.

findings.plain: The program ultimately served only about a third of the people who applied. Of 22,436 homeowners who applied, 8,131 were served, even though only a small share were found ineligible.
findings.quote: HRO served 36% of those applicants who initially applied to participate in the program, despite excluding only a small percentage based on eligibility.

findings.plain: Processing was slow. It took HRO about two years on average to process a single application and roughly six more months to start construction.
findings.quote: HRO took two years on average to process a single application and six more months to initiate construction.

findings.plain: The program missed its own deadline. Nearly 1,600 homes, about 40 percent, were not finished by the end-of-2016 target, and 565 homes had not even begun construction by then. The last home was finished in February 2023, more than a decade after the storm.
findings.quote: HRO established a construction completion deadline of 2016, but nearly 1,600 (40.1%) homes were not completed by this time.

findings.plain: Start to finish, projects took about three years on average from the day a homeowner applied to the day construction was done, with the longest taking almost a decade.
findings.quote: On average, construction projects took three years to complete from the date an application was submitted to the date construction finished.

findings.plain: Deadline policies and an acceleration initiative introduced in 2016 cut the time to start construction from 217 days to 104 days on average, but the time to complete construction rose from 164 days to 283 days, so overall completion times did not improve.
findings.quote: the introduction of new policies and initiatives also failed to reduce overall completion times.

findings.plain: Slow timelines drove people away and kept others out of their homes. 11,140 applicants withdrew or were withdrawn, and of the 860 applicants who were temporarily relocated during construction, 627 were displaced longer than the program's 14-month limit, for 24 months on average, with 15 homeowners displaced for over four years.
findings.quote: Of the 860 applicants who were temporarily relocated, 627 were displaced from their homes for longer than 14 months.

findings.plain: HRO's controls were weak. It did not consistently track contract completion terms in its case management system, and it had no timeframe or deadline policies in place when the program started, which likely contributed to delays.
findings.quote: HRO did not ensure that TPA and Home Improvement Contract terms were consistently and accurately tracked in CMS.

recommendations: For future disaster recovery programs, document timeframes and deadlines in policies and procedures at the start so staff and contractors can monitor application processing and construction and keep them on schedule.
Establish and track performance indicators in the recordkeeping system, including timeliness measures for the contractors handling application processing and construction management.
audits.agency_response: HRO acknowledged that Build It Back encountered significant implementation challenges and agreed with both recommendations, saying it was establishing a new standard for compliance and audit readiness for future disaster recovery programs.

audits.title: Update on NYPD's Implementation of DOI's 2023 Criminal Group Database Recommendations
audits.plain_title: Gang database reforms are half done, so watchdog adds 13 more
audits.agency: New York City Police Department
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation's (DOI) Office of the Inspector General for the New York City Police Department (OIG-NYPD) assessed how the NYPD has implemented recommendations from OIG-NYPD's 2023 report on the Criminal Group Database (CGD), reviewing database entries and paperwork for a sample of 531 individuals.
audits.background: OIG-NYPD's 2023 report on the gang database made 17 recommendations, of which NYPD accepted 11, rejected five and placed one under consideration. As of December 2022 the database held 16,141 people, 98% of them male, identified as Black or Hispanic and under 42.

findings.plain: The database shrank 39% between December 2022 and October 2025, from 16,141 people to 8,563, while its demographics stayed largely the same: predominantly Black and Hispanic men aged 18 to 34.
findings.quote:
as of October 2025, the numbers had 
declined by 39%, to 8,563.

findings.plain: Of the eight accepted recommendations reviewed in depth, four were fully implemented and four partially implemented. NYPD updated its policies in October 2023 consistent with the accepted recommendations, though gaps remain.
findings.quote: finding four have been fully implemented and four partially implemented.

findings.plain: Renewals and deactivations still are not reviewed by a supervisor or subject to a multilevel review process, contrary to a recommendation NYPD accepted in 2023.
findings.quote:
the renewal and deactivations are not 
reviewed by a supervisor or otherwise subject to a multilevel review process

findings.plain: Despite a new parental notification process for minors added to the database, the department failed to complete any notifications; NYPD says a new procedure putting the duty on the nominating detective is still pending.
findings.quote:
Despite the updated IUP and the Chief of Detectives Memorandum, the Department failed to 
complete any notifications.

findings.plain: Review delays got worse: at least 151 entries, including 48 minors, were between six and more than 60 months past due for renewal or deactivation review. After OIG-NYPD flagged the delays, NYPD says the maximum is now eight days.
findings.quote:
delays were even 
longer with at least 151 entries (48 minors and 103 adults) between 6 and 60+ months past due

findings.plain: A vendor coding error wrongly stretched the review period from two years to three for people added at 16 or 17 who turned 18 before their review; 48 of 59 minors reviewed were delayed six to 60 months. NYPD says the error is corrected.
findings.quote:
the automated review system incorrectly extended the review time from two years to three years if a 
person was activated at 16 or 17

findings.plain: Activation paperwork improved but some officers filled forms out incorrectly, including listing themselves as one of the two required independent sources, and source justifications were often boilerplate with no specific supporting information.
findings.quote:
there wer e reporting 
officers who listed themselves as one of the two sources.

numbers.label: People in the database as of October 2025
People in the database as of December 2022
Decline in database size since December 2022
Individuals in OIG-NYPD's review sample
Entries at least six months past due for review
New recommendations issued in this report

recommendations: Ensure all uniformed personnel authorized to nominate people into the database are trained on the Impact and Use Policy and the Chief of Detectives Memorandum.
Require the two independent reliable sources to give substantive explanations for their belief in an individual's criminal group membership and document those explanations on activation forms.
Clarify that the two independent sources must be different from the reporting officer.
Update the Impact and Use Policy to mirror the detailed guidelines in the Chief of Detectives Memorandum.
Establish a multilevel review process for renewals with supervisor sign-off on all renewal forms, as previously recommended and accepted, and list the required supporting documentation.
Require the nominating detective to notify a juvenile's parent or guardian within 60 days of activation into the database.
Ensure renewal and activation forms include a required field with the individual's next review date.
Create a written internal audit requirement to verify that parental notifications for minors are made, documented and recorded in a new database column.
Confirm whether anyone activated at 16 or 17 went more than two years without review because of the coding error, and review whether they should be renewed or deactivated.
Ensure supporting documentation is included for all renewals.
Conduct quarterly audits so no entries are past due for review, and immediately renew or deactivate any that are.
Review individuals renewed based on an arrest every six months to make sure renewals do not rest on arrests that were later sealed, at minimum exploring whether such an audit is feasible.
Collect, analyze and publish data annually on the number of entries added, renewed and deactivated.
audits.agency_response: NYPD promptly moved to reduce review backlogs when OIG-NYPD flagged them, saying the maximum delay is now eight days, corrected the vendor coding error and plans to shift parental notification duties to nominating detectives and strip sealed-arrest details from database forms.
audits.implementation_note: Of the 17 recommendations in the 2023 report, NYPD accepted 11, rejected five and placed one under consideration; of the eight accepted recommendations assessed here, four were fully implemented and four partially implemented, and of the remaining three accepted, two were implemented and one was not yet implemented.

audits.title: Twenty-Sixth Report of the Independent Monitor: The NYPD's Accountability Efforts
audits.plain_title: Few consequences for officers who made unlawful stops
audits.agency: New York City Police Department
audits.what_they_audited: The effectiveness of the New York City Police Department's (NYPD) internal accountability systems for unconstitutional stops, frisks and searches: how commands responded to audits by the department's Quality Assurance Section (QAS), whether the court-ordered Early Intervention Program (EIP) changed officer behavior and how the department's ComplianceStat meetings held commanders accountable.
audits.background: Accountability for unconstitutional stops is key to compliance with the federal court's orders in Floyd v. City of New York, Ligon v. City of New York and Davis v. City of New York. Each quarter QAS audits a sample of stop reports from every command, the court ordered an early warning system in 2020 to flag at-risk officers and the department launched ComplianceStat meetings in January 2024 to question borough and command staff on compliance.

findings.plain: There was little accountability for unconstitutional policing in 2024. Over the four quarters reviewed, QAS identified 4,458 improper stops, frisks or searches, but only eight officers received a Command Discipline and 110 got a negative entry through the Cop's Rapid Assessment Feedback Tool (CRAFT), the lowest sanction. In the other 97.5% of incidents the officer was instructed, trained or nothing was done.
findings.quote: Out of these 4,458 incidents, eight officers were given CDs and 110 officers were issued a

findings.plain: Commands responded to audit findings with training and instruction even for repeat offenders. In the 46 Precinct, where only 78% of audited stops, 57% of frisks and 60% of searches were lawful, one officer was instructed or referred for training 14 times in 12 months with no improvement, and nothing more severe was ever reported.
findings.quote: ...was instructed or referred for training 14 times...

findings.plain: The Early Intervention Program has not worked. Interventions directed by the Early Intervention Committee were minimal, follow-up was rare and officer behavior did not change.
findings.quote: EIP interventions did not impact officer behavior...

findings.plain: Officers flagged by the intervention program kept failing to document stops. For ten officers reviewed from the first quarter of 2024, the monitor found that of 43 encounters that should have had stop reports, only 17 did, leaving 60.5% of stops without reports.
findings.quote: leaving a staggering 60.5% of stops missing reports.

findings.plain: ComplianceStat pressure worked when sustained. Patrol Borough Brooklyn South was called in three times in four months for poor performance; by the third meeting an intensive borough effort had cut potentially undocumented encounters to 1% of audited videos, a precinct commander and two other supervisors were removed and one command's Neighborhood Safety Team was disbanded.
findings.quote: ...in another command, the NST team was disbanded.

findings.plain: At later ComplianceStat meetings covering Manhattan and Brooklyn North patrol boroughs, several borough and command executives were unprepared and could not answer basic questions about their specialized teams. Department leadership responded by disbanding the Brooklyn North Public Safety Team, relieving the executive responsible for compliance oversight and reassigning personnel.
findings.quote: ...command executives were unprepared for the meetings and unable to answer questions

numbers.label: Improper stops, frisks or searches identified by QAS in a year
Command Disciplines issued for those incidents
Negative CRAFT entries, the lowest sanction, in those incidents
Incidents met with only instruction, training or nothing
Stops missing reports among flagged officers reviewed
Stop reports audited by QAS over the four quarters reviewed

recommendations: Recognize that discipline and/or reassignment, for both officers and supervisors, may be necessary to address poor performance.
Hold supervisors accountable for identifying the unlawful actions of officers under their command.

Give the Early Intervention Program a strategic approach at the command level: commanders presenting to the committee should address not just the individual officer but what is being done to prevent other officers from engaging in triggering events.
Track the results of Early Intervention Program interventions and conduct an evaluation of the program.
audits.agency_response: The NYPD told the monitor it will begin examining how commands respond to Quality Assurance Section audits so officers with repeat deficiencies are not simply given the same training, and it acknowledged the monitor's concerns about the Early Intervention Program and is implementing new procedures. The police commissioner also issued a February 5, 2025 memorandum on discipline for repeated or intentional violations in connection with Level 3 stops.
audits.compliance_note: The monitor found meaningful accountability for unconstitutional stops, frisks and searches largely absent in 2024, with training substituted for discipline, but called the department's newer systems such as ComplianceStat and a revamped Early Intervention Program hopeful signs while saying it is too early to tell whether they will produce measurable improvement.

audits.title: Audit Report on the Office of the New York City Public Advocate’s Provision of Language Access Services
audits.plain_title: Does the public advocate serve New Yorkers in their languages?
audits.agency: Office of the New York City Public Advocate
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Office of the Public Advocate (PAO) provides services to people with a Non-English Language Preference (NELP) in the languages required by law, whether those services meet the NELP population's needs and whether NELP residents get the same access to government services as English speakers.
audits.background: Nearly half of all New Yorkers speak a language other than English at home and almost 25% of city residents aged five and over are not proficient in English. Local Law 30 of 2017 requires city agencies that provide direct public services to designate a Language Access Coordinator and develop a Language Access Implementation Plan.

findings.plain: The office generally provides the required language services, contracting with vendors for telephonic interpretation in over 240 languages and document translation in over 100 languages, and NELP residents generally get the same access as English speakers.
findings.quote: The language access services provided by PAO generally meet the needs of the Non-English Language Preference (NELP) population as intended, and the NELP population generally has the same access to government services as the English-speaking population.

findings.plain: The office was not fully compliant with Local Law 30. Its website did not say free language services were available and did not list the name and title of its Language Access Coordinator.
findings.quote: PAO’s website did not indicate whether the agency provides free language access services...

findings.plain: The reports the office publishes on its website, its most commonly distributed documents, could not be translated into the city's top 10 non-English languages. Only the report summaries could be translated, and the site did not tell visitors that translations were available on request.
findings.quote: they are not translatable documents—only the report summaries can be translated

findings.plain: The office had no Language Access Implementation Plan as the law requires. Its existing procedures left out most key elements, including annual staff training, emergency preparedness and a process for handling language access complaints.
findings.quote: PAO had not created or implemented an LAIP in compliance with LL30 prior to this audit.

findings.plain: When auditors first tested the website's translation feature in March 2025, the language dropdown menu showed blank options. The office fixed the bug promptly after being told, and a retest in April 2025 found it working.
findings.quote: the dropdown menu was not functioning properly, with language options appearing blank

findings.plain: By the August 2025 exit conference the office had made fixes, including creating a Language Access Implementation Plan, updating its website and documenting training for 12 staff members, and auditors assessed that it is now in compliance with Local Law 30.
findings.quote: Auditors confirmed that the implementations had been made and assessed that PAO is now in compliance with Local Law 30.

numbers.label: City residents aged five and over not proficient in English
Languages covered by the office's interpretation vendor
Languages the website translation feature can handle
Staff with documented language training by August 2025

recommendations: Periodically test website features to make sure they work as intended.
Going forward, make sure all frontline and managerial staff get annual language access training as Local Law 30 requires, and keep documentation such as attendance sheets and training materials.

Continue publishing reports directly on the website so the translation feature can translate them in full, or if that is not feasible, post a notice that published reports can be translated on request.
Post the newly created Language Access Implementation Plan in a conspicuous spot on the website.
Continue to keep the Language Access Coordinator's name and title posted on the website as required.
audits.agency_response: The Office of the Public Advocate agreed with the findings and all five recommendations, and during the audit provided documentation showing it had begun implementing them.

audits.title: College Readiness (Follow-Up)
audits.plain_title: Checkup on how city schools prepare students for college
audits.agency: New York City Public Schools
audits.what_they_audited: How far New York City Public Schools has gone in carrying out the four recommendations from a 2022 state audit of how well the school system prepares students for college.
audits.background: New York City Public Schools, the nation's largest school system, served about 900,000 students in the 2023-24 school year. The initial audit found that in a cohort of 71,210 students expected to graduate by August 2019, as many as 23% did not graduate on time, 38% did not persist in college for 6 months after enrolling and 45% of a 291-student sample were not college ready.

findings.plain: The school system has made significant progress since the initial audit. All four of the original recommendations have been implemented.
findings.quote: Of the initial report’s four audit recommendations, all four have been implemented.

findings.plain: Graduation rates still outpace college readiness. In 2024, 83% of high school students citywide graduated while only 52% were considered college ready, and the system has since added a grade point average component and a career component to its readiness metric.
findings.quote: In 2024, 83% of high school students citywide graduated, while only 52% were considered college ready.

numbers.label: High school students citywide who graduated in 2024
Students considered college ready in 2024

recommendations: The report makes no formal recommendations.
audits.implementation_note: Of the four recommendations in the 2022 audit, the follow-up found all four implemented.

audits.title: Follow-Up Audit on the Equal Employment Practices Commission’s Compliance with Its Charter Mandate to Audit City Agencies
audits.plain_title: Did the equal employment watchdog fix its audit lapses?
audits.agency: Equal Employment Practices Commission
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Equal Employment Practices Commission (EEPC) implemented the three recommendations from a 2020 audit and whether it is now meeting its City Charter mandate to audit every city agency's equal employment practices at least once every four years.
audits.background: EEPC is an independent oversight body that audits, reviews and monitors the equal employment practices of New York City government. The 2020 audit found EEPC had failed to audit 27 of the 141 city agencies under its jurisdiction during calendar years 2013 through 2016 and had erroneously claimed in annual reports that it met its mandate.

findings.plain: EEPC carried out all three recommendations from the 2020 audit, even though it had disagreed with two of them and never responded to the third.
findings.quote: the Equal Employment Practices Commission (EEPC) implemented all three recommendations made in the initial audit, despite its stated disagreement with two and non-response to the third

findings.plain: The commission caught up on its backlog and is meeting its mandate. It audited the 27 agencies it had skipped, completed audits of all 143 agencies under its jurisdiction for the 2018 to 2021 cycle and is on track to meet the mandate for the 2022 to 2025 cycle.
findings.quote: EEPC subsequently audited and evaluated the 27 City agencies that it had not audited during CYs 2013 through 2016; that it met its Charter mandate for the 2018–2021 cycle

findings.plain: The commission also resolved a long-running dispute over when an audit counts as done. At the auditors' urging it asked the city's Law Department, which said an audit can reasonably be considered complete when EEPC issues its final determination to an agency.
findings.quote: the Law Department stated that it was reasonable to interpret an audit as being completed upon EEPC’s issuance of an FD to an agency

findings.plain: In the current cycle EEPC issued 395 corrective actions to agencies whose equal employment programs fell short, and follow-up records showed 353 of them, or 89 percent, were satisfactorily implemented.
findings.quote: determined that 353 (89%) of the 395 CAs were satisfactorily implemented

findings.plain: A new problem: EEPC's website is badly out of date. None of the 124 final determinations auditors reviewed for the 2022 to 2025 cycle were posted online, and 10 of 40 sampled from the 2018 to 2021 cycle were also missing, undermining transparency.
findings.quote: none of the 124 FDs reviewed by the auditors for the 2022–2025 quadrennial cycle have been posted

findings.plain: Another new problem: the commission has no written policies or procedures for key audit practices, including how to create an audit plan or how to document policy changes such as its new definition of a completed audit.
findings.quote: There are no written policies or procedures that provide step-by-step instructions on how to create an audit plan

numbers.label: Previously skipped agencies that EEPC later audited
Final determinations issued in the 2018-2021 cycle
Corrective actions issued to agencies in the current cycle
Corrective actions satisfactorily implemented
Recent final determinations reviewed, none posted online

recommendations: Establish written procedures on when city agency audits open and close, in line with the Law Department's opinion.
Continue updating the website and make sure future updates happen in a timely manner.
Document all policy changes in writing and share them with the appropriate staff.
audits.agency_response: EEPC agreed with all three new recommendations and said it will implement them.
audits.implementation_note: Of the 3 recommendations in the 2020 audit, the follow-up found all 3 implemented.

audits.title: New York City Housing Authority Monitorship: Monitors' Report (Fifth Report)
audits.plain_title: New heat data: 84% of apartments lost heating service last winter
audits.agency: New York City Housing Authority
audits.what_they_audited: The federal monitors' fifth quarterly report on the New York City Housing Authority's (NYCHA) compliance with its 2019 agreement with the federal government, covering heat, elevators, pests and waste, mold and leaks, lead paint and inspections, plus organizational change. It reports data for May 1, 2025 to July 31, 2025 and serves as the annual heat report for the full 2024-2025 heating season.
audits.background: On January 31, 2019 NYCHA agreed with the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York (SDNY), the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and the City of New York to improve housing conditions, and a monitor was appointed to evaluate compliance. This is the first report in which NYCHA and the monitors had an agreed method for measuring heating failures inside individual apartments, so it is also the first to show apartment-level heat performance.

findings.plain: Measured for the first time at the apartment level, heating failures turned out to be near universal. In the 2024-2025 season 84% of occupied apartments had at least one heating service interruption, the highest since the monitorship began. The monitors caution this does not mean those apartments fell below the legal minimum temperature. NYCHA also had 388 unplanned heating outages, 104 more than the prior season.
findings.quote: 2025 season, 84% of occupied apartments experienced at least one

findings.plain: Heat came back faster when it failed. Average restoration time for verified in-apartment heating complaints fell from 26.3 hours in the 2022-2023 season to 13.9 hours, and NYCHA resolved 94% of central heating outages within 12 hours and 100% within 24 hours, meeting those requirements in the first season they applied.
findings.quote: restoration times from 26.3 hours in 2022‒2023 to 13.9 hours in

findings.plain: The heating system itself is aging and underfunded. NYCHA estimates it would need $4 billion in additional funding to repair or replace heating infrastructure at or past its useful life, and it is behind on boiler replacements, having done 146 of the required 297 as of July 31, 2025 and expecting to miss the December 31, 2026 deadline by about two months.
findings.quote: would require $4 billion in additional funding. Moreover, according

findings.plain: Mold repairs improved but remain far from compliance. Through the second quarter of Year 7, NYCHA met the agreement's mold timeframes 28% of the time, up from 8% in the same period of Year 6, against a 95% requirement. The monitors call it the first potential path to compliance in the monitorship.
findings.quote: blended obligation 28% of the time through the second quarter of

findings.plain: Lead testing neared the finish line. NYCHA had completed X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF) testing in 86.2% of apartments and expected to finish testing every apartment by the end of the year.
findings.quote: testing, having completed 86.2% of apartments, and

findings.plain: On pests, NYCHA hit two milestones and one setback. For the first time it met the requirement to send staff trained in integrated pest management to every pest complaint, and it began publishing estimated rat, mouse, cockroach and bed bug populations for each development on its website. But estimated populations for all four pests rose compared with the same period in Year 6, though they still met the agreement's reduction targets.
findings.quote: Year 7, NYCHA’s pest population estimates for rats,

findings.plain: NYCHA still shuts elevators down during protected hours with little warning, but a pilot showed a fix. There were 820 no-service conditions from planned outages during restricted hours this year, 383 fewer than the same period last year. At South Jamaica Houses, where NYCHA scheduled preventive maintenance and gave 24 hours' notice by robocall, no planned outages happened in restricted hours and residents told the monitors the elevators work better.
findings.quote: indicates that NYCHA should add other developments to the pilot

Unplanned heating outages, up 104 from the prior season
Average time to restore heat inside an apartment
Extra funding NYCHA estimates its heating system needs
Mold work orders finished within required timeframes
