recommendations: Repair or replace the aging heating infrastructure, which the high rate of heating service interruptions makes urgent.
Strengthen maintenance processes, improve data systems, improve performance on in-apartment heating failures and manage preventive and corrective maintenance more efficiently.
Expand the South Jamaica Houses elevator pilot to other developments and use the results to improve preventive maintenance scheduling across NYCHA.
Apply pest control methods more consistently and improve their quality so pest populations at developments actually fall.
Standardize across developments the way residents are told about second attempts to enter their apartments for annual inspections.
Sustain the workforce accountability work already under way, including managerial and nonmanagerial performance evaluations, revised job descriptions and better onboarding.
audits.agency_response: NYCHA is trying to recover the boiler replacement delays by adding construction shifts and resequencing work. It has responded positively to the monitors' inspection feedback, including adding training on inspection protocols to daily maintenance worker meetings, and has used a new missed appointments dashboard to cut missed skilled trades appointments from 7% in January 2025 to 4% in July 2025.
audits.compliance_note: The monitors say NYCHA has continued to build on the progress in their last report and should be commended, while mold, heat and pest management still require sustained focus. Under Paragraph 28 of the agreement, NYCHA does not yet meet the criteria for ending the monitorship.

audits.title: DOI Investigation into DOC Correction Intelligence Bureau Investigator Assisting Federal Agents with Immigration Enforcement
audits.plain_title: Jail investigator broke sanctuary laws by helping ICE
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) investigated allegations that Department of Correction (DOC) officers on a joint federal task force helped Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents arrest a person in custody, and examined DOC's guidance and training on the city's sanctuary laws.
audits.background: New York City local laws and mayoral executive orders, referred to as "Sanctuary City" laws, limit when local officials can share information with immigration authorities about non-citizens for civil immigration enforcement. DOC policy likewise prohibits employees from using city resources to assist federal civil immigration enforcement.

findings.plain: A DOC Correction Intelligence Bureau investigator assigned to the Homeland Security Investigations Violent Gang Task Force assisted immigration authorities in the February 2025 apprehension of a person released from Rikers Island, in violation of the city's sanctuary laws and DOC policy.
findings.quote:
did in fact assist immigration authorities in 
the apprehension of Concepcion, as alleged by the complainant, in violation of New York City’s Sanctuary 
City l aws and DOC policy.

findings.plain: DOI uncovered a second incident in which the same investigator gave federal immigration authorities information about another person in custody, including a screenshot with his booking photo, criminal charges and next court date, also in violation of city law and DOC policy.
findings.quote:
CIB Investigator A 
provided information to federal immigration authorities about another PIC, Pedro Mujica Villa Nueva, in 
furtherance of immigration enforcement

findings.plain: In the arrest case, immigration authorities presented neither a civil immigration detainer nor a judicial warrant, and the man's conviction for third-degree assault did not meet the "violent or serious crime" definition that could have permitted assistance.
findings.quote:
Immigration authorities did not present either a civil 
immigration detainer or a judicial warrant

findings.plain: In both instances the investigator did not understand that the help he provided furthered civil immigration enforcement rather than a criminal investigation, a failure DOI traced to a lack of training and guidance by DOC.
findings.quote:
CIB Investigator A’s failure to inquire further 
with respect to the purpose of the assistance that HSI asked that he provide was the result of a lack of 
training and guidance by DOC.

findings.plain: DOC provided no training to officers or staff on the sanctuary laws or its own related policy, and had issued no other guidance on interacting with law enforcement agencies involved in immigration enforcement before DOI raised the issue.
findings.quote:
DOC does not provide any training to its officers or staff about NYC “Sanctuary City” laws or DOC’s 
policy issued pursuant to those laws.

findings.plain: The two immigration enforcement assistance requests were not reported to the Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs or posted on the department's website as city law requires.
findings.quote:
not reported to the Mayor’s Office of Immigrant Affairs or posted on the Department’s website, as 
required by City Law.

numbers.label: Policy and procedure recommendations issued to DOC
Persons in custody whose information was improperly shared

recommendations: Provide updated guidance to DOC employees on the city's immigration enforcement laws and DOC policy, including in-person training and memorandums with DOC-specific scenarios.

Give staff specific guidance on responding to requests from law enforcement partners, including follow-up questions about the request's purpose and when to seek supervisory or general counsel approval.
Instruct all DOC staff to direct any immigration-related requests from other law enforcement authorities to the ICE Unit and the general counsel's office.
Amend Operations Order 9/19 to require the ICE Unit to regularly ask other DOC units whether they have received immigration enforcement-related requests and to require a written response.

Have senior DOC officials confer with senior officials at partner federal agencies to remind them that DOC staff are bound by city law and cannot assist civil immigration enforcement except in very limited circumstances.
Conduct a department-wide audit to determine whether there were other instances where the department, intentionally or not, assisted in immigration enforcement.
Report any previously unknown or unreported immigration enforcement-related requests to the Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs as the administrative code requires.
audits.agency_response: DOC accepted four recommendations, partially accepted two and is considering one. It has already conducted in-person training for intelligence and investigative staff, issued a department-wide teletype directing referral of immigration requests to its ICE Unit and legal division, and said a full agency-wide audit is impractical but targeted reviews will be considered.

audits.title: A Compilation of Audits of Agencies’ Oversight of Prime Vendors’ Use of Subcontractors on Health and Human Services Contracts
audits.plain_title: Five agencies share the same subcontractor oversight gaps
audits.agency: New York City Administration for Children's Services, Department for the Aging, Department of Health and Mental Hygiene and Department of Social Services
audits.what_they_audited: This is an overview report compiling a series of audits of how five health and human services agencies, the Administration for Children's Services (ACS), the Department of Homeless Services (DHS), the Human Resources Administration (HRA), the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH) and the Department for the Aging (NYC Aging), oversee the subcontractors their prime vendors hire.
audits.background: City health and human services agencies deliver services like foster care, homeless shelters and senior centers through contracts with providers called prime vendors, which sometimes hire subcontractors of their own. Because the city has no direct contract with subcontractors, oversight depends on agencies watching their prime vendors, and the comptroller's office launched this audit series in August 2023 after watchdog reports found a history of unapproved and unvetted subcontractors.

findings.plain: Four oversight deficiencies showed up at all five agencies, including failures to record subcontractors and their payments in city systems and to ensure timely payment, indicating the problems are systemic rather than unique to any one agency.
findings.quote: several deficiencies were found in multiple agencies, including four that were found at all five agencies, indicating that these issues were systemic in nature

findings.plain: At four agencies, prime vendors paid more than $8.6 million to 25 subcontractors that were never authorized to work on those contracts, including two used on contracts where the primes reported using no subcontractors at all.
findings.quote: subcontractors received more than $8.6 million in payments from prime contractors on contracts for which they did not obtain authorization to perform any work

findings.plain: Four agencies could not consistently show that subcontractors were vetted and background checked. Across the sampled contracts, 24 of 63 subcontractors, paid a combined $13.2 million, lacked evidence of vetting.
findings.quote: the auditors did not find sufficient evidence to indicate that vetting and background checks were consistently conducted on subcontractors by four of the agencies

findings.plain: Agencies did not make sure prime vendors got competitive bids. About half of the sampled subcontracts requiring written estimates lacked evidence of them, and the Human Resources Administration had no bid evidence for any of its 11 sampled subcontracts.
findings.quote: HRA had no evidence that bids were obtained for any of the 11 sampled subcontractors requiring them.

findings.plain: No agency ensured subcontractors were recorded and approved in the city's Payee Information Portal (PIP) on time. The Human Resources Administration had the worst delays, approving all of its sampled subcontractors at least 583 days after work started.
findings.quote: none of the five agencies ensured that all of the subcontractors on the sampled contracts were recorded and approved in PIP in a timely manner, if at all

findings.plain: Agencies do not monitor whether prime vendors pay subcontractors on time, and the Department for the Aging reimbursed primes $381,700 for subcontractor expenses the primes had never actually paid, surfacing only because caterers complained about nonpayment.
findings.quote: auditors found that NYC Aging paid primes $381,700 for subcontractor expenses that had not actually been paid

findings.plain: Of the $3.6 million paid to for-profit subcontractors on sampled contracts, only 4.7% went to certified Minority and Women-Owned Business Enterprises (M/WBEs), just four of the 22 for-profit firms used.
findings.quote: Payments made to these M/WBEs from FY2022 through FY2024 totaled $168,564—4.7% of the $3.6 million total paid to the for-profit subcontractors

numbers.label: Paid to unauthorized subcontractors across four agencies
Sampled subcontracts lacking required bid estimates
Shortest approval delay among HRA's sampled subcontracts
Aging agency reimbursements for costs primes never paid
For-profit subcontractor spending that went to M/WBEs

recommendations: Agencies should prevent payments to unapproved subcontractors by carefully reviewing prime vendors' invoices, periodically reviewing their general ledgers and requesting and reviewing subcontractors' agreements and invoices.
Agencies should make sure prime vendors submit subcontractor information, including agreements and payment details, in the PASSPort procurement system.
Agencies should document the process of vetting and running background checks on proposed subcontractors.
Agencies should make sure prime vendors use competitive bidding when selecting subcontractors.
Agencies should review subcontract agreements for prompt payment terms and make sure prime contractors pay subcontractors accordingly.
Agencies should make sure subcontractor costs were actually paid by prime vendors before reimbursing them, a recommendation that applied only to the Department for the Aging.
Agencies should implement the Department of Investigation's 2021 recommendations and comply with the Mayor's Office of Contract Services policies guiding their implementation.
Agencies should consider using more Minority and Women-Owned Business Enterprise contractors and encourage prime vendors to use more M/WBE subcontractors.
audits.agency_response: Responses varied by agency and recommendation: the Department for the Aging and DOHMH agreed with most recommendations, the Department of Social Services disagreed with several, ACS disagreed with reviewing general ledgers and did not address prompt payment, and DOHMH called two recommendations unnecessary.
audits.implementation_note: Of the seven 2021 Department of Investigation recommendations on subcontractor oversight directed at agencies, the audits found DOHMH had implemented all seven while the Department for the Aging had implemented one, with the other agencies in between.

audits.title: Audit Report on Department for the Aging’s Oversight of Prime Vendors’ Use of Subcontractors on Health and Human Services Contracts
audits.plain_title: Weak oversight of subcontractors on senior services contracts
audits.agency: New York City Department for the Aging
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Department for the Aging (NYC Aging) properly oversees the subcontractors its prime contractors hire on health and human services contracts, such as caterers serving meals at senior centers, to reduce the risk of fraud, misuse and waste of city funds.
audits.background: NYC Aging contracts with nonprofit and for-profit providers, called prime vendors, that sometimes hire subcontractors to deliver services like meals for older adults. Because the city has no direct contract with subcontractors, it relies on agencies to make sure primes get approval before hiring them, and this audit is one of a series covering five health and human services agencies prompted by a 2021 Department of Investigation report on corruption vulnerabilities in nonprofit human services contracts.

findings.plain: Prime vendors paid $2,251,857 to six subcontractors that NYC Aging never approved during fiscal years 2022 through 2024, and the agency has no way to independently confirm which subcontractors its vendors are using.
findings.quote: unapproved subcontractors received more than $2.2 million in payments from prime contractors

findings.plain: Even for approved subcontractors, auditors found no proof the agency vetted them. NYC Aging supplied a spreadsheet checklist of claimed background checks but no supporting evidence, and it did not enforce competitive bidding, with no bids on file for two of the four subcontracts that required them.
findings.quote: the auditors did not find any evidence, such as documents, to indicate that vetting and background checks were conducted by NYC Aging

findings.plain: Subcontractors were not consistently recorded in the Payee Information Portal (PIP), the city system meant to track them. For sampled subcontracts, approval in the system came 29 to 215 days after the subcontract's start date.
findings.quote: delays in approval ranged from 29 to 215 days after the subcontract start date

findings.plain: The agency has no mechanism to make sure subcontractors get paid on time. For one sampled contract, 47 of 53 invoices from a meals subcontractor were paid more than 30 days after the invoice date, with delays running as long as 580 days past the 30-day target.
findings.quote: 47 (89%) of the invoices were paid more than 30 days after the subcontractor’s invoice date

findings.plain: NYC Aging paid primes almost $400,000 to reimburse subcontractor expenses that the primes had never actually paid. Two caterers complained of nonpayment, and one prime vendor still owes a caterer $224,790 for meals delivered to homebound seniors.
findings.quote: the audit found that NYC Aging paid primes almost $400,000 for subcontractor expenses that had not actually been paid

findings.plain: Six of the seven recommendations the Department of Investigation (DOI) made in 2021 about agency oversight of subcontractors have not been implemented, with the agency saying it is waiting for guidance from the Mayor's Office of Contract Services (MOCS).
findings.quote: NYC Aging has not implemented six of the seven agency-directed recommendations related to oversight of subcontractors

findings.plain: Only 4.9 percent of the $2.3 million paid to for-profit subcontractors on sampled contracts went to Minority and Women-Owned Business Enterprises (M/WBEs), just one of the nine for-profit subcontractors was certified, and missing records made a broader analysis impossible.
findings.quote: Payments made to the M/WBE from FY2023 through FY2024 totaled $113,819—4.9% of the total $2.3 million paid to the nine for-profit subcontractors

numbers.label: Paid to unapproved subcontractors, fiscal 2022-2024
Paid to primes for subcontractor bills not actually paid
Still owed to a caterer feeding homebound seniors
Longest delay approving a subcontractor in city systems
Share of for-profit subcontractor spending going to M/WBEs

recommendations: Prevent payments to unapproved subcontractors by carefully reviewing invoices from prime vendors, periodically reviewing their general ledgers and requesting and reviewing subcontractors' agreements and invoices.
Make sure prime vendors submit subcontractor information, including subcontract agreements and payment information, in PASSPort as required.
Document the process of vetting proposed subcontractors and running background checks.
Make sure prime vendors use competitive bidding when selecting subcontractors.
Review subcontract agreements for prompt payment terms and make sure prime contractors pay their subcontractors according to those terms.
Make sure costs for subcontractor goods and services were actually incurred by prime vendors before the city reimburses them.
Implement DOI's 2021 recommendations to city agencies and comply with the policies and directives MOCS and the Mayor's Office of Risk Management and Compliance created to guide that work.
Consider increasing use of M/WBE contractors and encourage prime vendors to increase their use of M/WBE subcontractors.
audits.agency_response: NYC Aging did not submit a written response to the draft report or its recommendations, saying on June 13, 2025 that it had no response to the report.

audits.title: Audit Report on the Department of Social Services’ Oversight of Prime Vendors’ Use of Subcontractors on Health and Human Services Contracts
audits.plain_title: Poor tracking of subcontractors on social services contracts
audits.agency: New York City Department of Social Services
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Department of Social Services (DSS), which oversees the Human Resources Administration (HRA) and the Department of Homeless Services (DHS), properly oversees the subcontractors its prime contractors hire on health and human services contracts, to reduce the risk of fraud, misuse and waste of city funds.
audits.background: DSS is the umbrella agency for HRA, which serves over three million low-income New Yorkers through public benefit programs, and DHS, which runs the shelter system. Prime vendors on these contracts sometimes hire subcontractors, and this audit is one of a series covering five health and human services agencies prompted by a 2021 Department of Investigation report on corruption vulnerabilities in nonprofit human services contracts.

findings.plain: Neither HRA nor DHS made sure prime vendors recorded their subcontractors in the Payee Information Portal (PIP) on time. Recording delays ran 67 to 471 days for HRA and 34 to 305 days for DHS, and many approvals were still pending as of August 2024, with the approvals that did happen taking as long as 583 days.
findings.quote: For HRA, delays in the recording of the subcontractors in PIP from the sub-agreement start date ranged from 67 to 471 days.

findings.plain: Payments to subcontractors mostly went unrecorded in city systems. For sampled HRA contracts, only $1.4 million of $9.8 million in subcontractor payments showed up in HHS Accelerator, and DHS primes failed to record $2.4 million in payments in any system.
findings.quote: just $1.4 million of $9.8 million in total payments made to subcontractors were reported in HHS Accelerator (no payments were recorded in PIP)

findings.plain: Neither agency makes sure subcontractors get paid on time. On sampled DHS contracts, 63 of 327 invoices were paid late, and on sampled HRA contracts, 41 of 101 invoices totaling $2.4 million were paid 33 to 165 days after the invoice date.
findings.quote: 41 of the 101 sampled invoices—in total, $2.4 million of approximately $8 million—were paid late

findings.plain: On HRA contracts, prime vendors paid $1,683,863 to six subcontractors the agency never approved, including organizations providing housing and educational support to asylum seekers. DSS argued these were 'vendors' rather than subcontractors, but the auditors found they clearly met the city's definition of subcontractors.
findings.quote: the prime vendors paid $1,683,863 to unapproved subcontractors without HRA’s knowledge

findings.plain: HRA could not always show it vetted approved subcontractors, some approval forms were filled out incorrectly and no competitive bids were on file for any of the 11 subcontracts that required them.
findings.quote: The auditors found no evidence of bids for any of the 11 subcontracts, as the prime contractors did not submit them.

findings.plain: Three of the seven recommendations the Department of Investigation (DOI) made in 2021 about agency oversight of subcontractors had not been implemented by either agency, with the Mayor's Office of Contract Services (MOCS) saying citywide policies are still being developed.
findings.quote: three of the seven agency-directed recommendations have not been implemented

findings.plain: On sampled DHS contracts, Minority and Women-Owned Business Enterprises (M/WBEs) got $22,245, or 4.32 percent, of the $514,404 paid to for-profit subcontractors, while the sampled HRA contracts used no for-profit subcontractors at all, and incomplete records made a broader analysis impossible.
findings.quote: Payments made to these M/WBEs during the three-year period totaled $22,245, accounting for 4.32% of the $514,404 amount paid to all four for-profit subcontractors

numbers.label: Paid to unapproved subcontractors on HRA contracts
Subcontractor payments on sampled HRA contracts
DHS subcontractor payments not recorded in any system
Longest delay recording an HRA subcontractor in PIP
Share of DHS for-profit subcontractor spending to M/WBEs

recommendations: Prevent payments to unapproved subcontractors by carefully reviewing invoices submitted by primes, periodically reviewing prime vendors' general ledgers and requesting and reviewing subcontractors' agreements and invoices.
Make sure prime vendors submit subcontractor information, including subcontract agreements and payment information, in PASSPort as required.
Document the process of vetting proposed subcontractors and running background checks.
Make sure prime vendors use competitive bidding when selecting subcontractors.
Review subcontract agreements for prompt payment terms and make sure prime contractors pay their subcontractors according to those terms.
Implement DOI's 2021 recommendations to city agencies and comply with the policies and directives MOCS and the Mayor's Office of Risk Management and Compliance created to guide that work.
Continue to increase use of M/WBE contractors and encourage prime vendors to increase their use of M/WBE subcontractors in human services contracts.
audits.agency_response: DSS partially agreed with two recommendations and disagreed with five, arguing among other things that it follows existing city invoice review policy and that the unapproved organizations were vendors rather than subcontractors. The auditors urged DSS to reconsider and implement the recommendations.

audits.title: The Administration for Children’s Services’ Oversight of Prime Vendors’ Use of Subcontractors on Health and Human Services Contracts
audits.plain_title: Weak oversight of subcontractors on children's services contracts
audits.agency: New York City Administration for Children's Services
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Administration for Children's Services (ACS) properly oversees the subcontractors that its prime vendors hire on health and human services contracts, which cover services like foster care, juvenile justice and early education. Auditors examined a sample of four contracts held by three prime vendors over fiscal years 2022 through 2024.
audits.background: ACS contracts with non-profit and for-profit providers called prime vendors, which sometimes hire subcontractors of their own, for example to run group homes for foster children outside the city. Because the city has no direct contract with subcontractors, it relies on agencies like ACS to make sure prime vendors pick competent subcontractors and manage the risks, and this audit is one of a series covering five health and human services agencies.

findings.plain: Prime vendors paid more than $1.8 million to subcontractors that ACS had never approved to work on the sampled contracts, in some cases without the agency's knowledge.
findings.quote: unauthorized subcontractors were paid over $1.8 million during the audit scope period of Fiscal Years 2022 through 2024

findings.plain: Although ACS policy requires vetting and background checks for subcontracts worth $20,000 or more, auditors found no documents showing that this vetting actually happened for the sampled contracts.
findings.quote: the auditors did not find evidence that this was conducted for the sampled contracts

findings.plain: ACS did not make sure subcontractors were entered and approved in the city's Payee Information Portal (PIP) on time. For two sampled subcontracts, approval came 76 to 204 days after the subcontractor had already started work.
findings.quote: delays in approval ranged from 76 to 204 days after the subcontract start date

findings.plain: None of the sampled prime vendors reported their payments to subcontractors in the Payee Information Portal as required, which made it impossible for auditors to fully analyze how subcontractors were used.
findings.quote: the audit found that none of the sampled prime vendors did this

findings.plain: ACS has no way to make sure subcontractors get paid on time. Of 13 sampled payments to subcontractors, seven were made more than 30 days after the invoice, and one subcontractor was paid as late as 216 days after invoicing.
findings.quote: A review of 13 payments to subcontractors on the sampled contracts found that seven (56%) were paid more than 30 days after receipt of invoices

findings.plain: ACS has not implemented four of the seven 2021 Department of Investigation recommendations aimed at strengthening agency oversight of subcontractors on city contracts.
findings.quote: The auditors found that ACS has not implemented four of the seven recommendations.

findings.plain: Neither of the two for-profit subcontractors used on the sampled contracts was a certified Minority and Women-owned Business Enterprise (M/WBE), and poor recordkeeping made it impossible to measure M/WBE use across all of the agency's human services contracts.
findings.quote: none of the monies spent on sampled contracts’ for-profit subcontractors went to Minority and Women-Owned Business Enterprises

numbers.label: Paid to unapproved subcontractors, fiscal years 2022-2024
Longest delay approving a subcontractor in the city portal
Sampled subcontractor payments made late
Total paid to seven subcontractors on sampled contracts

recommendations: Prevent payments to unapproved subcontractors by periodically reviewing prime vendors' general ledgers along with subcontract agreements and invoices.
Make sure prime vendors submit subcontractor information, including agreements and payment details, in the PASSPort procurement system.
Document the process of vetting and running background checks on proposed subcontractors.
Review subcontract agreements for prompt payment terms and make sure prime vendors pay their subcontractors promptly.

Implement the Department of Investigation's 2021 recommendations to city agencies and comply with related policies from the Mayor's Office of Contract Services and the Mayor's Office of Risk Management and Compliance.
Consider using more Minority and Women-owned Business Enterprise contractors and encourage prime vendors to do the same with their subcontractors.
audits.agency_response: ACS agreed with four recommendations, disagreed with the recommendation to review prime vendors' general ledgers, arguing it never paid unapproved subcontractors, and did not clearly address the recommendation on prompt payment.
audits.implementation_note: Of the seven 2021 Department of Investigation recommendations on subcontractor oversight that applied to agencies, the audit found ACS had not implemented four.

audits.title: The Department of Health and Mental Hygiene’s Oversight of Prime Vendors’ Use of Subcontractors on Health and Human Services Contracts
audits.plain_title: Weak tracking of subcontractors on health department contracts
audits.agency: New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH) properly oversees the subcontractors that its prime vendors hire on health and human services contracts, such as running programs at neighborhood clinics. Auditors examined sampled contracts covering fiscal years 2022 through 2024.
audits.background: DOHMH contracts with non-profit and for-profit providers called prime vendors, which sometimes hire subcontractors of their own, and since the city has no direct contract with subcontractors it relies on agencies to oversee how primes use them. This audit is one of a series covering five health and human services agencies, launched after watchdog reports found weak oversight of subcontracting on city contracts.

findings.plain: Prime vendors paid about $2.9 million to eight subcontractors that were not approved to work on the sampled contracts. DOHMH said the vendors had been approved, but under the wrong contract numbers.
findings.quote: subcontractors not approved to work on the sampled contracts received about $2.9 million in payments from prime contractors

findings.plain: DOHMH could not fully show it vetted subcontractors. Auditors found insufficient evidence of vetting for two of eight sampled subcontractors that required it, an outdated background questionnaire for one large subcontract and incomplete approval forms for six of 21 subcontracts.
findings.quote: the auditors did not find sufficient evidence for two of the eight sampled subcontractors that DOHMH did this

findings.plain: The agency did not make sure prime vendors got competitive bids. For three of the 13 sampled subcontractors that required a bidding process, there was no evidence three written estimates were obtained.
findings.quote: The auditors found no evidence that three bids were obtained for three of the 13 sampled subcontractors that required a bidding process.

findings.plain: Subcontractors were entered and approved in the city's Payee Information Portal (PIP) far too late. For 19 of 21 sampled subcontractors, recording came 35 to 574 days after work started, and DOHMH's approval came as much as 706 days, almost two years, after the start date.
findings.quote: the vendors recorded the subcontracts in PIP ranging from 35 to 574 days after the subcontract’s start date

findings.plain: Payments to subcontractors were barely recorded in the city system. Prime vendors' ledgers showed $3,691,056 paid to 16 subcontractors, but only about 1% of that was recorded in the Payee Information Portal.
findings.quote: only $35,628 (1%) of these payments were recorded in PIP

findings.plain: DOHMH does not make sure subcontractors get paid on time and has no agencywide process for handling their complaints. Of 18 sampled invoices, 17 were paid 32 to 214 days late, and doulas in a city childbirth support program complained of waiting months for payment.
findings.quote: The auditors found 17 of the 18 invoices were paid late.

findings.plain: Only 5.1% of the money paid to for-profit subcontractors on the sampled contracts, $32,500 of $634,114, went to a certified Minority and Women-owned Business Enterprise (M/WBE).
findings.quote: only 5.1% of the monies spent on sampled contracts’ for-profit subcontractors went to Minority and Women-Owned Business Enterprises

numbers.label: Paid to subcontractors not approved on sampled contracts
Longest delay approving a subcontractor in the city portal
Share of subcontractor payments recorded in the city system
Sampled subcontractor invoices paid late
For-profit subcontractor spending that went to M/WBEs

recommendations: Make sure payments for subcontracting expenses go only to vendors DOHMH has approved as subcontractors on those specific contracts.

Prevent payments to unapproved subcontractors by carefully reviewing invoices submitted by prime vendors and continue periodically reviewing prime vendors' general ledgers, subcontract agreements and invoices.
Make sure prime vendors submit subcontractor information, including agreements and payment details, in the PASSPort procurement system.
Make all reasonable efforts to ensure the city's Financial Management System accurately reflects subcontractor approvals and industry classifications.
Document the process of vetting and running background checks on proposed subcontractors.
Make sure prime vendors use competitive bidding when selecting subcontractors.
Review subcontract agreements and make sure prime contractors pay their subcontractors promptly.
Consider using more Minority and Women-owned Business Enterprise contractors and continue encouraging prime vendors to use more M/WBE subcontractors.
audits.agency_response: DOHMH agreed with six recommendations and called the other two unnecessary, saying it already documents subcontractor reviews and already prioritizes Minority and Women-owned Business Enterprise vendors. Auditors urged the agency to implement both anyway.
audits.implementation_note: Of the seven 2021 Department of Investigation recommendations on subcontractor oversight directed at agencies, the audit found DOHMH had implemented all seven.

audits.title: DOI Investigation into Theft Involving Pension Funds Managed by the NYC Employees' Retirement System (NYCERS) and Related Recommendations
audits.plain_title: How a pension examiner stole $624,000 from retirees' accounts
audits.agency: New York City Employees' Retirement System
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) examined internal control failures at the New York City Employees' Retirement System (NYCERS) after a criminal investigation found a NYCERS benefits examiner stole about $624,000 from two pensioners' accounts.
audits.background: NYCERS, established in 1920, is the largest municipal public employee retirement system in the United States, with more than 430,000 active members and retirees. It suspends pension payments when checks are returned or a pensioner does not confirm they are still alive, then reactivates accounts and pays retroactive benefits.

findings.plain: Between February 2021 and January 2024, Gregory Mathieu, an Associate Retirement Benefits Examiner in the unit that verifies whether pensioners are alive, used forged electronic fund transfer (EFT) authorizations, manipulated member profiles and unauthorized account reactivations to divert about $624,000 from two retirees' accounts.
findings.quote:
exploited internal control 
weaknesses to fraudulently divert approximately $624,000 in pension funds from two retirees' 
accounts.

findings.plain: The case revealed critical vulnerabilities in NYCERS' internal controls, particularly in segregation of duties, system access controls and verification procedures.
findings.quote:
This case revealed critical vulnerabilities in NYCERS ’ internal controls, particularly 
regarding segregation of duties, system access controls, and verification procedures.

findings.plain: A $99,999.99 payment on one victim's account was returned several times, a potential fraud risk factor, but NYCERS did not flag the account or give it extra scrutiny.
findings.quote: NYCERS did not flag the account or otherwise subject it to additional scrutiny.

findings.plain: NYCERS protocols did not require bank account verification for EFT forms received by mail, and the payroll unit processed Mathieu's fraudulent request without independent checks. The same bank account used for two unrelated pensioners should have been a warning sign.
findings.quote: NYCERS protocols also do not require account verifications for EFTs received by mai l.

findings.plain: NYCERS did not keep an audit trail of account access that would have shown when Mathieu got into pension systems, and it failed to notify DOI when one victim reported in person that he had not authorized banking changes.
findings.quote:
NYCERS did not maintain an audit 
trail of account access that would have shown when Mathieu accessed various NYCERS systems

findings.plain: In separate investigations, DOI and NYCERS found rising attempted fraud through account takeovers and fraudulent loan requests on the MyNYCERS online platform, worsened by pandemic-era disruptions; more than half of members have not re-registered on the platform.
findings.quote:
more than half of NYCERS 
members have not re-registered on the MyNYCERS platform.

numbers.label: Stolen from two pensioners' accounts
Restitution the former employee agreed to pay
Recovered by NYCERS from the defendant's account
Active NYCERS members and retirees
Recommendations DOI made to strengthen controls

recommendations: Improve internal controls with regular review of reactivated suspended accounts, especially those paying $3,000 or more a month, periodic audits of retroactive payments and returned-payment patterns and regular assessment of access controls.
Periodically review all accounts suspended for three years to determine whether members are still alive, including contacting family and checking obituaries and probate court records.
Expand bank account verification to cover electronic fund transfer requests received by mail.
Provide enhanced training for NYCERS employees, including regular ethics training stressing personal responsibility in fraud prevention.
Develop internal fraud algorithms that alert staff to duplicate bank accounts or shared contact information across profiles and to transfer requests going to high-risk banks tied to past fraud.
Maintain electronic audit logs of all account access and changes, including who made them.
Require two-factor authentication when members contact NYCERS to change account information.
Notify members by email or text immediately when someone logs into their account, with device, browser and location details.
Monitor IP addresses and review or block logins from geographic regions inconsistent with prior use.
Replace mail, email and fax submission of sensitive documents with a secure upload portal using two-factor authentication and time-locked session links.
Require identity confirmation by the relevant United States consulate plus a NYCERS video interview for reactivation requests from members living overseas.
audits.agency_response: NYCERS cooperated with the investigation and has already made reforms, including two-tier approval for account reactivations, restricted access to suspended account data and the mailroom, in-person or video confirmation for reactivations, a new anti-fraud policy and an anonymous whistleblower hotline.

audits.title: Review of the Department of Sanitation’s Commercial Waste Zone Request for Proposals and Carter Selection Process
audits.plain_title: How sanitation picked carters for commercial waste zones
audits.agency: New York City Department of Sanitation
audits.what_they_audited: This is a review rather than a full audit. It examined whether the Department of Sanitation's (DSNY) request for proposals and selection of private carting companies for the Commercial Waste Zone program complied with Local Law 199 of 2019, and looked at the safety, labor and violation histories of the carters that were chosen.
audits.background: More than 90 private carting companies collect the city's commercial waste, an industry DSNY describes as disorganized and hazardous, with private garbage trucks involved in at least 43 fatalities between January 2010 and May 2019. Local Law 199 of 2019 divided the city into 20 commercial waste zones with up to three carters each, and DSNY announced 18 winning carters in January 2024, though as of January 2025 only one zone had been implemented.

findings.plain: On the basic legal requirements, DSNY complied: its request for proposals incorporated the 13 evaluation factors in Local Law 199, no zone got more than three carters, no carter got more than 15 zones, scoring was calculated accurately and evaluators justified their scores.
findings.quote: DSNY’s RFP and carter selection processes were designed to meet the requirements of LL199

findings.plain: The carters with the worst traffic and safety records fared well in selection. Eight of the 10 carters with the most violations were chosen, selected carters averaged 241 violations each over four years versus 73 for those not selected, and auditors found no evidence violation history significantly affected suitability.
findings.quote: An analysis of the 10 carters that amassed the most violations during the period reviewed by DSNY revealed that eight of them were selected for the CWZ program.

findings.plain: DSNY awarded four zones to Cogent Waste Solutions, which holds the record for the largest payout of fines to the Business Integrity Commission, $500,000, after being charged with nearly 5,000 violation counts including overcharging customers. DSNY has since assigned an independent monitor to Cogent and a related company.
findings.quote: had the highest-ever recorded payout of $500,000 in fines for violations issued by BIC in January 2023

findings.plain: Twelve of the 15 carters proposed as subcontractors had safety violations, totaling 1,490 from February 2018 through July 2022, and three subcontractors accounted for nearly 70% of them.
findings.quote: a total of 1,490 violations were issued to the 15 subcontractors

findings.plain: Several selected carters also had labor problems and lawsuits: five awarded carters had 14 labor violations, and 12 of the 18 awarded carters faced 200 civil complaints from 2018 to 2022, mostly over vehicle accidents and injuries.
findings.quote: 12 carters faced a total of 200 civil complaints from 2018 to 2022

findings.plain: Maximum prices businesses can be charged vary widely within the same zone with no explanation in the proposals. In the Staten Island zone the highest maximum monthly rate was 145% above the lowest, which conflicts with the law's goal of fair and transparent pricing.
findings.quote: In the Staten Island zone, the maximum price listed by one carter was more than double the price listed by another carter within that zone.

findings.plain: The program's work is concentrated and rankings did not decide awards: four carters filled more than 70% of zone assignments, pricing carried the heaviest weight at 40 of 100 points, and the highest ranked carter won the zone in only three of 20 cases.
findings.quote: Of the 20 zones, the highest ranked carters were selected for only three zones.

numbers.label: Safety violations for Action Carting, awarded 14 zones
Cogent's record fine payout to the integrity commission
Safety violations issued to 15 proposed subcontractors
Gap between highest and lowest max rate in Staten Island
Share of zone assignments filled by just four carters

recommendations: Track indicators like vehicle miles traveled, safety violations, complaints and vehicle inspections to gauge whether the law's purposes are being met, and publish them quarterly in the Mayor's Management Report.
Investigate why prices charged by carters differ so widely within certain zones and whether the differences keep businesses from getting carting services at a reasonable rate.
Closely monitor the performance of Cogent Waste Solutions and New York Recycling to ensure compliance with the Commercial Waste Zone agreement.
Make sure the independent monitor assigned to Cogent and New York Recycling submits its required investigation reports to DSNY.
audits.agency_response: DSNY agreed with the two suggestions about monitoring Cogent and New York Recycling, partially agreed with quarterly public tracking, saying the law's annual reporting already covers it, and disagreed with investigating price differences, saying the law does not require carters to charge the same prices.

audits.title: Status Report on Remedial Relief
audits.plain_title: Monitor's blueprint for the Rikers remediation manager's role
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: The court-appointed independent monitor's second report on remedial relief for the city's contempt in Nunez v. City of New York, laying out a framework for selecting and structuring the new remediation manager position, summarizing candidate vetting and compiling the parties' objections to the court's proposed remediation manager order.
audits.background: The court held the city in contempt of 18 provisions of the Nunez court orders in November 2024 and on May 13, 2025 ordered the appointment of a remediation manager to direct a phased action plan for the contempt areas while the commissioner retains responsibility for the hundreds of other provisions. The monitoring team facilitated months of negotiations over candidates and the governing order.

findings.plain: The monitor cautioned that a receiver or remediation manager is an extreme and rarely used remedy, and that evidence on whether solutions devised by other correctional receivers work and last is mixed, largely anecdotal and context specific.
findings.quote: ...sustainability of the solutions devised by other correctional receivers is mixed, largely anecdotal

findings.plain: The remediation manager's office must build the department's own capacity to meet the 18 contempt provisions rather than becoming another entrenched layer of bureaucracy on top of the obstacles that have long blocked reform.
findings.quote: the Office of the Remediation Manager itself must not become another entrenched

findings.plain: The court identified the key blockers of compliance as insufficiently resourced leadership, lack of continuity in management, failures of supervision, lack of skill or imagination to implement transformative plans and unwillingness to cooperate with the monitor; the monitoring team adds that staff deployment and staff competency must also be essential objectives.
findings.quote: ...deployment and staff competency must also be essential objectives for the Remediation

findings.plain: The monitoring team and the parties evaluated almost 30 confidential applications for the remediation manager position, and on August 29, 2025 the monitor submitted the parties' recommended candidates to the court confidentially.
findings.quote: evaluated almost 30 confidential applications for the Remediation

findings.plain: The monitor concluded the department remains in a state of flux, with urgent safety issues persisting against a backdrop of uncertainty that includes the pending motion for reconsideration, unresolved objections to the proposed order and the November 2025 city elections.
findings.quote: The Department of Correction remains in a state of flux.

numbers.label: Nunez court order provisions covered by the contempt finding
Confidential applications for the remediation manager position

recommendations: The remediation manager's team must consist of members with bona fide credentials in sound correctional practice and in stimulating the culture change needed for the department to improve practice and sustain progress.

The court should permit the monitoring team to file a submission on September 24, 2025 with the outcome of the parties' still-pending negotiations over an information-sharing provision of the proposed order.
audits.agency_response: The city's objections and proposed revisions to the court's draft remediation manager order are attached as an appendix, and the monitor reports that all parties participated fully and made good faith efforts to find areas of agreement.
audits.compliance_note: The monitor reports that urgent, time-sensitive issues tied to the jails' elevated risk of harm remain at the forefront while the department awaits the remediation manager appointment and other court decisions.

audits.title: Audit Report on the Department of Education’s Compliance with Regulations Regarding English Language Learners Audit
audits.plain_title: Schools shortchanged English language learners on required services
audits.agency: New York City Department of Education
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the New York City Department of Education followed state regulations and its own policies for identifying English language learner students, placing them in the right programs, providing required instruction and keeping records.
audits.background: State regulations require school districts, including New York City's, to give English language learner students equal access to all school programs and services. The department reported 174,014 English language learners in the 2023-24 school year, up 16.8% from 2021-22.

findings.plain: For nearly half of sampled English language learner students, the department did not provide required courses or the minimum minutes of instruction.
findings.quote: for 145 of 301 (48.2%) sampled ELL students, DOE did not provide required courses, or the minimum number of minutes of ENL, or bilingual instruction time

findings.plain: About 40% of sampled students were served by at least one teacher who lacked the certifications required for teaching English language learners.
findings.quote: 122 (40.5%) students were served by one or more teachers who did not have the required certifications

findings.plain: The department does not track whether teachers complete the professional development hours in language acquisition that state rules require, relying instead on teachers to self-report to the state.
findings.quote: DOE does not monitor whether educators meet the required CTLE hours or the percentage of CTLE hours devoted to language acquisition

findings.plain: Schools failed to keep the forms documenting parents' program choices for nearly a third of sampled students, and 34 students were placed, or may have been placed, in the wrong program.
findings.quote: DOE did not retain ELL Parent Survey and Program Agreement Forms or Default Program Placement Letters in students’ files for 110 of 349 (31.5%) sampled ELL students

findings.plain: Instead of creating required bilingual education programs, the department improperly requested waivers. Of 150 waiver requests for the 2024-25 school year, 146 exceeded the five-year limit, affecting 9,527 students in 17 districts.
findings.quote: Of those 150 waivers, 146 exceeded the five-year exemption limit.

findings.plain: Parents of many sampled students were not given information about program options at their child's school or elsewhere in the district, and the department does not centrally record or analyze parent survey responses.
findings.quote: DOE did not inform the parents/guardians of 101 (28.9%) sampled students about ELL program options

findings.plain: The department did not consistently complete the identification process for potential English language learners on time, including the home language survey, the state identification test and a required Spanish language assessment.
findings.quote: DOE did not administer the NYSITELL to 1,447 of the 43,266 (3.3%) eligible students

numbers.label: English language learners in the 2023-24 school year
Sampled students denied required courses or minutes
Sampled students taught by uncertified teachers
Waiver requests that exceeded the five-year limit
Students affected by improper waiver requests
Sampled students missing program choice records
Eligible students never given the Spanish assessment

recommendations: Finalize rules for a tracking and monitoring system for bilingual education and English as a new language programs to make sure students are adequately served.
Implement and further develop a system to monitor English as a new language units of study so students receive all required minutes from a certified teacher.
Continue recruiting qualified teachers for English language learner classes and encourage current staff to earn the needed certifications.
Develop a centralized system to track teachers' required professional development hours and designate a team to monitor compliance and provide periodic status reports.
Continue regular audits and inspections during school support visits to make sure critical paperwork is completed, kept in student records and entered accurately in the department's data system.
Improve oversight of waiver requests, evaluate recruitment efforts and expand bilingual programs in high-demand districts to reduce reliance on waivers.
Set standardized procedures so all schools give parents complete and accurate program information on the parent survey and agreement forms.
Establish a centralized process to collect, analyze and act on data from the parent survey and agreement forms across all schools.
Develop a centralized tracking system for waitlist and transfer requests and strengthen oversight so bilingual program preferences are honored promptly.
Implement a school-level monitoring system to make sure the identification process for English language learners is completed as required.
audits.agency_response: The Department of Education agreed with nine of the 10 recommendations and disagreed with one, on centrally tracking teachers' professional development hours, saying teachers certify their own compliance to the state.

audits.title: Final Audit Letter Report on the New York City Office of Collective Bargaining’s Responses to Requests
audits.plain_title: How the collective bargaining office handles workers' inquiries
audits.agency: New York City Office of Collective Bargaining
audits.what_they_audited: In this final audit letter report, auditors reviewed how the Office of Collective Bargaining receives, tracks and responds to questions and complaints from city workers about union representation, checking whether responses were timely and well documented from July 2022 through December 2024.
audits.background: The Office of Collective Bargaining was created in 1967 to handle issues related to public employees' union representation. It is intended to function as a neutral agency that resolves questions about union representation and adjudicates disputes over collective bargaining, retaliation and unions' duty of fair representation.

findings.plain: Before 2024 the office's tracking of responses was inadequate. Records showed only 54% of people who contacted the office got a follow-up from an agency attorney within the informal five business day target, and 38% had no record of any contact.
findings.quote: only 54% of individuals received a follow-up contact from an OCB attorney within the agency’s informal target of five business days, and 38% of people had no record of contact at all

findings.plain: The office also did not adequately track requests for Pro Se information packets, which go to city employees pursuing claims against their union or the city without a lawyer. Of 35 people who requested one before 2024, the log shows only 11 were sent one.
findings.quote: Of the 35 individuals who requested one, OCB’s Log indicates that only 11 individuals were sent one.

findings.plain: After the office switched its tracking log from Microsoft Access to Microsoft Excel in January 2024, recordkeeping and responsiveness improved markedly. All 94 inquiries logged in calendar year 2024 got an attorney response within five business days, most within one day.
findings.quote: all 94 inquiries received a response from an OCB attorney within the five-day target, including 84 (89%) who were contacted within one business day

findings.plain: The 2024 log also shows the office became more responsive on information packets: every caller who requested a Pro Se packet that year was sent one.
findings.quote: according to the Log, all 40 callers who requested a Pro Se packet were sent one

numbers.label: Share contacted within five business days before 2024
Share with no record of contact at all before 2024
Inquiries logged in calendar year 2024, all answered on time
Share of 2024 inquiries answered within one business day

recommendations: Document the office's procedures for responding to inquiries and complaints, including how calls and responses are recorded and a target timeframe for a response.
Continue to ensure that all inquiries and complaints get timely responses and that all relevant information is documented according to those procedures.
audits.agency_response: The Office of Collective Bargaining agreed with the audit's findings and both recommendations.

audits.title: DOI's Findings Regarding "Skimming" of Electronic Benefit Transfer Cards that Provide Vital Funds to Low-Income New Yorkers and Related Recommendations
audits.plain_title: Benefit card skimming cost the city $48.6 million in reimbursements
audits.agency: New York City Department of Social Services
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) examined the theft of Cash Assistance (CA) and Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits through "skimming" of Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) cards administered by the city Department of Social Services (DSS).
audits.background: About 1.8 million low-income families and individuals in New York City receive cash and food benefits through state-issued EBT cards. The cards use a magnetic stripe, which makes them vulnerable to skimming devices placed secretly on card readers, and DOI began looking into the problem in June 2022 after hundreds of client reports of drained accounts.

findings.plain: Between August 2023 and March 2025, the Department of Social Services issued $48.6 million in reimbursements for reported stolen SNAP and cash assistance benefits.
findings.quote:
Between August 2023 and March 2025, DSS issued a total of $48.6 million in 
reimbursements for reported stolen SNAP and CA benefits.

findings.plain: In that period DSS processed 142,178 SNAP reimbursement applications and approved 96,048, paying $43.7 million, plus 60,337 cash assistance applications with 27,176 approved and $4.9 million paid. The true loss is likely higher because those figures exclude unreported thefts.
findings.quote:
The actual loss to New Yorkers is likely much greater, 
because th ese figures do  not include unreported losses

findings.plain: Skimming devices capture card numbers, PINs and names and transfer the data remotely by Bluetooth, so thieves never return to the store and benefits can be drained almost immediately, making the fraud hard for law enforcement to trace.
findings.quote:
there is no need to return to the retail location to collect the skimmer, and there is little if any delay in using 
the data to steal clients’ benefits after capturing the data.

findings.plain: In a recent operation, DOI and law enforcement partners found about 55 skimming devices placed on point-of-sale terminals at local retailers.
findings.quote:
found approximately 55 skimming devices that had been 
placed on POS terminals at local retailers

findings.plain: Since December 2024, federal funding to reimburse stolen SNAP benefits is no longer available, leaving thousands of victims without a way to recover benefits stolen after that date.
findings.quote:
Since December 2024, federal funding for 
reimbursements for stolen SNAP funds is no longer available

findings.plain: DOI concluded the best prevention is replacing magnetic-stripe EBT cards with chip-enabled cards, which generate a unique encrypted code for each purchase. California began issuing chip cards in January 2025 and four New York State bills would mandate the change.
findings.quote:
the best way to prevent much of this fraud is to use chip-enabled EBT cards rather than the existing 
EBT cards with magnetic stripes.

numbers.label: Reimbursed for stolen benefits, August 2023 to March 2025
Low-income New Yorkers receiving these benefits
SNAP reimbursement applications processed
SNAP reimbursement applications approved
Skimming devices found in a recent operation

recommendations: New York should urgently install EMV chips in EBT cards to reduce skimming theft, by amending the social services law to require the state Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance (OTDA) to do so or by OTDA acting without legislation.

OTDA should work with the EBT card vendor to create an alert that notifies clients when an out-of-state or suspicious transaction is pending and requires them to authenticate it through the app or an automated call.
OTDA should work with the vendor on a real-time text alert when a client's PIN is changed, on by default with the option to opt out.
OTDA should create an alert triggered by repetitive transactions at common locations between midnight and 2 a.m. and promptly report it to law enforcement.
DSS should continue working with the United States Department of Agriculture and law enforcement to promptly remove and confiscate identified or suspected skimming devices.
DSS should continue its early skimming detection and analytics work and keep informing the public of risks and precautions, including through flyers and public seminars.
audits.agency_response: DSS partnered with DOI on the investigation and has taken steps to warn clients, including a website video, multilingual fact sheets and a joint seminar with the Kings County District Attorney's Office. DSS also submitted a memorandum supporting state chip-card legislation.

audits.title: DOI's 2024 Annual Anti-Corruption Report
audits.plain_title: Complicated city rules can create corruption risk
audits.agency: New York City agencies (citywide)
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) asked city agencies, through a questionnaire, whether their own regulatory and enforcement processes create openings for corruption. This annual report covers October 1, 2023, to September 30, 2024, and analyzes responses from 51 agencies.
audits.background: Mayoral Executive Order No. 105 makes the DOI commissioner the city's independent inspector general and requires DOI to prepare an annual anti-corruption report describing corruption risks agencies identify and how they plan to address them. Unlike DOI's other reports, this one is not the product of DOI's own investigative work but summarizes what agencies say about themselves, with individual responses aggregated or anonymized.

findings.plain: Of the 51 agencies that answered the questionnaire, 24 said they review applications for licenses, permits, certifications, grants or registrations, while only seven review applications for public benefits or services such as food stamps, childcare vouchers or cash assistance.
findings.quote:
Out of the 51 respondents, 24 (47.1%) reported they review applications for 
licenses, permits, certifications, grants, and/or registrations

findings.plain: Most agencies showed an understanding of the corruption risks in their own processes, but several agencies denied that any risk of corruption or fraud existed, which DOI said seems implausible given its experience.
findings.quote:
there were several agencies that denied any risk of corruption or fraud 
existed, a claim that seems implausible based on DOI’s experience.

findings.plain: In application and determination processes, agencies most often pointed to falsified or altered documents as the corruption risk. In compliance and enforcement, the risk cited most often was bribery of inspectors or other enforcement staff.
findings.quote:
With respect to 
application and determination processes, agencies overwhelmingly pointed to the 
submission of fraudulent documents or misrepresentation of information as the 
primary fraud and corruption risk.

findings.plain: About two-thirds of respondents said they conduct inspections, issue violations or take other steps to enforce regulations, and several rely on the city's 311 system or public complaints to learn about noncompliance rather than proactive monitoring.
findings.quote:
several 
agencies stated that they rely on the City’s 311 reporting system or public complaints 
to address allegations of noncompliance, while others reported engaging in proactive 
monitoring.

findings.plain: Only a third of responding agencies track complaints from the public about their programs, even though those complaints can reveal burdens or complexities that push people toward workarounds.
findings.quote:
Only 17 (33.3%) of the agencies that 
responded to the questionnaire answered in the affirmative.

findings.plain: Agencies described applications that are complicated because multiple agencies must sign off, there is no online submission option or the paperwork is heavy. At least two agencies said their process is so technical that applicants need a third-party expert to guide them.
findings.quote:
At least two agencies reported that the 
application process was so complicated and technical as to require the assistance of a 
third-party s ubject matter expert to guide the applicant through the process.

findings.plain: Sixteen agencies suggested reforms, including more staff, changes to burdensome or confusing rules and moving applications online. Agencies split evenly on whether more staffing would reduce corruption risk.

numbers.label: Agencies that answered DOI's questionnaire
Agencies reviewing license or permit applications
Agencies that inspect or enforce regulations
Agencies that track public complaints
Agencies that offered reform suggestions
Low end of reported application fees

recommendations: City agencies should stay alert to the corruption and fraud risks built into any municipal process, review those processes regularly and put risk mitigation measures in place.

Agencies should streamline application and determination processes where they can, while still collecting the information and approvals they need, so that applicants have less motive to work around a slow or burdensome process.
Agencies should evaluate the regulations they implement and enforce with corruption risk in mind, weighing that risk against how necessary the process is.

In designing regulatory, application and enforcement processes, agencies should make sure the rules are strong enough to do their job without imposing burdens so heavy that they raise the risk of fraud.
audits.agency_response: The report is built on the agencies' own questionnaire responses. Agencies described integrity controls already in place, including anti-corruption training, multi-level reviews and audits, and 16 agencies proposed reforms.

audits.title: Peer Review Final Report
audits.plain_title: Outside auditors gave the comptroller's audit bureau a pass rating
audits.agency: New York City Comptroller Bureau of Audit
audits.what_they_audited: This is a peer review letter rather than a standard comptroller audit: a team from the Association of Local Government Auditors examined the New York City Comptroller Bureau of Audit's internal quality control system for the period July 1, 2022 through June 30, 2025. The reviewers came from audit offices in Virginia Beach, Hanover County and Seattle.
audits.background: The reviewers followed the standards and guidelines in the Peer Review Guide published by the Association of Local Government Auditors and tested whether the bureau's internal quality control system provided reasonable assurance of compliance with Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States. Organizations can receive a rating of pass, pass with deficiencies or fail.

findings.plain: The bureau earned the top rating on the three-level scale of pass, pass with deficiencies or fail.
findings.quote: The NYC Comptroller Bureau of Audit has received a rating of pass.

findings.plain: The reviewers concluded the bureau's internal quality control system was well built and working as intended during the review period.
findings.quote: adequately designed and operating effectively to provide reasonable assurance of compliance with Government Auditing Standards

findings.plain: The reviewers singled out areas where the office excels, including organized and thorough work with a logical flow and well written reports.
findings.quote: Audit reports contain a succinct Executive Summary, are well written, detailed and contain well developed findings and value-added audit recommendations.

recommendations: The report makes no formal recommendations.
audits.agency_response: In a reply letter, Deputy Comptroller for Audit Maura Hayes-Chaffe thanked the peer review team, noting this was the office's first peer review in partnership with the Association of Local Government Auditors and calling it a very positive and effective process.

audits.title: Management of the Student-School Matching Algorithm
audits.plain_title: How well the city runs its high school admissions algorithm
audits.agency: New York City Public Schools
audits.what_they_audited: Whether New York City Public Schools adequately managed the admissions process and the computer algorithm that matches students to high schools. The audit covered selected high school admissions processes for school years 2018-19 through 2024-25.
audits.background: New York City Public Schools, the nation's largest school district, serves about 900,000 students at about 1,600 public schools. Students apply to high school through one application listing up to 12 programs, and a deferred acceptance matching algorithm assigns offers based on student choices, seat availability, admissions priorities and a randomly assigned lottery number.

findings.plain: For admissions into the 2023-24 school year there were 7,000 students in temporary housing, such as homeless students, and there is no assurance they got the admissions priority they were entitled to because the algorithm does not account for both a student's current and prior address as the Chancellor's Regulations require.
findings.quote: there is no assurance these students were appropriately prioritized in the matching algorithm because the algorithm does not account for both the current and prior address

findings.plain: The district may be missing low-income students who are supposed to get priority at certain programs. In a sample of 39 students, auditors found 31 who were likely low-income because they lived with another student who was, yet the district had not identified them as low-income.
findings.quote: It is likely more students are low-income but have not been identified.

findings.plain: In admissions for the 2023-24 school year, auditors found more than 200 instances where students who should have been manually placed in a school program either were not placed or were not placed appropriately under the district's own practices and business rules.
findings.quote: over 200 instances where students should have been manually placed in a school program but were either not manually placed or were not placed appropriately

findings.plain: Despite the complexity of the matching process, the district had no written policies guiding most of how the algorithm is run, which are needed to make sure it works as intended and that errors get caught and fixed.
findings.quote: for most of the algorithm processes, NYCPS had no written policies to guide implementation

findings.plain: The district did not publish legally required public reports on applications, offers and available seats on time, and it posted incomplete enrollment reports, undercutting the goals of the local law that mandated them.
findings.quote: NYCPS did not publish reports timely, as required by Local Law 72 of 2018

numbers.label: Students in temporary housing in 2023-24 admissions
Of 39 sampled students, likely low-income but not identified
Manual placements missed or done improperly for 2023-24
Students applying to high school each year, at minimum

recommendations: Improve management of the matching algorithm so students get the admissions priority they are entitled to, including students in temporary housing, low-income students and students who need manual placements.

Develop and implement written policies and procedures for the matching process so students are treated consistently and appropriately, in line with the Chancellor's Regulations and other requirements.
Create policies and procedures to make sure complete and timely reports are publicly posted as required by Local Law 72 of 2018.

audits.auditor: Special master (NYC special education hearing orders)
audits.title: Special Master Program Monitoring Report
audits.plain_title: Two years on, 59% of the special education court order is unmet
audits.agency: New York City Public Schools
audits.what_they_audited: A periodic monitoring report to the court, filed as a slide deck, on how far the New York City Public Schools (DOE) has gotten in meeting the obligations imposed by the court's order of July 19, 2023 in L.V. v. D.O.E. It includes an independent assessment of the four technology systems the obligations depend on.
audits.background: In a special education due process proceeding an Impartial Hearing Officer (IHO) can order services for a student or payment on the student's behalf, and the department must carry the order out within 35 days unless the order sets a different timeline. The department runs an Implementation Unit (IU) to authorize those payments and arrange those services. Obligation #39 of the 2023 order requires the special master to report to the court every 120 days on whether each obligation has been fulfilled, what is blocking the unfulfilled ones and what steps come next.

findings.plain: As of July 8, 2025, the department had fulfilled 21 of the 51 obligations tracked and 30 were still unfulfilled.
findings.quote: As of July 8, 2025, twenty-one (21) obligations

findings.plain: Every unfulfilled obligation was past due, some by more than a year, leaving 59% of the July 2023 order unmet two years after it was issued.
findings.quote: DOE has yet to fulfill 59% of the obligations from the 7/19/23 order.

findings.plain: Two obligations were tentatively fulfilled since the March 2025 report: collecting documentation from parents and notifying the Implementation Unit when a case is settled. The evidence was contained in business requirements documents for the new hearing system.
findings.quote: In recent weeks, DOE has tentatively fulfilled two obligations from the LV order

findings.plain: IBM and the department set December 15, 2025 as the go-live date for the Impartial Hearing Management System (IHMS), with final design sign-off due August 29, 2025. The special master remained concerned that the schedule left almost no room for problems, particularly for migrating data out of existing systems.
findings.quote: IBM and DOE/DIIT have set a Go-Live date of 12/15/2025 for IHMS. The work plan

findings.plain: Technology is the choke point. Of the 40 obligations being monitored, 19 depend on specific technology systems, and the delayed hearing management system is the one most of them rest on.
findings.quote: has been the most delayed and is the lynchpin for many of the LV Orders.

findings.plain: Polaris, the custom-built invoicing tool, was working. It went live with 57 vendors in late December 2024 and invoices were being processed within five days, with a July release planned to bring the vendor total toward 200.
findings.quote: been positive with the team processing invoices through the system within 5 days of

findings.plain: A pilot letting vendors email the Implementation Unit generated 3,557 tickets between February 11 and May 9, 2025, but only 26% drew a confirmation from a parent or parent representative and most of the email came from three vendors.
findings.quote: system generated 3,557 tickets but only 26% of the tickets received a confirmation

numbers.label: Obligations fulfilled as of July 8, 2025
Obligations not yet fulfilled
Share of the July 2023 order still unmet
Go-live date set for the new hearing system
Vendors using the new Polaris invoicing tool
Vendor email tickets logged February 11 to May 9, 2025
Tickets confirmed by a parent or representative

recommendations: Obligation 5, hearing officer web form: include hearing officers in user acceptance testing of the new hearing management system.
Obligation 8b, multiple-file uploads: update the policy so parents can submit payment documentation as multiple files, and communicate the change internally and publicly.
Obligation 10, timesheet solution: test the invoicing application on multiple browser types to match what the public will use.
Obligation 13, monitoring service orders: set up a working group that meets regularly on the functionality needed in the special education system.
Obligation 14a, customer support hotline: keep improving the SupportHub tool and process in response to community feedback.
Obligation 16a, parent notifications: draft the requirements and content for the automated service that emails parents at key milestones.

Obligation 16c, deploying notifications publicly: see obligation 16a.
Obligation 20, nursing postings: provide copies of the communications sent to the health agencies.
Obligation 24b, DAITS enhancements: confirm that further enhancements to the older tracking system will be postponed so resources can support the new hearing system.
Obligation 30, operating procedures manual: have the communications lead revise the draft manual and share an updated version with plaintiffs and the special master.
Obligation 33, new services process: create a working group for the hearing system and special education system teams to work out the integration between them.
Obligation 27, case status indicator: make sure the parent-facing status function is tested with parents during user acceptance testing.
Obligation 31, document management: clarify and define the process and technologies for capturing and storing documentation from parents.
Obligation 34, document management tool: see obligation 13.
Obligation 32, mobile timesheets: share the mobile testing results for Polaris with the special master.
Obligation 2b, monthly performance reporting: gather and integrate the data assets and tell the parties when future performance reports will be delivered.
Obligation 9, payment documentation: keep reviewing the content of the implementation website and align it with the SupportHub site.
Obligation 12a, high-priority orders: gather data on high-priority cases, share it with the special master and determine lessons learned from missed cases.
Obligation 12b, service communications: produce and share a communications plan for service orders and action items.
