Obligation 35, home instruction: create a process document for confirming that ordered home instruction was actually provided.

audits.implementation_note: Of the 51 obligations in the July 19, 2023 court order, 21 were fulfilled and 30 were not yet fulfilled as of July 8, 2025, two more than at the March 2025 report.

audits.title: New York City Department of Homeless Services – Oversight of Contract Expenditures of Church Avenue Merchants Block Association, Inc.
audits.plain_title: Oversight of spending by a women's shelter contractor
audits.agency: New York City Department of Social Services
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the New York City Department of Homeless Services (DHS) effectively monitored its contract with Church Avenue Merchants Block Association, Inc. (CAMBA) to make sure the costs the nonprofit reported were allowable, supported and related to the program. The audit covered July 2020 through June 2023.
audits.background: Since 2011 DHS has contracted with CAMBA, a city-based nonprofit, to run the 200-bed Magnolia House Women's Shelter, serving homeless women including those with mental illness and substance abuse disorders. Over the three fiscal years ended June 30, 2023, CAMBA claimed $27.9 million in reimbursable expenses under the contracts.

findings.plain: Auditors identified $4,501,692, about 16.1% of all costs CAMBA reported over three fiscal years, that did not comply with the applicable fiscal manuals and the shelter contracts.
findings.quote: we identified $4,501,692—accounting for approximately 16.1% of all CAMBA’s reported costs—that did not comply with the requirements

findings.plain: That total included $2,126,980 in salaries and fringe benefits that were not supported by staff sign-in and sign-out logs, were overallocated to the shelter contracts or were unrelated to the shelter program.
findings.quote: $2,126,980 in compensation costs (salaries and related fringe benefits) that were not supported by Magnolia staff sign-in/sign-out logs

findings.plain: It also included $1,835,545 in contracted services and other expenses that were unsupported, overallocated to the program or not reimbursable, plus $539,167 in related indirect costs.
findings.quote: $1,835,545 in contracted services costs and other expenses that were unsupported, overallocated to the Magnolia program, or non-reimbursable

findings.plain: DHS approved CAMBA's security contracts without evidence they were competitively bid, as required.
findings.quote: DHS approved CAMBA’s security contracts without evidence that they were competitively bid, as required

findings.plain: DHS did not complete required expenditure reviews or make sure year-end closeouts were done on time, a control that would improve its reviews and help recover overpayments. The auditors said the findings point to a significant deficiency in DHS' monitoring of its CAMBA contracts.
findings.quote: a significant deficiency in DHS’ monitoring and oversight of its contracts with CAMBA

numbers.label: Reported costs that did not comply with the rules
Share of CAMBA's reported costs that were non-compliant
Unsupported, overallocated or unrelated compensation costs
Expenses CAMBA claimed over three fiscal years

recommendations: Review and recover, as appropriate, the $4,501,692 in reported expenses that did not comply with the fiscal manuals and the shelter contracts.

Review the eligibility of claimed expenses under the fiscal manuals and providers' contracts, making sure providers such as CAMBA keep documentation to support claimed expenses, maintain required inventories and complete year-end closeouts on time.

audits.title: Oversight of Contract Expenditures of Bowery Residents’ Committee (Follow-up)
audits.plain_title: Follow-up on oversight of a homeless shelter contractor
audits.agency: New York City Department of Social Services
audits.what_they_audited: How far the New York City Department of Homeless Services (DHS) has gotten in carrying out the 11 recommendations from a 2021 audit of its oversight of contract spending by the Bowery Residents' Committee (BRC), a nonprofit shelter operator.
audits.background: DHS contracted with BRC to run the 200-bed Jack Ryan Residence, an emergency shelter for mentally ill and chemically addicted homeless adults. The initial audit, issued in December 2021, found DHS was not effectively monitoring the contract and identified $1,428,199, or 6.05% of all reported costs over three fiscal years, that did not comply with the applicable fiscal manuals and the contract.

findings.plain: DHS has made some progress on the problems identified in the initial audit, but more work remains.
findings.quote: DHS officials have made some progress in addressing the issues we identified in the initial audit report; however, more work needs to be done.

findings.plain: Of the 11 recommendations in the initial report, DHS implemented two, partially implemented seven and did not implement two.
findings.quote: Of the initial report’s 11 audit recommendations, two were implemented, seven were partially implemented, and two were not implemented.

numbers.label: Recommendations in the initial 2021 audit
Non-compliant costs found in the initial audit
Share of reported costs that were non-compliant

recommendations: Officials are asked, but not required, to report within 30 days on any actions planned to address the unresolved issues in the follow-up report.
audits.implementation_note: Of the 11 recommendations in the 2021 audit, the follow-up found 2 implemented, 7 partially implemented and 2 not implemented.

audits.title: Audit of the Queens Borough Public Library’s Emergency Preparedness
audits.plain_title: How prepared the Queens library is for emergencies
audits.agency: Queens Borough Public Library
audits.what_they_audited: In this final audit letter report, auditors examined whether the Queens Public Library is adequately prepared to plan for and respond to emergencies, keep its operations running and serve the public during major disasters and other events.
audits.background: The Queens Public Library is an independent nonprofit with 66 locations that served over 5.6 million visitors in fiscal year 2023. Under the federal Stafford Act, libraries can receive disaster assistance if they provide critical services during a major disaster, and the library's borough-wide reach positions it as an access point for information and services in emergencies.

findings.plain: The library served the public during emergencies. Open branches acted as cooling centers on all 14 days heat emergencies were declared from June through August 2024, and on freezing days auditors found seven visited branches adequately heated with working free Wi-Fi.
findings.quote: From June through August 2024, heat emergencies were declared on 14 days. QPL branches that were open for business served as cooling centers on those days.

findings.plain: The library put flood protection and mitigation measures in place at two of its three branches located in the 100- and 500-year floodplains, but provided nothing showing similar protections at the Seaside branch.
findings.quote: QPL did not provide information or documentation indicating it implemented any flood protection and mitigation measures for Seaside.

findings.plain: Backup generators exist at only three locations, though officials said all locations have battery backup for their information technology servers.
findings.quote: QPL has backup generators at three locations—the Queens Central Library, Flushing, and Hunters Point

findings.plain: The library's Disaster Recovery Plan has been tested and updated, but nothing formally requires testing it at least annually, and test reports noted areas for improvement such as documenting step-by-step recovery procedures.
findings.quote: Without a specified requirement for testing, there is potential for the Plan to go untested even if there are changes to the QPL’s procedures or communication structure.

findings.plain: Although the library's evacuation plan requires fire drills at least twice a year, officials had no reports of any drills conducted during calendar year 2024 for the 15 branches auditors sampled.
findings.quote: QPL officials stated that they did not have any reports for drills conducted during Calendar Year 2024

findings.plain: A survey of branches revealed potential communication and training gaps: 52 of 61 open branches (85.2%) did not respond at all, and among the nine that did, some reported missing active shooter or other emergency training and three said the central office did not inform them of emergency alerts in their area.
findings.quote: one branch reported that they did not receive active shooter training, and four branches reported that they did not receive any other safety or emergency preparedness training

numbers.label: Library locations in the Queens system
Visitors served in fiscal year 2023
Summer 2024 heat emergency days with cooling center branches
Share of branches that did not answer the audit survey

recommendations: Consider installing flood protection and mitigation measures at the Seaside branch because of its floodplain location.
Consider installing generators or other backup power systems at additional branches so libraries can keep operating and serve the public during emergencies.
Request that the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency conduct an Infrastructure Survey Tool assessment to identify and document the library's overall security and resilience.
Ensure the Disaster Recovery Plan includes a requirement to test, review and update the plan at least annually.
Address the areas of improvement noted in Disaster Recovery Test Reports.
Ensure twice-yearly fire drills are conducted at all branches and implement a centralized process for keeping documentation of each completed drill.

Implement a centralized notification system to quickly relay information to all branch managers and staff, including local emergency updates and instructions on public health, weather or security situations.
audits.agency_response: The library agreed with five of the seven recommendations, partially agreed with one and did not address the recommendation about the federal security assessment, saying it already conducts its own periodic cybersecurity assessments through certified vendors.

audits.title: Final Audit Letter Report on the Teachers’ Retirement System of the City of New York’s (TRS) Other Than Personal Services (OTPS) Expenditures
audits.plain_title: Teachers' pension fund spending mostly proper but poorly documented
audits.agency: Teachers' Retirement System of the City of New York
audits.what_they_audited: In this final audit letter report, auditors examined whether the Teachers' Retirement System's other than personal services expenditures, meaning nonsalary costs like office supplies, travel and payments to outside vendors, followed the system's policies and city rules and were necessary, reasonable and well supported by documentation. They reviewed a sample of 54 expenditures from fiscal years 2023 and 2024.
audits.background: The Teachers' Retirement System is one of the largest municipal public pension systems in the United States, serving over 220,000 members, retirees and beneficiaries who worked for the city's public schools, the City University of New York and participating charter schools. For fiscal year 2024 it reported approximately $132 billion in assets and $47 million in other than personal services expenditures.

findings.plain: Overall, the retirement system's nonsalary spending largely followed its own policies and relevant rules, and the expenses were necessary and reasonable. But auditors said the system should improve how it approves and documents this spending.
findings.quote: TRS’ OTPS expenditures were, for the most part, spent in accordance with internal policies and procedures and other relevant rules and regulations

findings.plain: The system paid 11 of 54 sampled invoices (20%) more than 30 days after the invoice date without justification, and could not produce an invoice to substantiate one payment at all.
findings.quote: 11 (20%) of the 54 sampled OTPS invoices were paid more than 30 days after the invoice dates, without justification

findings.plain: For six payments to consultants totaling $35,587, the system could not provide a contract or other documentation to substantiate the rates of pay it was charged.
findings.quote: For six payments totaling $35,587, TRS was unable to provide documentation (such as a contract) to substantiate the consultants’ rates of pay

findings.plain: Despite saying after a March 2022 internal audit that it would stop, the system kept buying gift cards, purchasing an unknown number totaling $16,060 on agency credit cards in violation of a comptroller's directive.
findings.quote: TRS purchased an unknown number of gift cards, totaling $16,060, using agency credit cards

findings.plain: Most of the sampled out-of-town travel spending for fiscal year 2024, $52,427 of $77,944, was not sufficiently documented. Auditors also flagged expenses that might not be necessary or allowable, including alcoholic beverages, premium hotel rooms and meals bought when the conference already provided them.
findings.quote: for $52,427 (67%) of the $77,944 out-of-town travel expenses sampled for FY2024, the auditors found that some of these expenses were not sufficiently documented

findings.plain: The system did not enforce the directive that caps conference travel at two employees per conference and two out-of-town conferences per employee each year, and no post-travel attendance reports were provided for any sampled trip. It also could not support $31,291 of sampled fiscal year 2023 travel expenses.
findings.quote: TRS registered five employees to attend “2023 NCTR 101st Conference,” and allowed two employees to attend three different conferences

numbers.label: Nonsalary spending reported for fiscal year 2024
Sampled expenditures reviewed from fiscal years 2023-2024
Consultant payments lacking documented pay rates
Gift cards bought on agency credit cards
Fiscal 2024 travel spending not sufficiently documented

recommendations: Ensure invoices are received before initiating payment and properly maintain the invoices that are received and paid.
Process payments to vendors within 30 days after receiving the invoices.
Immediately stop the practice of purchasing gift cards.
Ensure all out-of-town travel is justified and the associated costs are approved.
Request and obtain all necessary documents before processing payments and reimbursements to avoid paying unnecessary expenses.
Comply with the directive's limits on how many employees attend the same conference and how many conferences each employee attends per year.
Obtain post-travel attendance reports from everyone who attends out-of-town conferences to show how what they learned benefits the system.
audits.agency_response: The Teachers' Retirement System agreed to implement three of the seven recommendations and disagreed with the other four, in several cases saying its current practices already address the findings. Auditors reiterated those recommendations, noting the system had not provided supporting evidence.

audits.title: Audit of the New York Public Library’s Emergency Preparedness
audits.plain_title: New York Public Library helps in crises but has planning gaps
audits.agency: New York Public Library
audits.what_they_audited: This audit letter report examined whether the New York Public Library is adequately prepared to plan for and respond to emergencies, keep its operations running and serve the public during major disasters and other events.
audits.background: The New York Public Library is a private nonprofit with 92 locations across the Bronx, Manhattan and Staten Island, and it served nearly 8 million visitors in fiscal year 2024. Federal law and the American Library Association recognize the role libraries play in responding to disasters.

findings.plain: The library served the public during emergencies, with branches acting as cooling centers on hot days and warm places on freezing days, and free Wi-Fi working at every branch auditors tested.
findings.quote: NYPL served the public in numerous ways during emergencies but needs to improve certain aspects of its emergency preparedness

findings.plain: The library refused to give auditors its business continuity, disaster recovery and information technology incident response plans or evidence they were tested, citing security concerns. Auditors noted the city charter entitles the comptroller's office to such records, and a belated offer to inspect the plans allowed only 30 minutes.
findings.quote: NYPL did not provide the auditors with its Business Continuity Plan, Disaster Recovery Plan, or IT Incident Response Plan, or evidence that these plans were tested.

findings.plain: Most branches did not conduct the required annual fire drill: 70 of 81 locations, or 86.4%, had no drill logged for calendar year 2024.
findings.quote: 70 (86.4%) of the 81 locations list did not conduct a fire drill during Calendar Year 2024

findings.plain: Sampled branches did not complete required emergency preparedness documents. The library produced all requested key documents for only eight of 17 sampled branches.
findings.quote: NYPL provided all requested key documents for only eight (47.1%) sampled branches

findings.plain: Of the 66 branches that answered an auditor survey, 17 said the central office did not inform them of emergency alerts in their area.
findings.quote: 17 branches stated that the Central Office did not inform them of emergency alerts in their area

findings.plain: The library has not implemented, and told auditors it will not implement, flood protection measures at the Aquilar branch, its only location in the 500-year floodplain, even though the branch is being renovated.
findings.quote: NYPL has not implemented flood protection and mitigation measures at Aquilar, the only branch located in the 500-year floodplain

numbers.label: Visitors served in fiscal year 2024
Locations across the Bronx, Manhattan and Staten Island
Locations with no fire drill logged in 2024
Sampled branches with all required safety documents on file
Time auditors were given to inspect the withheld plans

recommendations: Ask the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to conduct an infrastructure survey assessment of the library's overall security and resilience.
Test, review and update the business continuity plan, cybersecurity plan and information technology incident response plan at least annually.
Consider implementing a mesh Wi-Fi network, which supports communications in hard-to-reach areas and can be used in emergency response.
Make sure annual fire drills are conducted at all locations.
Establish a centralized tracking and reporting system so all branches submit their required security plans, checklists, safety surveys and resource lists.
Make sure critical emergency alerts from New York City Emergency Management are promptly relayed to all branch managers and staff.
Consider flood protection and mitigation measures at the Aquilar branch given its floodplain location.
audits.agency_response: The library agreed with six of the seven recommendations and disagreed with one, on mesh Wi-Fi, saying its fiberoptic network makes mesh Wi-Fi impracticable for emergency response communications.

audits.title: Final Audit Letter Report of the Civil Service Practices by the Civil Service Commission
audits.plain_title: How the Civil Service Commission handles job appeals
audits.agency: Civil Service Commission
audits.what_they_audited: In this letter report, auditors assessed how effectively the Civil Service Commission minimizes vacancies in city agencies and improves the quality of the city workforce. They reviewed the 1,918 appeal cases the commission handled between July 2021 and April 2024.
audits.background: The commission is an independent, non-mayoral city agency authorized by the New York City Charter to hear and decide appeals from determinations made by other city agencies, mainly appeals from people disqualified from civil service exams or job lists and appeals of agency disciplinary decisions.

findings.plain: The commission is meeting its legal duty to hear and decide civil service appeals from applicants who were disqualified from exams or removed from civil service titles.
findings.quote: CSC is fulfilling its statutory requirements to review (hear and decide) Civil Service appeals for disqualified applicants under Section 50 of the Civil Service Law

findings.plain: Of the 1,918 appeals the commission accepted between July 2021 and April 2024, 95% were pre-employment cases from people who disagreed with their disqualifications, and 1,724 were closed with final decisions before April 2024.
findings.quote: 1,818 cases (95%) were pre-employment cases filed by individuals who disagreed with their disqualifications from Civil Service lists

findings.plain: The commission has not set timeframes for reviewing cases, but in 244 of 248 sampled cases it followed up to get the information needed, granting extensions to agencies and appellants when appropriate.
findings.quote: in 244 (98%) cases, CSC followed up to obtain additional case information as documented in case files

findings.plain: The commission sent acknowledgement letters to appellants within an average of two days of receiving a case, and the vast majority went out within a week.
findings.quote: 93% of the cases had acknowledgement letters issued in seven days or less

findings.plain: Deciding an appeal took anywhere from less than three months to over 15 months, mostly because agencies or appellants were slow to provide documents. In four cases the delay stemmed from inadequate commission oversight, and the commission now audits every open case every 30 days.
findings.quote: the time from submission to case closing ranged from less than three months to over 15 months

findings.plain: The auditors noted that the number of appeals and the time it takes to decide them do not affect the city's ability to fill vacancies.
findings.quote: the number of appeals received and the length of time CSC takes to adjudicate them does not impact the City’s ability to fill vacancies

numbers.label: Case numbers received, July 2021 to April 2024
Cases accepted and reviewed as appeals
Cases closed with final decisions before April 2024
Average time to send case acknowledgement letters

recommendations: Continue auditing all open cases in the Law Manager system every month to make sure cases are processed in a timely and appropriate way.
Set timeframes for reviewing cases so they are processed in a timely manner.
audits.agency_response: The commission agreed with both of the audit's recommendations in its June 12, 2025 written response.

audits.title: Final Audit Letter Report on the New York City Fire Pension Fund’s Other Than Personal Services Expenditures
audits.plain_title: Fire pension fund spending mostly proper but controls are weak
audits.agency: New York City Fire Pension Fund
audits.what_they_audited: In this final audit letter report, auditors examined whether the Fire Pension Fund's other than personal services expenditures, meaning nonsalary operating costs like supplies, travel and vendor contracts, were spent during fiscal years 2023 and 2024 in accordance with its policies and other rules, and whether the spending was necessary and related to its mission.
audits.background: The Fire Pension Fund is one of the five New York City retirement systems, administering pension benefits for more than 28,000 active members, retirees and beneficiaries of the fire department. Its fiscal year 2024 administrative expenses totaled $11 million, including $4.4 million in other than personal services expenditures.

findings.plain: Overall, the fund's nonsalary spending largely followed the rules and was necessary and mission-related, but auditors found several weaknesses in the fund's controls over that spending.
findings.quote: FPF’s OTPS expenditures were, for the most part, spent in accordance with relevant rules and regulations, and were necessary and related to its mission

findings.plain: Five fund employees attended two out-of-town conferences in fiscal year 2024 at a cost of $11,195, but the fund did not provide the required justification for all five attendees.
findings.quote: FPF did not provide justification for all five employees who attended the conferences

findings.plain: The fund misreported certain expenses in its annual financial reports, counting $2.4 million of investment-related expenses and $56,991 of member-related payments as nonsalary operating spending. That overstated those expenditures and the reported gains of its investment portfolio.
findings.quote: FPF reported $2.4 million of investment-related expenses as OTPS expenditures in its ACFRs for FYs 2023 and 2024

findings.plain: The fund recorded information technology consultant costs in the wrong year, which after review of additional documentation meant its nonsalary spending was overstated in fiscal year 2023 and understated in fiscal year 2024 by $930,000.
findings.quote: FPF OTPS expenditures were overstated in FY2023 and understated in FY2024 by $930,000, as opposed to $303,287

findings.plain: The fund did not divide key financial duties among different staff, a safeguard against error or fraud. A single person issued purchase orders, assigned budget codes, prepared payment vouchers and processed payments in the banking system.
findings.quote: FPF designated one person to issue purchase orders, assign budget codes, prepare payment vouchers, and process checks and electronic fund transfers (EFT) in the banking system

findings.plain: The fund also recorded some transactions in its general ledger months late, paid three of 54 sampled invoices more than 30 days after the invoice date without justification and has no implemented policies and procedures for procurement and travel expenses.
findings.quote: FPF does not have policies and procedures for procurement and travel expenses.

numbers.label: Nonsalary spending in fiscal year 2024
Investment expenses misreported as nonsalary spending
Amount misstated across fiscal years 2023 and 2024
Cost of two conferences lacking full justification
Active members, retirees and beneficiaries served

recommendations: Obtain post-travel attendance reports from everyone who attends out-of-town conferences to show how what they learned benefits the fund.
Stop reporting investment and member-related payments as other than personal services expenditures.
Accurately report expenditures in the period the expenses are incurred.
Segregate duties for the expenditure process or implement compensating controls such as management review and dual authorization.
Promptly record payment transactions in the general ledger.
Process payments to vendors within 30 days of receiving the invoices.
Establish and implement internal procurement and travel policies and procedures.
audits.agency_response: The fund agreed with two recommendations, partially agreed with one and did not explicitly agree or disagree with the remaining four, in some cases citing its small staff and plans for a new accounting system. Auditors reiterated those recommendations.

audits.title: Final Audit Letter Report on the New York City Police Pension Fund’s Other Than Personal Services Expenditures
audits.plain_title: Police pension fund lacked controls over its office spending
audits.agency: New York City Police Pension Fund
audits.what_they_audited: This audit letter report examined whether the New York City Police Pension Fund's spending on things other than salaries, such as leased vehicles, travel and vendor payments, followed its policies and city rules in fiscal years 2023 and 2024 and was necessary to its mission.
audits.background: The fund is one of the five New York City retirement systems and administers pension benefits for more than 90,000 active members, retirees and beneficiaries of the police department. Its administrative expenses totaled $34 million in fiscal year 2024, including $15.7 million in spending other than salaries and fringe benefits.

findings.plain: Most of the fund's spending followed its policies and relevant rules, but auditors found several control weaknesses.
findings.quote: the auditors also found several weaknesses in PPF’s controls over its OTPS expenditures that could be improved

findings.plain: The fund paid $69,814 over two years to lease vehicles for three executives without keeping required documentation of business use. Auditors concluded the vehicles were not economical or necessary, noting the city's other four pension funds do not lease vehicles for their executives.
findings.quote: the leased vehicles are not economical and necessary to PPF’s mission

findings.plain: The fund paid $4,009 in sales tax to two vendors even though it is exempt from New York State sales tax.
findings.quote: PPF paid $4,009 in Sales Tax on five sampled invoices issued by two vendors

findings.plain: Nine of 64 sampled invoices, or 14%, were paid more than 30 days after the invoice date without justification.
findings.quote: nine (14%) were paid more than 30 days after the invoice dates without justification

findings.plain: The fund reported expenditures on a cash basis instead of the accrual basis required under generally accepted accounting principles.
findings.quote: PPF did not report expenditures on an accrual basis as required, instead reporting on a cash basis

findings.plain: The fund could not document $31,710 in out-of-town travel expenses, improperly reimbursed employees $2,473 and has no internal travel policy.
findings.quote: PPF did not maintain required documentation for out-of-town travel expenses totaling $31,710

numbers.label: Non-salary spending in fiscal year 2024
Paid for three leased executive vehicles and related costs
Sales tax paid despite the fund's tax exemption
Out-of-town travel spending without required documentation
Improper reimbursements to employees
Active members, retirees and beneficiaries the fund serves

recommendations: Make sure spending other than salaries is economical and necessary to the fund's mission.
Reevaluate vehicle use policies in light of general city requirements and document each business use of leased vehicles, noting the time, place and business purpose.
Inform vendors of the fund's sales tax exemption and exclude sales tax from payments.
Review and recoup all prior payments that included sales tax.
Pay vendors within 30 days of receiving invoices.
Report expenditures accurately in the period the expenses are incurred.
Create an internal travel policy covering how travel is requested, approved, funded and reimbursed, in line with the comptroller's travel directive.
Make sure all out-of-town travel expenses are economical, necessary and consistent with the comptroller's travel directive.
audits.agency_response: The fund agreed with four of the eight recommendations. It did not explicitly agree or disagree with the other four, saying it would review its processes and make changes it deems necessary, and maintained that its leased vehicles remain integral to its mission.

audits.title: Final Letter Report on the Audit of the Brooklyn Public Library’s Emergency Preparedness
audits.plain_title: Brooklyn Public Library helps in emergencies but lacks a full plan
audits.agency: Brooklyn Public Library
audits.what_they_audited: This letter report examined whether the Brooklyn Public Library is adequately prepared to plan for and respond to emergencies, keep its operations running and serve the public during major disasters and other events.
audits.background: The Brooklyn Public Library is a private nonprofit with 60 branches serving a borough of 2.7 million residents, and it reported nearly 5.9 million visitors in fiscal year 2024. Federal law and the American Library Association recognize the role libraries play in responding to disasters.

findings.plain: The library served the public during emergencies, with branches acting as cooling centers on hot days and warm places on freezing days, and free Wi-Fi working at every branch auditors tested.
findings.quote: BPL served the public in numerous ways during emergencies but needs to improve certain aspects of its emergency preparedness

findings.plain: On one heat emergency day, four branches listed as cooling centers were closed, two of them because of extreme heat inside the buildings.
findings.quote: four branches listed as cooling centers were closed on July 16, 2024: two due to extreme heat in the building and two for maintenance or repairs

findings.plain: Three of the six branches located in floodplains, Brighton Beach, Gerritsen Beach and Sheepshead Bay, have no flood protection or mitigation measures despite the significant impact of Hurricane Sandy on those locations.
findings.quote: BPL did not implement any flood protection and mitigation measures for the other three branches located in the floodplain

findings.plain: The library has many individual safety policies but no comprehensive emergency plan that assigns responsibilities for protecting people, property and operations in an emergency.
findings.quote: it lacks a comprehensive emergency plan that provides incident stabilization and assigns responsibilities

findings.plain: The library did not test or update its business continuity plan annually as required, skipping tabletop exercises for three straight years and leaving the plan unrevised since 2021.
findings.quote: The BPL conducted tabletop exercises in August 2021 and January 2025, but did not test the plan in 2022, 2023, or 2024.

findings.plain: Some branches did not conduct required twice-yearly fire drills, and branches that answered an auditor survey reported gaps in safety training and emergency alerts from the central office.
findings.quote: For CY2023, seven (13.5%) of the 52 branches did not conduct biannual drills

numbers.label: Visitors served in fiscal year 2024
Branch locations throughout Brooklyn
Heat emergency days, June through August 2024
Branches skipping twice-yearly fire drills in 2023
Surveyed branches reporting no safety or emergency training

recommendations: Conduct facility assessments at all branches before the summer cooling and winter heating seasons to make sure heating and cooling systems work.
Consider installing generators or other backup power systems at additional branches so libraries can serve the public during emergencies.
Consider flood protection and mitigation measures at the Brighton Beach, Gerritsen Beach and Sheepshead Bay branches given their floodplain locations and past storm impacts.
Create a comprehensive public safety and emergency plan that assigns responsibilities for specific actions to protect people, property, operations and the environment.
Train all staff on the comprehensive plan and the business continuity plan, test the plans at least once a year and update them as necessary.
Make sure twice-yearly fire drills are conducted at all locations.
Implement a centralized notification system to quickly relay emergency information and instructions to all branch managers and staff.
audits.agency_response: The library agreed with all seven recommendations, noting for several that work is under way, including a consolidated comprehensive emergency plan it expects to publish in the first quarter of fiscal year 2026.

audits.title: Audit Report on the New York City Law Department’s Timeliness in Reviewing Agency Contracts
audits.plain_title: Slow Law Department reviews of city contracts
audits.agency: New York City Law Department
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Law Department reviews city agencies' procurement contracts in a timely manner, looking at contracts reviewed from January 2023 through October 2024.
audits.background: The Law Department, headed by the Corporation Counsel, must approve the form of all city contracts and leases. Its Contracts and Real Estate Division, with 15 attorneys who also have other responsibilities, evaluates and approves city agreements totaling approximately $10 billion annually. Officials say a review generally takes three to four weeks.

findings.plain: For non-mayoral and certain mayoral agency contracts tracked in the Law Manager system, the department blew past its own three-to-four-week norm on 38.1% of contracts in the first nine months of 2024 and 36.1% in 2023, with some reviews running months late.
findings.quote: the department took more than four weeks to review and approve 115 (38.1%) of the 302 contracts

findings.plain: In a random sample of 50 mayoral agency contracts processed through the Procurement and Sourcing Solutions Portal (PASSPort), eight (16%) took more than four weeks to review and approve.
findings.quote: the Law Department took more than four weeks to review and approve eight contracts, with delays ranging from one day to nearly two months

findings.plain: Delays were largely the Law Department's own doing. In a sample of 15 delayed contracts, it was solely responsible nine times and partially responsible three times, with officials citing resource constraints, a mayoral push to prioritize human services contracts and lengthy negotiations.
findings.quote: The Law Department was solely responsible for delays in nine instances and partially responsible for delays in three instances.

findings.plain: In one case, the Queens County District Attorney's Office repeatedly asked for an expedited review of a contract for software it called critical to law enforcement operations, but the Law Department did not approve it until nearly two months after the existing contract expired.
findings.quote: the Law Department did not approve this contract until July 26, 2024—more than three-and-a-half months after it was received

findings.plain: The department does not monitor pending contract reviews, flag overdue ones or analyze closed requests, so it cannot tell whether reviews are timely, identify the causes of delays or take corrective action.
findings.quote: the Law Department does not monitor pending requests or flag those approaching or past due

findings.plain: The Mayor's Office of Contract Services (MOCS) has not fixed a PASSPort glitch that hides when contracts are returned to agencies for revision, and it never produced contract milestone data the auditors requested repeatedly over two months.
findings.quote: MOCS has not corrected a PASSPort glitch that inhibits the Law Department’s ability to track whether and when contracts are returned to Mayoral agencies and how long they take to respond

numbers.label: Approximate annual value of contracts the division reviews
Law Manager contracts reviewed late in 2024
Sampled PASSPort contracts reviewed late
Attorneys in the division that reviews contracts

recommendations: Record key milestones in Law Manager or its planned successor LegalStratus or otherwise track them, including when agencies submit contracts, attorneys are assigned, contracts are returned or approved and agencies respond.
Ask the Mayor's Office of Contract Services to create standard aging reports and reports of closed contracts showing key milestone dates.

Use Law Manager, LegalStratus and PASSPort to generate biweekly aging reports that flag requests nearing or past the expected review timeframe, and to generate historical reports of closed requests to measure timeliness, identify the causes of delays and take corrective action.
Assess whether staffing levels are adequate.
Keep working with the Mayor's Office of Contract Services on issues including the PASSPort glitch involving returned contracts and the system's reporting capabilities.
audits.agency_response: The Law Department disagreed with the report's findings but agreed with three of the five recommendations and partially agreed with two, saying that recording every interaction would be unduly burdensome. Auditors replied that they asked only for key milestones to be tracked.

audits.title: Case Management (Follow-Up)
audits.plain_title: Follow-up on case management services for older New Yorkers
audits.agency: New York City Department for the Aging
audits.what_they_audited: How far the New York City Department for the Aging (DFTA) has gotten in carrying out the eight recommendations from a 2023 audit of its case management program, which helps older people with functional impairments get the services and benefits they need to age safely at home.
audits.background: DFTA contracts with community-based organizations to provide case management, with more than 31,000 seniors receiving over 515,000 hours of services in the city fiscal year ended June 30, 2024. The initial audit, issued in July 2023, found DFTA did not provide adequate oversight of the program: providers did not always follow DFTA's standards, clients spent significant time on waitlists and referrals were not always prioritized so those with the greatest needs got services first.

findings.plain: DFTA has made some progress on the problems identified in the initial audit.
findings.quote: DFTA has made some progress in addressing the problems identified in our initial audit report.

findings.plain: Of the eight recommendations in the initial report, DFTA implemented one, partially implemented four and did not implement three.
findings.quote: Of the initial report’s eight audit recommendations, one was implemented, four were partially implemented, and three were not implemented.

findings.plain: Waitlists remain: as of February 2025, DFTA officials said 338 people were waiting for case management and 475 were waiting for home care.
findings.quote: as of February 2025, there were 338 people on the case management and 475 on the home care wait lists

numbers.label: People on the case management waitlist, February 2025
People on the home care waitlist, February 2025
Seniors who received case management in fiscal 2024, at minimum
Value of case management contracts for fiscal 2025, at minimum

recommendations: DFTA officials are asked, but not required, to report within 30 days on any actions planned to address the unresolved issues in the follow-up report.
audits.implementation_note: Of the 8 recommendations in the 2023 audit, the follow-up found 1 implemented, 4 partially implemented and 3 not implemented.

audits.title: Twenty-Fifth Report of the Independent Monitor: The NYPD's Community Response Team's Stop, Frisk, and Search Practices
audits.plain_title: Quality-of-life police teams made unlawful stops at high rates
audits.agency: New York City Police Department
audits.what_they_audited: The stop, frisk and search practices of the New York City Police Department's (NYPD) Community Response Team (CRT) units from July to December 2024, using three methods: a review of 100 body-worn camera (BWC) videos from randomly selected CRT officers, a review of 50 videos officers had labeled as Level 2 investigative encounters and an assessment of 50 CRT stop reports.
audits.background: The NYPD established the CRT in July 2022 to focus on quality-of-life issues; its officers wear modified uniforms of khaki pants and blue shirts and drive unmarked cars. An initial monitor review in early 2024 found the teams focused on illegal motorcycles, demonstrations and unlicensed marijuana shops rather than Terry stops, but community complaints and a significant expansion of the teams prompted this second audit.

findings.plain: The teams' role has shifted: rather than addressing specific quality-of-life conditions or answering calls for service, CRTs now operate like the department's Neighborhood Safety Teams (NST) and Public Safety Teams (PST), doing proactive enforcement.
findings.quote: CRTs appear to be another version of NSTs or PSTs, engaging in proactive enforcement

findings.plain: CRT officers overwhelmingly made stops based on their own observations rather than 911 or 311 calls: 96% of the stop reports CRT officers prepared in the third quarter of 2024 were self-initiated.
findings.quote: 96% of stop reports prepared by CRT officers...

findings.plain: CRT officers stopped, frisked and searched people unlawfully at higher rates than patrol officers. In this audit 84% of CRT stops, 64% of frisks and 59% of searches were lawful, compared with 92%, 89% and 77% for patrol officers in the monitor's prior report.
findings.quote: 84% for stops, 64% for frisks, and 59% for searches

findings.plain: Supervisory review was largely absent. Reviewing supervisors found a legal basis for all but one of 50 reported CRT stops and deemed every reported frisk and search lawful, even though the monitor found unlawful stops, frisks and searches in the same sample.
findings.quote: There was a lack of meaningful NYPD supervisory review of CRT stops.

findings.plain: Officers mislabeled Terry stops as lower-level encounters and skipped required stop reports. Of 13 encounters on body-worn camera that the monitor determined were Terry stops, only four (31%) had stop reports prepared at the time.
findings.quote: only four (31%) had stop reports prepared documenting the encounters.

findings.plain: The people stopped were overwhelmingly Black and Hispanic men: 97% of the persons stopped, frisked and searched during Terry stops in this audit, and 90% of all persons CRT officers encountered across the three samples.
findings.quote: Ninety-seven percent of the persons stopped, frisked, and searched by CRT officers during...

findings.plain: CRT traffic stops frequently turned into searches that found almost nothing, and officers often sought consent to search without a lawful basis. Of 119 traffic stops in the audit, 75 (63%) involved a search, contraband was recovered in only two (2.7%) and in 38.3% of consent search requests nothing in the video supported the request.
findings.quote: In 38.3% of consent searches, there was nothing evident in the BWC footage

numbers.label: CRT stops found lawful in the audit
CRT stop reports that were self-initiated, third quarter of 2024
Persons encountered who were Black or Hispanic men
Audited traffic stops that involved a search
Traffic-stop searches that found contraband
Consent search requests with no apparent founded suspicion

recommendations: CRT officers should reach the same compliance levels the monitor set for Neighborhood Safety Team officers: at least 85% by the end of the third quarter of 2025 and at least 90% by the end of the year.

The department should tell the monitor what steps it will take to keep officers within the bounds of the Fourth Amendment during traffic stops and consent searches, including any additional training, directives or monitoring that may be required.
As the department finalizes its Fourteenth Amendment compliance plans, it should ensure an analysis of CRT operations is included in the plan's implementation.
audits.agency_response: The City argued that traffic stops and consent searches are beyond the scope of the monitorship; the monitor responded that the Fourth Amendment applies equally to vehicle stops and pedestrian stops. The department agreed with the monitor that the seven mislabeled encounters in the Level 2 sample were Terry stops.
audits.compliance_note: The monitor found CRT stops, frisks and searches lawful less often than those by patrol officers and comparable to the NST and PST specialized units, and directed the teams to reach at least 85% compliance by the end of the third quarter of 2025 and 90% by year end.

audits.title: Final Audit Letter Report on the New York City Employees’ Retirement System’s (NYCERS) Other Than Personal Services (OTPS) Expenditures
audits.plain_title: How the city employees' pension system spends its non-payroll money
audits.agency: New York City Employees' Retirement System
audits.what_they_audited: In this audit letter report, auditors checked whether the New York City Employees' Retirement System (NYCERS) spent its Other Than Personal Services (OTPS) money, meaning expenses unrelated to salaries and benefits such as supplies, travel and vendor contracts, according to its own policies and city rules, and whether the spending was necessary, reasonable and well documented. They reviewed a sample of 77 OTPS expenditures from fiscal years 2023 and 2024.
audits.background: NYCERS is one of the five New York City retirement systems and administers pension benefits for more than 350,000 active members, retirees and beneficiaries. For fiscal year 2024 it reported about $101 billion in assets and spent $130 million on administrative expenses, of which $70 million (53.8%) was OTPS spending.

findings.plain: Most spending followed the rules. The auditors found the money was generally spent in line with internal policies and other regulations and that the expenses were necessary and reasonable, but NYCERS needs better procedures for approving and documenting them.
findings.quote: NYCERS’ OTPS expenditures were, for the most part, spent in accordance with internal policies and procedures and other relevant rules and regulations

findings.plain: NYCERS could not produce purchase orders or contracts for two consultants who were paid a combined $52,250, so it could not show the purchases were approved under the city's Procurement Policy Board rules for small purchases.
findings.quote: NYCERS did not provide purchase orders or contracts for two consultants whose payments totaled $52,250.

findings.plain: Vendors were often paid late. City rules require payment within 30 days of receiving an invoice, but 33 of the 77 sampled invoices, or 43%, were paid later than that with no documented justification.
findings.quote: 33 (43%) of the 77 sampled OTPS invoices were paid more than 30 days after the invoice dates, without justification

findings.plain: NYCERS paid the same $2,000 invoice twice, first with an incorrect purchase order and account number in September 2023 and again with the correct information in January 2024.
findings.quote: NYCERS officials acknowledged that this was a duplicate payment

findings.plain: Travel spending did not consistently follow Comptroller's Directive #6. Of 30 out-of-town trips totaling $54,906 that were reviewed, four employees attended conferences without documented justification, and NYCERS paid for expenses that appeared unnecessary such as extra-legroom seats, lodging above the GSA rate and plane tickets to Washington D.C. instead of Amtrak tickets.
findings.quote: NYCERS also did not provide justification for expenses that appeared to be unnecessary, such as payments for seats with extra legroom, lodging costs that exceeded the GSA rate, and plane tickets to Washington D.C., instead of Amtrak tickets.

findings.plain: NYCERS did not appear to hold its trustees to the travel rules, saying that four trustees who attended six conferences are not required to get approval for travel or file post-conference reports.
findings.quote: In addition, NYCERS appeared not to enforce Directive #6 requirements for trustees who attended conferences.

numbers.label: OTPS spending in fiscal year 2024
Consultant payments with no purchase order or contract
Sampled invoices paid more than 30 days late
Invoice paid twice
Cost of the 30 out-of-town trips reviewed

recommendations: Make sure a purchase order or contract is created for every small or micro purchase.
Pay vendors within 30 days of receiving their invoices.
Recoup the $2,000 overpayment from the vendor or have it credited to NYCERS' account.
Make sure all out-of-town travel costs are approved, including lodging that exceeds GSA rates and extra-legroom charges.
Get all necessary documents before processing payments and reimbursements to avoid paying unnecessary expenses.
Get post-travel attendance reports from everyone who attends out-of-town conferences to show how what they learned benefits NYCERS.
audits.agency_response: NYCERS agreed with five of the six findings and recommendations and disagreed with one, saying its trustees are not employees and do not need formal travel approval or post-travel reports. The auditors maintained that NYCERS should still collect post-travel reports from everyone who attends conferences.

audits.title: Audit of the Behavioral Health Emergency Assistance Response Division’s Effectiveness in Responding to Individuals with Mental Health Crises and Meeting Its Goals
audits.plain_title: Is the city's non-police mental health crisis team reaching people?
audits.agency: New York City Mayor's Office of Community Mental Health
audits.what_they_audited: Auditors examined whether the Behavioral Health Emergency Assistance Response Division (B-HEARD), the pilot program that sends social workers and Emergency Medical Technicians (EMTs) instead of police officers to 911 mental health calls, is meeting its goals and effectively serving patients. The program is administered by the Mayor's Office of Community Mental Health (OCMH) and run jointly with the fire department's Emergency Medical Services, New York City Health + Hospitals and the police department.
audits.background: B-HEARD was established as a pilot in 2021 as a health-centered alternative to the traditional response to mental health crises, which sends New York City Police Department officers and an ambulance with two EMTs. Its goals include routing 911 mental health calls to a health-centered response, reducing unnecessary use of police resources, increasing connection to community-based care and reducing unnecessary hospital transports; its fiscal year 2024 budget was $35.9 million.

findings.plain: The pilot is limited in when it operates, where it operates and which calls qualify, so many people who might need a B-HEARD team instead get the traditional response of police officers and an ambulance.
findings.quote: The Behavioral Health Emergency Assistance Response Division (B-HEARD) pilot program is limited in its hours of operation, its geographic distribution, and in the types of calls considered eligible for a response.

findings.plain: Because the program only runs from 9am to 1am, more than 14,000 calls that qualified for a B-HEARD team between January 2022 and September 2024 got a traditional response simply because they came in overnight.
findings.quote: Over 14,000 calls determined to be eligible for a B-HEARD team did not receive one because the calls were received during the overnight hours, when the pilot does not operate.

findings.plain: Even during operating hours, about a third of qualifying calls got no B-HEARD response. OCMH does not track why, though officials said team unavailability is the most likely reason.
findings.quote: 13,042 (35%) of the 37,113 calls determined to be eligible for B-HEARD did not receive program services.

findings.plain: The program fields just 18 teams split across two shifts and covers only 31 of the city's 78 police precincts across four boroughs, with no coverage in Staten Island.
findings.quote: The B-HEARD program is currently active in 31 (40%) of the 78 precincts in the City.

findings.plain: Of the 96,291 mental health calls received in pilot areas during program hours over fiscal years 2022 to 2024, more than 60% were counted as ineligible, a figure that includes calls that were never triaged at all, for instance because no fire department call-taker was available.
findings.quote: Of these, 59,178 calls (over 60%) were considered “ineligible” for a B-HEARD response by OCMH.

findings.plain: The share of B-HEARD responses that included a mental health assessment, which teams are expected to conduct, fell from 55% in fiscal year 2022 to 25% in fiscal year 2024, and OCMH does not track the reasons assessments are not done.
findings.quote: During FY2022, only 55% of the calls that B-HEARD teams responded to resulted in a mental health assessment of the patient. This number decreased to 31% in FY2023 and 25% in FY2024

findings.plain: OCMH's data collection is too weak to tell whether the program is working. It does not track why calls are not triaged, why eligible calls get no B-HEARD response, how often police officers request a B-HEARD team or whether people receive treatment after the initial crisis intervention.
findings.quote: The auditors found that OCMH’s overall tracking of program and performance data is inadequate.

numbers.label: Mental health 911 calls in pilot areas, fiscal 2022-2024
Calls deemed eligible for a B-HEARD response
Eligible calls that got no B-HEARD response
Eligible calls received outside program hours
B-HEARD teams covering two shifts
Program budget for fiscal year 2024
Responses with a mental health assessment in fiscal 2024

recommendations: Formally assess the citywide need for B-HEARD mental health response teams.
Work with partner agencies to expand the program's reach and number of teams in line with established need, including covering the overnight hours.

Work with the fire department to explore additional ways, such as tuition assistance, livable wages or loan forgiveness, to recruit enough qualified EMS responders so all eligible calls are triaged and answered.

Work with partner agencies to develop performance metrics and collect the data needed to evaluate the program, including reasons calls are ineligible or untriaged, reasons eligible calls get no response, police responses caused by team unavailability and reasons assessments are not performed.
Work with the fire department to require EMS responders to consistently update the final call type on every call so eligible-call counts are accurate.
Continue developing ways to increase contact with and assessments of patients when B-HEARD teams respond.
Continue working with the New York State Office of Mental Health and Health Department to expand community-based care centers across all five boroughs.
audits.agency_response: OCMH agreed with three recommendations, partially agreed with three and disagreed with one, on updating final call types, calling it infeasible and outside its role. It also disputed any need for increased oversight or improved metrics and said many issues were outside its purview, positions the auditors strenuously disagreed with.

audits.title: Nineteenth Report for the Monitoring Period July 1, 2024 to December 31, 2024
audits.plain_title: Rikers shows momentum under new leadership but violence stays high
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: The court-appointed independent monitor's 19th compliance assessment of the Department of Correction under the Nunez consent judgment and remedial orders, covering July through December 2024, including the department's use of force, its management of people with a propensity for violence, body-worn cameras and compliance with dozens of specific court order provisions.
audits.background: The report was filed nearly 10 years after the consent judgment took effect in fall 2015, days after the court's May 13, 2025 order creating a remediation manager to address the city's contempt. Five commissioners have led the agency in that time, at least 10 remedial orders have been issued and the monitor describes 2021 to 2023 as a period of extraordinary instability and danger in the jails.

findings.plain: The monitor found the department appears to be emerging from its crisis phase, with tangible momentum toward reform since Commissioner Maginley-Liddie's appointment in December 2023, though the road to sustainable reform remains very long.
findings.quote: As will be described throughout this report, the Department appears to be emerging from

findings.plain: Of the 39 court order provisions rated or updated in the report, the commissioner's team moved the department from non-compliance into partial compliance on 10, sustained progress on 15 already in partial or substantial compliance, made progress on seven others and left seven with no progress.
findings.quote: moved the Department out of Non-Compliance and into Partial Compliance

findings.plain: Key measures of violence and use of force remain far above where they stood when the consent judgment took effect: the systemwide use of force rate was 9.13 in 2024 versus 3.96 in 2016, and the fight rate was 9.95 versus 5.11.
findings.quote: substantially higher than those observed at the time the Consent Judgment went into effect

findings.plain: After ten years, the monitor sees signs that staff practice on use of force has started to change, but says it is too early to draw definitive conclusions and the department has made little progress in reducing how often staff use force.
findings.quote: certain signs that Staff practice has started to change

findings.plain: Excessive and unnecessary uses of force remain pervasive, and the risk of harm in the jails remains high for both incarcerated people and staff.
findings.quote: ...unnecessary uses of force are still pervasive

findings.plain: The commissioner's administration catalyzed improvements including restored collaboration with the monitor, stronger leaders, better searches and contraband recovery, an improved restrictive housing unit, faster staff discipline, upgraded body-worn cameras and steps against staff absenteeism.
findings.quote: ...administration has demonstrated greater acknowledgement and ownership of core problems and

numbers.label: Provisions subject to compliance ratings or updates in the report
Provisions moved from non-compliance into partial compliance
Systemwide monthly use of force rate in 2024, up from 3.96 in 2016
Systemwide monthly fight rate in 2024, up from 5.11 in 2016

recommendations: Staff must reduce unnecessary uses of force, including head strikes and dangerous takedowns.
Improved security practices must be embedded into staff practice through the department's security plan work.
The department must continue reducing staff absenteeism and improve deployment of staff to housing unit and other facility posts that engage the incarcerated population.
Officers and captains must properly manage and supervise housing units to reduce interpersonal violence and assaults on staff.
Staff must be properly deployed to housing unit posts to ensure supervision and service delivery, and facility leadership must be more directly involved in identifying and fixing poor practice.
The department must reduce investigative caseloads by triaging incidents so administrative reviews handle simpler cases and resources go to incidents needing in-depth investigation.
Accountability for staff misconduct must be imposed closer in time to the incidents in which misconduct occurs.
audits.agency_response: The monitor writes that the commissioner's administration has shown greater acknowledgement and ownership of core problems than past leadership, which it calls critical for institutional change.
audits.compliance_note: Of the 39 provisions assessed, the department newly reached partial compliance on 10 and sustained progress on 15, but the monitor stresses that violence and use of force rates remain substantially higher than when the consent judgment took effect and the risk of harm remains high.

audits.title: Twenty-Fourth Report of the Independent Monitor: Compliance Snapshot of NYPD’s Stop, Frisk, and Search Practices
audits.plain_title: NYPD stop and frisk compliance snapshot for 2024
audits.agency: New York City Police Department
audits.what_they_audited: A visual "compliance snapshot" of how well New York City Police Department (NYPD) stops, frisks and searches complied with the federal court's requirements in Floyd v. City of New York, Ligon v. City of New York and Davis v. City of New York, based on the monitor team's audits of stop reports and body-worn camera videos through 2024.
audits.background: The independent monitor oversees the NYPD's compliance with federal court orders in the Floyd, Ligon and Davis stop and frisk cases. The monitor's audits assess whether stops, frisks and searches complied with the Fourth Amendment, reviewing samples of 100 stop reports per month and 225 body-worn camera videos per quarter.

findings.plain: Compliance rose over the first three quarters of 2024. In the third quarter, the monitor's audits found 91% of reported stops, 79% of frisks and 78% of searches were lawful.
findings.quote: 91% of stops, 79% of frisks, and 78% of searches were assessed as lawful

findings.plain: Stops that officers initiated on their own observations were far less lawful than stops responding to 911 or 311 calls or witness information. For the first three quarters of 2024, self-initiated stops were lawful 79% of the time, with frisks at 60% and searches at 66%.
findings.quote: ...complainant information were lawful, and 79% of self-initiated stops were lawful.

findings.plain: Most NYPD commands fell short of even an 85% lawfulness rate for frisks and searches: in the third quarter of 2024 only 46% of commands cleared that bar for frisks and only 27% did for searches.
findings.quote: In other words, most NYPD commands did not achieve minimum...

findings.plain: Supervision was a critical gap. The monitor found 11% of stops, 26% of frisks and 26% of searches unlawful in the third quarter of 2024, while NYPD reviewing supervisors approved nearly everything, flagging only 3% of stops, 1% of frisks and 7% of searches. The NYPD's own Quality Assurance Section audits, by contrast, had improved and closely mirrored the monitor's findings.
findings.quote: ...approved close to 100% of all stops, frisks, and searches and barely identified any...

findings.plain: Officers often did not document stops. About 38% of stops identified in the monitor's audits over 2022 to 2024 went unreported, and in the fourth quarter of 2024 officers failed to complete stop reports for 30% of stops the audit identified.
findings.quote: approximately 38% of stops in the Monitor’s audits have gone...

findings.plain: Stops prompted by complainants or radio runs led to arrests far more often than self-initiated stops. In the fourth quarter of 2024 the arrest rate was 41% for complainant stops and 42% for radio run stops, versus 11% for self-initiated stops and just 7% for self-initiated stops for suspected weapon possession.
findings.quote: the arrest rate for RR stops was 42%; the arrest rate for all SI stops was 11%

findings.plain: Housing Bureau officers had lower compliance than the department overall: in the first half of 2024, 77% of their stops, 52% of frisks and 48% of searches were lawful, though trespass arrests showed high compliance (98% had an objective credible reason to approach and 99% had probable cause).
findings.quote: 77% of stops, 52% of frisks, and 48% of searches were assessed as lawful

numbers.label: Reported stops found lawful, third quarter of 2024
Stops that went unreported, 2022 through 2024
Stops missing a stop report, fourth quarter of 2024
Arrest rate for self-initiated weapon stops, fourth quarter of 2024
Commands with search compliance above 85%, third quarter of 2024

recommendations: The report makes no new formal recommendations.
audits.compliance_note: The monitor found compliance improving during 2024 but still short of the court's requirements: most commands did not reach 85% lawfulness for frisks and searches, supervisors approved nearly all stops including unlawful ones and underreporting of stops continued to be a problem.

audits.title: DOI's Investigation of Excessive Workers' Compensation Claims by City Department of Correction Employees
audits.plain_title: Correction employees' injury claims cost the city over $340 million
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) examined the volume and cost of workers' compensation claims filed by New York City Department of Correction (DOC) employees, after several city agencies including the City Law Department raised concerns about the claims.
audits.background: Under New York law employers must pay workers' compensation benefits when an employee is disabled by an on-the-job injury, and the city self-insures, meaning awards are directly funded by public money. The Law Department represents the city in proceedings before the state Workers' Compensation Board.

findings.plain: In fiscal year 2024 the city paid more than $340 million for workers' compensation claims by correction department employees, compared with just under $225 million for claims by employees of all other mayoral agencies combined.
findings.quote: it paid just under $225 million for claims by  employees of all other

findings.plain: Over fiscal years 2022 through 2024, the city's total spending on claims by correction employees passed the billion-dollar mark.
findings.quote: compensation claims by DOC employees exceeded $1 billion.

findings.plain: Between fiscal 2015 and fiscal 2024, workers' compensation expenses for correction employees grew about 337%, from roughly $78 million to roughly $341 million, while expenses for all other mayoral agencies combined grew only 65%.
findings.quote: expenses for DOC employees grew by approximately 337%

findings.plain: Correction employees led all mayoral agencies in claims filed, with 3,547 new claims in fiscal 2024. Many claims that drove the increase were for permanent partial disability, where employees can collect lump-sum Schedule Loss of Use awards while continuing to draw their usual wages.
findings.quote:
many 
DOC employees who receive SLU awards have also continued to receive their usual 
wages on top of significant payments

findings.plain: DOI and federal prosecutors announced charges against one current and two former correction officers for allegedly fraudulent claims. DOI said it cannot yet conclude that other employees are submitting false claims but that the pattern raises serious concerns that fraud goes beyond the three charged.
findings.quote:
the pattern of claims by 
DOC employees as described above raises serious concerns that fraud in the workers’ 
compensation space goes well beyond these three charged employees.

numbers.label: Paid for DOC employees' claims in fiscal year 2024
Paid for all other mayoral agencies' claims that year
Total DOC claim costs over fiscal years 2022-2024
Growth in DOC claim expenses, fiscal 2015 to 2024
New claims filed by DOC employees in fiscal 2024

recommendations: The Law Department should appoint a Director of Claims Integrity to identify potentially fraudulent workers' compensation claims by city employees and serve as a liaison referring possible fraud to DOI.
The Law Department should evaluate the anti-fraud training it gives city employees who review and approve workers' compensation claims, in coordination with DOI, to decide whether changes are needed.

The correction department should appoint a Director of Workplace Safety to monitor accident statistics, examine safety conditions at its facilities, develop clear safety protocols and train employees on workplace safety.
The correction department should update and reissue Directive #1004, its procedures for filing workers' compensation claims.
audits.agency_response: The Law Department accepted both of its recommendations, the first contingent on city funding for the new position. The correction department said it will consider appointing a workplace safety director and accepted the recommendation to update its claims-filing directive.

audits.title: Audit Report on the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene’s Oversight of Doula Programs in Underserved Neighborhoods
audits.plain_title: Are the city's free doula programs improving birth outcomes?
audits.agency: New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene
audits.what_they_audited: Auditors assessed how the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH) runs the Citywide Doula Initiative (CDI), which provides free doula support to people in underserved neighborhoods, shelters and foster homes, and whether the program is increasing access to doula services and reducing negative birth outcomes for clients from March 2022 through June 2024.
audits.background: City laws require DOHMH to expand access to doula services and to provide them at no cost to residents of marginalized neighborhoods in all five boroughs. DOHMH contracted with seven vendors to provide CDI doula services, with $4,066,429.32 approved for services and training from March 2022 through June 2024, in a city where Black non-Hispanic women accounted for 17.7% of live births in 2021 but 39.7% of pregnancy-associated deaths.

findings.plain: The program is reaching its target areas. All 33 neighborhoods identified as underserved by the city's Taskforce on Racial Inclusion & Equity now have access to CDI doula services, and use of the services has grown quickly.
findings.quote: the number of CDI doula visits conducted during the second quarters of Calendar Years 2022 through 2024 has increased an average of 75% each year

findings.plain: Black and Hispanic women who used CDI doulas had better birth outcomes than Black and Hispanic women citywide, with lower rates of C-sections, low birth weight and pre-term births. CDI clients also breastfed exclusively at a 53% rate versus 40.4% citywide, and no pregnancy-associated deaths were reported among CDI clients during the audit period.
findings.quote: among both Black and Hispanic women, CDI clients fared better than those in the general population in all three categories of negative birth outcomes relating to C-sections, low birth weights, and pre-term births

findings.plain: Results were weaker for Asian American/Pacific Islander (AAPI) and White clients, though far fewer of them participated in the program, so there was much less data to go on.
findings.quote: Birthing outcomes of White CDI clients varied when compared to citywide birth outcome rates, while birthing outcomes of AAPI CDI clients were worse than citywide birth outcome rates.

findings.plain: Pregnant people living in homeless shelters are not getting doula services as reliably as other clients. About half of doulas surveyed said shelter clients were difficult or impossible to reach, with some shelters denying entry and others requiring caseworker approval that delays services.
findings.quote: Clients residing in shelters are not receiving doula services with the same level of consistency as CDI clients not residing in shelters, either because doulas are delayed waiting for case worker approvals or because some shelters outright deny doulas access to their clients.

findings.plain: There are not enough doulas who speak languages other than English. Clients requested services in another language 321 times, and while six of the seven vendors could serve clients in Spanish, fewer than half could cover other languages.
findings.quote: Vendors that responded to the survey reported a need for non-English-speaking doulas.

findings.plain: Some hospitals still get in doulas' way. In DOHMH's own survey, doulas reported being prevented from helping clients use the restroom, supporting mobility out of bed or staying with clients during delivery.
findings.quote: DOHMH’s assessment and the audit’s review of the Doula Assessment survey found that a significant portion of doulas were prevented from providing certain care.

findings.plain: DOHMH stores program data across multiple datasets instead of one comprehensive one, which makes it labor intensive to analyze whether the program is achieving its goals.
findings.quote: However, the agency does not maintain a single comprehensive dataset containing key data (e.g., doula services provided, clients served, birth outcomes) relating to the CDI.

numbers.label: Underserved neighborhoods with access to CDI doula services
Average yearly growth in CDI doula visits
Approved for CDI services and training, March 2022-June 2024
CDI live births exclusively breastfed, versus 40.4% citywide
Client requests for services in a language other than English
Doulas who said shelter clients were hard or impossible to reach

recommendations: Make all reasonable efforts to collect or use available provisional citywide birth outcome data so CDI client rates can be compared with citywide rates sooner.
Consolidate data collection into more efficient reporting to determine how well doula services reduce negative birth outcomes and maternal mortality.
Increase the number of doulas who speak languages other than English.
Continue working with the Department of Homeless Services to increase doula access to clients in shelters.
Continue promoting doula-friendly policies in the Maternity Hospital Quality Improvement Network hospitals and expand the incorporation of doulas into hospital birthing teams.
Build client satisfaction surveys into data collection and evaluate satisfaction by vendor, analyzing differences in practice that may affect satisfaction.
Conduct additional studies of outcomes for AAPI and White women to understand why the program appears to help them less.
audits.agency_response: DOHMH agreed with six of the seven recommendations and disagreed with one, on studying outcomes for AAPI and White women, saying the program's focus is Black and Hispanic birth outcomes and the sample sizes for those groups were very small. The auditors responded that the worse outcomes for those clients should not be dismissed without closer consideration.

audits.title: Audit of the New York City Department of Buildings’ Enforcement of Building Codes
audits.plain_title: How the buildings department enforces the building code
audits.agency: New York City Department of Buildings
audits.what_they_audited: Auditors examined whether the Department of Buildings (DOB) enforces building codes for one- and two-family properties in an equitable way, so that no communities are disproportionately impacted, covering calendar years 2022, 2023 and the first quarter of 2024. The audit was prompted by housing advocates' concerns that small property owners, particularly in communities of color, are hit hardest by violations and fines.
audits.background: DOB regulates more than 1,000,000 buildings and over 40,000 active construction sites, issuing summonses through the Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings (OATH) when properties violate the construction codes. If an immediately hazardous violation is not certified as corrected within 60 days, owners can be issued a Failure to Comply summons that repeats every 60 days, and owners who miss their hearings face default judgments with maximum penalties.

findings.plain: DOB's enforcement of existing one- and two-family homes is essentially driven by anonymous 311 complaints. The agency identified no other routine way of checking whether such properties comply with the code, so it cannot tell whether the most-penalized communities actually have the most violations or just the most complaints.
findings.quote: The audit found that the Department of Buildings (DOB) relies almost exclusively on 311 complaints for its enforcement actions, and that certain communities were disproportionately impacted by penalties that were assessed as a result.

findings.plain: The penalties fell hardest on lower-income areas. Black households were among the two largest demographic groups in seven of the 10 community districts with the most one- and two-family properties carrying $20,000 or more in accumulated penalties.
findings.quote: seven of the 10 community districts with the most one- and two-family properties with high accumulated penalties had median household incomes below the Citywide median
