findings.plain: DOB issued 13,466 OATH violations with $38.3 million in fines against one- and two-family properties in 2022 and 2023, and most of the penalty dollars came from illegal conversions and from owners who missed their hearings.
findings.quote: Overall, default judgments accounted for 63% ($24.3 million out of $38.3 million) of the total penalties imposed during the audit scope for one- and two-family properties

findings.plain: Some homeowners were fined for failing to fix violations they legally could not fix yet, because the correction plans they had submitted were still awaiting DOB approval. Three more owners were fined within 60 days of getting plan approval, leaving little time to do the work.
findings.quote: In four cases, homeowners still had seven plans pending with DOB when they were issued eight FTC violations with fines totaling $17,500.

findings.plain: Plan reviews are getting much slower and vary widely by borough. In the first quarter of 2024 the citywide average from plan submission to approval for major alterations was 124 business days, ranging from an average of 100 business days in Staten Island to 175 in the Bronx, and penalties keep accruing until the violation is fixed.
findings.quote: the number of days taken by DOB for its plan reviews increased 80% Citywide, as the number of applications filed Citywide also increased by 106%

findings.plain: DOB has no time targets for completing plan reviews and, since April 2022, has stopped publicly reporting its plan review and approval times, tracking them internally only.
findings.quote: The audit found that DOB has not established time targets for plan reviews and permit approvals.

findings.plain: The Homeowner Relief Program, which gives eligible owners a chance to fix problems without a summons, appears to have had limited success: of 9,167 substantiated complaints handled under the program, only 19% were confirmed corrected and most were never re-inspected at all.
findings.quote: 5,504 (60%) remained open with no evidence of an attempted re-inspection by DOB

numbers.label: Fines against one- and two-family homes, 2022-2023
OATH violations issued to one- and two-family homes
Share of penalty dollars from default judgments
Fines issued while correction plans awaited DOB approval
Average plan approval time citywide, early 2024
Homeowner Relief Program complaints never re-inspected

recommendations: Re-evaluate the total reliance on complaints to drive code enforcement and consider additional approaches.
Consider ways to track the source of complaints and other remedies to make sure the 311 complaint system is not abused to target certain communities.
Change processes so Failure to Comply summonses are not issued while correction plans are still pending DOB review, or within 60 days of DOB approving a plan.
Establish education and engagement strategies in the communities most affected by illegal conversions, emphasizing the financial impact of violations, fines and penalties.
Work with OATH to educate the public about the financial consequences of defaulting on summonses.
Restore the practice of publicly reporting service levels, including plan approval times, on the agency's website tracker.
Identify why review times vary among the boroughs, work to reduce those variances and minimize review times, and set time targets for plan reviews.
Set key performance indicators for the Homeowner Relief Program to assess its effectiveness.
Formally survey participants in homeowner-assistance initiatives about their satisfaction and possible improvements.
audits.agency_response: DOB agreed with three recommendations, partially agreed with two and disagreed with four, including the calls to look beyond complaints, track complaint sources, hold off on Failure to Comply summonses while plans are pending and set plan review time targets. DOB also argued the finding of disproportionate impact on lower-income districts was unfounded; the auditors responded that DOB was conflating intent with impact.

audits.title: Oversight of Horizon and Crossroads Juvenile Centers
audits.plain_title: How the city runs its two juvenile detention centers
audits.agency: New York City Administration for Children's Services
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the New York City Administration for Children's Services (ACS) adequately operates the Horizon and Crossroads juvenile detention centers for court-placed youth, meeting federal, state and city health and safety standards and providing required services. The audit covered October 2018 through December 2023.
audits.background: ACS runs the city's two secure juvenile detention facilities, Horizon in the Bronx and Crossroads in Brooklyn, providing medical, mental health, case management and educational services to detained youth. Between October 2018 and March 2023, 3,643 youth were admitted to the two facilities, and police data show the number of people under 18 accused of major crimes increased sharply in the city from 2021 to 2024.

findings.plain: ACS did not adequately make sure intake and case management services happened on time. Only 53% of sampled youth got the required initial intake interview within 24 hours, and one youth did not get an interview until 76 days after admission.
findings.quote: Only 53% of the youth sampled received an initial intake interview within 24 hours, as required. One youth did not receive an interview until 76 days after being admitted to the facility.

findings.plain: Case managers often missed required check-ins: 94% of sampled youth did not get all their required daily face-to-face meetings with their case manager, some assessments were not completed and service records were incomplete or missing.
findings.quote: 94% of the youth sampled did not receive all their daily face-to-face meetings with their case manager, as required.

findings.plain: ACS under-reported incidents to the state Office of Children and Family Services (OCFS): 37% of 9,693 unique incidents recorded in ACS' own database were never reported to OCFS through the state's Juvenile Detention Automated System.
findings.quote: 37% of 9,693 unique incidents at the two detention facilities were not reported to OCFS through JDAS

findings.plain: Serious incidents were reported late. A youth setting a garbage can on fire was not reported for 24 hours though immediate reporting is required, 14 incidents including sexual abuse and assault were reported 1 to 22 days late, and a May 2020 escape attempt at Crossroads was not reported until 2 days later.
findings.quote: 14 incidents including sexual abuse, assault, harassment, employee misconduct, and contraband were required to be reported within 24 hours—but were reported from 1 to 22 days late.

findings.plain: Contraband prevention is falling short. Reported contraband incidents rose from 62 in 2019 to 706 in 2023, an increase of more than 1,038%, and auditors watched an ACS official pass through security at Horizon with two cell phones despite a policy barring employees from bringing personal phones inside.
findings.quote: The number of reported contraband incidents increased from 62 in 2019 to 706 in 2023—over a 1,038% increase.

findings.plain: School attendance oversight was inadequate: both facilities showed chronic absenteeism across all educational programs and ages, with 13-73% of days absent, even though classes are on site and ACS staff are responsible for walking students to class.
findings.quote: Both facilities exhibited chronic absenteeism levels across all educational programs and ages, ranging from 13-73% days absent.

numbers.label: Youth admitted to the two facilities, October 2018 to March 2023
Sampled youth who got an intake interview within 24 hours
Sampled youth missing required daily case manager meetings
Of 9,693 incidents never reported to the state
Contraband incidents in 2023, up from 62 in 2019
Range of school days absent across programs

recommendations: Make sure ACS policies for intake, housing and case management are communicated to staff, and set up monitoring to ensure compliance.
Report all incidents in ACS' internal database to the Office of Children and Family Services through the state system, and monitor the timeliness and accuracy of that reporting.
Establish monitoring procedures and periodic reviews to make sure all incidents are entered into the state system on time and accurately.
Evaluate and strengthen, as needed, policies and practices for preventing and detecting contraband.
Work with New York City Public Schools, the Office of Children and Family Services and other stakeholders to minimize youth absenteeism from school.

audits.title: Street Construction-Related Permits (Follow-Up)
audits.plain_title: Follow-up on oversight of street construction permits
audits.agency: New York City Department of Transportation
audits.what_they_audited: How far the New York City Department of Transportation (DOT) has gotten in carrying out the nine recommendations from a 2022 audit of how it manages street construction-related permits, which cover work such as street openings, sidewalk construction and canopy installation.
audits.background: DOT is responsible for more than 6,300 miles of streets and highways and issues 150 different types of sidewalk and roadway construction permits. The initial audit, issued in June 2022, found DOT did not always make sure permittees complied with permit requirements, including that 41,761 street opening permits that should have been inspected were not, that follow-up on corrective action requests lacked set time frames and documentation and that DOT did not verify insurance or restrict non-emergency work on recently resurfaced streets.

findings.plain: DOT has made some progress on the issues identified in the initial report.
findings.quote: DOT officials made some progress in addressing the issues we identified in the initial report.

findings.plain: Of the nine recommendations in the initial report, DOT implemented two, partially implemented six and did not implement one.
findings.quote: Of the initial report’s nine recommendations, two were implemented, six were partially implemented, and one was not implemented.

numbers.label: Uninspected street opening permits flagged in initial audit
Miles of streets and highways DOT oversees, at minimum
Types of construction permits DOT issues

recommendations: DOT officials are asked, but not required, to report within 30 days on any actions planned to address the unresolved issues in the follow-up report.
audits.implementation_note: Of the 9 recommendations in the 2022 audit, the follow-up found 2 implemented, 6 partially implemented and 1 not implemented.

audits.title: Audit Report on the New York City Department of Education/School Construction Authority’s Asbestos Management Program
audits.plain_title: Are schools getting their required asbestos inspections?
audits.agency: New York City Department of Education and School Construction Authority
audits.what_they_audited: Auditors checked whether the Department of Education (DOE) and School Construction Authority (SCA) are inspecting every public school building for asbestos hazards every three years and every six months as the federal Asbestos Hazard Emergency Response Act (AHERA) requires, and whether asbestos found in inspections is documented and management plans are kept up as mandated.
audits.background: Asbestos fibers, once airborne and inhaled, can cause severe diseases including asbestosis, lung cancer and mesothelioma, and AHERA was enacted in 1986 to protect students, teachers and school staff from exposure. As of March 2024, about 1,431 of the roughly 1,700 New York City school buildings, about 80%, were identified as containing asbestos containing materials (ACM) and are subject to AHERA's inspection requirements.

findings.plain: DOE has been out of compliance with the federal asbestos law for decades. Since 1997, across nine three-year inspection cycles, DOE conducted an average of only 11% of the required triennial inspections, with one cycle at 0%.
findings.quote: The audit found that DOE is not in compliance with Asbestos Hazard Emergency Response Act (AHERA) regulations and has not been for many years.

findings.plain: In the most recent three-year cycle, from March 2021 to March 2024, just 18% of schools with known asbestos got the required triennial reinspection, leaving 1,175 buildings unassessed. DOE typically does 200 to 250 inspections every three years but needs about 480 per year to comply.
findings.quote: only 257 of the 1,431 buildings (18%) with identified ACM received the triennial inspection required by AHERA

findings.plain: The required twice-a-year surveillance inspections are also mostly not happening. From May 2023 to April 2024, only 22% of the required periodic inspections were completed, and compliance was similarly low in every borough.
findings.quote: a total of 620 of the required 2,862 periodic surveillance inspections were performed

findings.plain: DOE has no centralized system for tracking this work. It did not start tracking periodic inspections until March 2023, previously relying on outdated management plans and, in some schools, custodians who lacked the training AHERA requires.
findings.quote: DOE maintains no centralized recordkeeping system with reporting features to support compliance with AHERA.

findings.plain: Evidence of mandatory asbestos training was inadequate or missing for most of 2020 through 2023, and the required annual notifications to parents, teachers and employee organizations were sent only to DOE email addresses, so auditors could not verify all stakeholders were reached.
findings.quote: DOE did not maintain training records during most of the period from 2020 to 2023, and while complete records exist for 2024, DOE lacked training certificates for all custodians in the previous years

findings.plain: Poor coordination between DOE and SCA has left 57 school buildings with asbestos status listed as to be determined, and delays in certifying buildings as asbestos-free led to unnecessary spending. One Queens school got its certification 13 years after opening, after DOE had paid for inspections it may not have needed.
findings.quote: In April 2022, DOE spent about $31,000 on one triennial and one periodic inspection because the ACM status had not been determined for over 10 years.

numbers.label: School buildings identified as containing asbestos
Schools with a triennial inspection, March 2021-March 2024
Required six-month inspections completed, May 2023-April 2024
Average share of required triennial inspections done since 1997
School buildings with asbestos status listed as to be determined
Spent on inspections at one school lacking asbestos-free certification

recommendations: Improve awareness and understanding of AHERA compliance among school officials and the designated compliance officer.
Develop and adopt comprehensive policies and procedures for asbestos management in schools, including internal reporting and review mechanisms to ensure full compliance.

Develop a plan with specific milestones to bring triennial and periodic inspections up to date, including a historical review of inspection data, a phased plan prioritizing buildings with the longest gaps, adequate resources and consultants, and a detailed schedule covering all 1,431 buildings.
Implement a recordkeeping system with reporting features to ensure accountability and compliance.
Document ongoing inspection and management-plan efforts to minimize potential penalties and demonstrate good-faith compliance.
Make sure all custodians and asbestos handlers are adequately trained and keep evidence of that training.
Make sure all stakeholders are adequately notified of asbestos-related activities.
Develop a standard procedure for promptly determining a school's asbestos status, including timely receipt and monitoring of asbestos-free certification letters from SCA.
SCA should keep the asbestos status of all new school buildings and additions current, and investigate and address delays in providing asbestos-free certification letters to DOE.
audits.agency_response: DOE and SCA both agreed with every recommendation. DOE officials did not dispute the low inspection rates but asserted there was no risk of asbestos exposure given its abatement practices, a position the auditors disagreed with.

audits.title: Eleventh Annual Report of DOI's Office of the Inspector General for the NYPD
audits.plain_title: Police watchdog's year in review: half its fixes adopted
audits.agency: New York City Police Department
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation's (DOI) Office of the Inspector General for the New York City Police Department (OIG-NYPD) issued its annual report, required by Local Law 70, reviewing each of its 23 investigative reports and one statement of findings issued between 2015 and December 31, 2024 and the status of 240 recommendations.
audits.background: Local Law 70 established OIG-NYPD as part of DOI to oversee the New York City Police Department (NYPD). The annual report tracks the office's investigations and how NYPD and the Civilian Complaint Review Board (CCRB) have responded to its recommendations; recommendations made in 2024, with responses due in 2025, are not assessed.

findings.plain: NYPD has fully implemented 120 of the 238 recommendations OIG-NYPD issued to it through 2024, about 50%, and accepted in principle or partially implemented 46 more, about 19%. Two recommendations to the CCRB have also been implemented.
findings.quote:
NYPD has fully implemented 12 0 of 2 38 
recommendations issued to them , or approximately 50%; and accepted in principle  or partially implemented  46 
recommendations, or approximately 19%.

findings.plain: In its May 2024 Public Oversight of Surveillance Technology (POST) Act report, the office found NYPD issued no new Impact and Use Policies for five surveillance technologies introduced in 2023 and used grouping too expansively by folding the Digidog robot into an existing policy. Of seven recommendations, NYPD accepted five and rejected two.
findings.quote:
OIG -NYPD found that NYPD utilized grouping in an overly 
expansive manner by addressing Digidog within an existing IUP, rather than issuing an individual IUP.

findings.plain: The December 2024 POST Act report on drones found NYPD's unmanned aircraft policy did not describe all the capabilities of its drone fleet or accurately reflect operations in practice. NYPD accepted all ten recommendations.
findings.quote:
the UAS IUP did not describe all the capabilities of its drone fleet or provide 
a complete and accurate picture of NYPD UAS operations in practice.

findings.plain: The office's review of NYPD's Community Response Team found the quality-of-life unit had no mission statement, no unit-specific policies and procedures and striking gaps in data collection and analysis. NYPD accepted six of seven recommendations and rejected one.
findings.quote:
CRT had no mission statement, no policies and procedures specifically related to the unit, and striking gaps in 
data collection and analysis.

findings.plain: Beyond its investigations, OIG-NYPD participated in 147 outreach events across the city in 2024 to promote awareness of its work and hear policing concerns.
findings.quote: participating in 147 events (virtual and in -person) across the City to promote awareness of its work

numbers.label: Recommendations whose status the report discusses
Recommendations NYPD has fully implemented, of 238
Accepted in principle or partially implemented
Investigative reports issued since 2015
Outreach events in 2024

recommendations: The report makes no new formal recommendations; it reviews the office's prior reports and tracks the status of the 240 recommendations already issued to NYPD and the CCRB.
audits.agency_response: Per the report, NYPD has accepted or implemented nearly 70 percent of OIG-NYPD's recommendations, including accepting five of seven from the May 2024 POST Act report, all ten drone recommendations and six of seven Community Response Team recommendations.
audits.implementation_note: Of 238 recommendations issued to NYPD through 2024, 120 were fully implemented (about 50%) and 46 were accepted in principle or partially implemented (about 19%); two recommendations to the CCRB were implemented.

audits.title: Safeguarding NYCHA Residents: A Review of Select Safety Measures at Senior Buildings & Compliance with Fire Guard Requirements
audits.plain_title: Guards at public housing senior buildings often just weren't there
audits.agency: New York City Housing Authority
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) examined oversight of contracted security guards at New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) senior buildings, which house residents 62 and older, and compliance with fire guard requirements at NYCHA developments.
audits.background: The investigation was prompted by March 2022 media reports on security lapses at NYCHA's Corsi Houses in East Harlem, where the front door did not lock. NYCHA contracted with FJC Security, doing business as Allied Universal Security Services, for guard services, and the city fire code requires round-the-clock fire guards in buildings with uncorrected fire safety deficiencies.

findings.plain: In DOI's surveillance of randomly selected senior buildings, 64 of 94 scheduled security guards, about 68%, were absent for all or part of their required shift. Fifty-four abandoned their post for an average of about two hours and five never showed for their entire eight-hour shift.
findings.quote:
64 of the 94 scheduled security guards (approximately 68%) were absent for all or part of their 
required shift

findings.plain: Some absent guards falsified handwritten timesheets to indicate they worked a full shift, causing NYCHA to be billed for services that were not provided.
findings.quote:
falsified their handwritten timesheets to indicate that they had worked 
their entire shift, jeopardizing the safety of NYCHA residents

findings.plain: During in-person inspections, about nine of 28 lobby doors, roughly 32%, were not secure, and 44 of 63 senior buildings, about 70%, had closed-circuit cameras that were inoperable or could not be viewed remotely.
findings.quote:
44 of the 63 Senior Buildings (approximately 70%) had CCTV 
cameras that were inoperable or unable to be viewed remotely.

findings.plain: At fire watch sites, only 23 of 60 scheduled fire guards, about 38%, were present at their posts for the duration of DOI's inspections, and guards kept abandoning posts even after DOI shared its findings with NYCHA.
findings.quote:
only 23 of 60 
scheduled fire guards (approximately 38%) were present at their assigned posts for the duration of 
the inspection

findings.plain: Scheduled fire guards were absent during three fires at the Douglass, Taft and Ingersoll Houses, two of which caused minor injuries, and the guards had falsified timesheets claiming to be present.
findings.quote: Scheduled fire guards were absent during three fires that occurred in three different buildings

findings.plain: Over the contract term from October 2019 to February 2024, both NYCHA and Allied Universal failed to consistently exercise required oversight. NYCHA's Office of Safety and Security failed to consistently conduct or document field inspections for multiple consecutive years.
findings.quote:
failed, among other things, to consistently conduct field inspections of the security and 
fire guards, and to document the inspections that it did conduct, for multiple consecutive years of the 
contract term.

numbers.label: Guards absent for all or part of their shift
Fire guards present for the full inspection period
Senior buildings with broken or unviewable cameras
Lobby doors found not secure
In-person inspections of senior buildings
Recommendations issued to NYCHA

recommendations: Require guard vendors to provide a smartphone app with geofencing and electronic timekeeping that alerts vendor managers when guards leave their post, with QR code scans along patrol routes and backup call-in procedures when the app is down.

Require vendors to provide geofencing and electronic timekeeping records as invoice backup, with the vendor's invoicing system configured to block invoices when records show a guard did not complete the scheduled shift.
Include in guard contracts a definition of "post abandonment" specifying the minimum number of minutes, such as no more than 15 minutes.
Provide security guards a designated desk or podium bearing NYCHA's insignia in the lobby to serve as their central duty location.
Require property management to post lobby signage with contact information for NYCHA's Office of Safety and Security for emergencies and complaints about guards.
Require a minimum number of documented unannounced monthly inspections of guard performance and biweekly briefings up the chain on vendor performance.

Revise the field inspection form so inspectors check that lobby and stairwell doors are secure with working self-closing hardware and that cameras work with unobstructed views, and train inspection staff accordingly.
Revise the manual so the safety office immediately reports security infrastructure deficiencies it cannot fix to property management, which must generate a work order ticket within 12 hours.
Revise the field inspection report form to require electronic delivery, such as scanning and uploading or submission through NYCHA's ServiceNow platform.
Revise the manual to define the Security Manager role and specify the titles and duties of employees responsible for managing the guard contracts.
Establish a process to receive and verify invoices, certified payroll, electronic timekeeping and geofencing records and confirm they accurately reflect hours worked before paying.
Require biweekly vendor invoices and retain relevant camera footage until invoices are reviewed and approved so NYCHA can cross-reference them when needed.
audits.agency_response: NYCHA accepted eight recommendations and accepted four in part, saying it will build the technology, invoicing and post-abandonment requirements into future contracts but that changing current contracts would be too costly and time consuming.

audits.title: Twenty-Second Annual Report of the Commission
audits.plain_title: Police corruption watchdog: faster cases, weaker interviews
audits.agency: New York City Police Department
audits.what_they_audited: This is the annual monitoring report of the Commission to Combat Police Corruption (CCPC), not a financial audit. The Commission read the case files of a random sample of closed New York City Police Department (NYPD) Internal Affairs Bureau (IAB) investigations, 46 closed in 2022 and 35 closed in 2023, to judge whether they were fair, thorough, accurate and impartial, and it also reprints a summary of its March 2024 review of how the Department carried out the recommendations of the 2019 Independent Panel on the Disciplinary System.
audits.background: The Commission was created in 1995 by Mayoral Executive Order No. 18 to monitor how the NYPD gathers information, investigates allegations and sets policy to detect, control and deter corruption among its members. IAB is the bureau inside the Department that investigates allegations of corruption and serious misconduct against members of the service, and the Commission monitors it by attending briefings, steering committee meetings and case reviews and by reading closed case files.

findings.plain: Investigations moved faster than at any point the Commission has tracked. Cases reviewed in 2022 took 8.9 months on average, the shortest in eight years of reviews, and the 2023 average of 10.4 months fell to 8.6 months once a single 73-month case was set aside.
findings.quote:
In 2022 and 2023, the Commission observed the lowest average length of time IAB 
investigations were pending since we began tracking this metric.

findings.plain: The Commission's satisfaction rate fell in all seven areas it tracks in the 2023 sample, after mostly small declines in 2022. It attributes the drop partly to dropping failed drug tests from its sample and partly to turnover among IAB executives and group commanders.
findings.quote:
In 2023, our 
satisfaction rates decreased in all seven areas.

findings.plain: Interview quality remains the weakest part of IAB's work. The Commission found problems in 13 of the 46 cases reviewed in 2022 and 13 of the 35 reviewed in 2023, most often failure to ask follow-up questions and failure to cover all relevant issues, with questioning that at times seemed designed only to elicit a denial.
findings.quote:
we identified interview quality issues in 13 of the 46 cases we 
reviewed in 2022 and 13 of the 35 cases we reviewed in 2023

findings.plain: Investigators repeatedly failed to interview people who were available to them. The Commission flagged missed civilian or officer interviews in 12 cases from the 2022 sample and 13 cases from the 2023 sample, and in some property cases officers who had access to the missing property were never made subjects.
findings.quote:
The Commission noted deficiencies related to the failure to interview witnesses in 12 of 
the cases reviewed in 2022.

findings.plain: The Commission disagreed with more case outcomes than in any of the previous four years. It found three cases in the 2022 sample where the overall disposition was wrong, and in the 2023 sample it identified three cases where allegations closed as unsubstantiated should have been substantiated; IAB agreed with its assessment in two of those.
findings.quote:
We disagreed with more overall dispositions of investigations in this review than we have 
had in the prior four years.

findings.plain: Body-worn camera footage has been a clear benefit to IAB investigations, but officers who failed to record properly were rarely punished beyond a warning, even though the Department's own penalty guidelines call for the forfeiture of one to five days.
findings.quote:
it did not appear that penalties beyond 
warnings were given in a majority of these cases

findings.plain: Long stretches of inactivity persisted in some files even when cases closed on time, and supervisors' directions were not always carried out. Eight investigations in the 2023 sample sat for more than 30 days with no explained activity, and in six 2023 cases team leaders ordered steps that were never taken and never explained.
findings.quote:
there were eight investigations that we reviewed in 2023 
that had unexplained gaps of longer than 30 days

numbers.label: Closed 2022 cases the Commission reviewed
Closed 2023 cases the Commission reviewed
Average length of investigations, 2022 sample
Average months pending, 2023 sample
Commission agreed with the disposition, 2022 sample
Commission agreed with the disposition, 2023 sample
Most serious allegation substantiated, 2023 sample

recommendations: Conduct investigations promptly and without lapses in activity, but do not sacrifice quality for speed; IAB has directed each group commander to name backup investigators who can take over when the primary investigator is unavailable.
Identify subject officers as early as possible, and in property cases treat every officer who had access to the missing property as a subject unless there is a specific reason to exclude them.

Interview civilian witnesses without delay and interview witness officers close in time to the incident absent a strategic reason; the assigned investigator should personally contact the complainant, and civilians should be shown body-worn camera footage that contradicts their account unless there is a strategic or privacy reason not to.
Document in the case file, preferably on the worksheet summarizing the interview, any reason for departing from best interview practices.

Train newly assigned investigators in interviewing techniques and give all investigators routine refresher courses; the current Department Advocate should put this training in place with the attorneys in that office.
Have supervisors who are skilled at interviewing help less experienced investigators, both in preparing for interviews and during the questioning.

Include every allegation against a subject in the investigation even if it will end up unsubstantiated, and notify subjects' commanding officers of any allegation IAB did not fully investigate or address.
Before conducting surveillance, have investigators discuss the objectives with supervisors and plan the surveillance for the times they are most likely to observe what they are looking for.

When summarizing recorded interviews, include only what can be heard on the audio, record anything said outside the recording on a separate worksheet or clearly mark it as before or after the recording, and have supervisors confirm the summaries are accurate and complete.

Search for relevant video as soon as the complaint comes in, have supervisors check within the first one to two weeks that a video canvass was done, and follow up quickly on cameras whose footage could not be accessed.

Promptly perform investigative steps directed in team leader or commanding officer reviews, document any reason a step was not taken, and admonish or discipline investigators who skip a step without a legitimate reason.

Follow the penalty ranges in the Department's disciplinary guidelines, known as the Matrix, when officers negligently fail to activate body-worn cameras in cases where footage would have been relevant, or at minimum monitor whether warnings alone are enough to change behavior.
audits.agency_response: The Commission gives the Department a draft of each annual report for comment before publication, and it reports that in response to this draft the Department said it is building and testing a search function for its Trial Decisions Library. In the Independent Panel review reprinted here, the Department defended keeping the Citizen's Liaison inside the Department Advocate's Office and said that recording informal contacts about disciplinary cases was unnecessary and would be burdensome.
audits.implementation_note: The report reprints the Commission's March 2024 review of the Department's implementation of the 13 recommendations of the 2019 Independent Panel and reports that, since that review, none of the Commission's three public reporting recommendations had been adopted and only two of its proposed additions to the disciplinary Matrix, penalty ranges for failing to notify IAB and for fraternization, appeared in the revised version.

audits.auditor: Special master (NYC special education hearing orders)
audits.title: Special Master Program Monitoring Report
audits.plain_title: Special education fixes stall: one obligation met in four months
audits.agency: New York City Public Schools
audits.what_they_audited: A periodic monitoring report to the court, filed as a slide deck, on how far New York City Public Schools (NYCPS) has gotten in meeting the obligations imposed by the court's order of July 19, 2023 in L.V. v. D.O.E. It includes an independent assessment of the four technology systems the obligations depend on.
audits.background: When a special education hearing is held, an Impartial Hearing Officer can order that a service be provided or a payment be made on a student's behalf, and the school system then has 35 days to carry the order out unless the order says otherwise. NYCPS runs an Implementation Unit (IU) to authorize the payments and arrange the services. Obligation #39 of the 2023 order requires the special master to report to the court every 120 days on whether each obligation has been fulfilled, what is blocking the unfulfilled ones and what comes next.

findings.plain: As of March 7, 2025, 19 of the 51 tracked obligations had been fulfilled and 32 remained unfulfilled. Only one had been fulfilled since the November 2024 report, a recruiting and hiring strategy, and every remaining obligation was past due as of January 19, 2025.
findings.quote: have been fulfilled, while thirty-two (32) remain

findings.plain: Work on the Impartial Hearing Management System (IHMS), the system most of the obligations depend on, had nearly stopped while the project waited for funding for its second phase. Funding for the change request was approved on February 26, 2025, but the contract and comptroller steps remained.
findings.quote: OMB approved the funding for change request on 2/26/2025

findings.plain: The independent technology assessment estimated that even in a best case the remaining development and testing of the hearing system would not finish until the first quarter of 2027.
findings.quote: remaining development and testing will be the first quarter 2027.

findings.plain: SupportHub, the new customer support platform, went live on January 8, but the special master's survey of attorneys and parents who used it found no one rated it very helpful and about half reported it unhelpful or a bad experience.
findings.quote: and 0% found it very helpful. About 52% did

findings.plain: The school system had not carried out everything the judge ordered at the December 5, 2024 conference on public communications and process changes, and the special master attached a status report tracking the outstanding items.
findings.quote: report tracking these items. In short, NYCPS has not satisfied all of the directives

findings.plain: Polaris, the new custom-built invoicing tool, launched with 57 vendors in late December 2024 and processed 207 invoices in January, 98% of them within five days, though the special master's team had not yet reviewed technical documentation to verify the results.
findings.quote: from Polaris now and processed 207 invoices in January, (98% within 5 days).

findings.plain: Hiring was moving: the school system reported 100 of the 148 needed implementation positions filled with full-time or temporary staff. audits.title: Audit Report on Controls over Payroll, Personnel, and Purchasing at the 14 Queens Community Boards
audits.plain_title: Payroll, leave and purchasing lapses at Queens community boards
audits.agency: Queens Community Boards
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the 14 Queens community boards maintained adequate controls over their payroll, personnel and purchasing functions in compliance with applicable city rules, regulations and official guidance. The audit covered July 1, 2021 through March 15, 2023, with employee leave data extended to November 25, 2024.
audits.background: New York City is divided into 59 community districts, each served by a community board, a local advisory body created by the New York City Charter with up to 50 unsalaried volunteer members. Each board employs a district manager who runs the district office, and board operations are funded through the city budget.

findings.plain: Eleven of the 14 Queens community boards had at least one reportable problem, generally involving excess annual leave accruals and payroll and invoicing procedures. Boards 5, 8 and 9 had no reportable issues.
findings.quote: 11 of the 14 Community Boards in the borough had at least one problem

findings.plain: Seven district managers had annual leave balances above the two-year maximum for managers as of November 25, 2024. The excess was not converted to sick leave as required and waivers to carry it over were not consistently granted. One manager had accumulated over 1,600 hours of excess leave.
findings.quote: One District Manager accumulated over 1,600 hours in excess leave.

findings.plain: Those excess balances carry a real cost. Even with excess leave converted to sick leave, auditors estimated separation payouts for the seven district managers would run from over $27,000 to $66,000 each and total more than $293,000 across the borough's boards.
findings.quote: the total pay-out amounts for the District Managers would range today from over $27,000 to $66,000 each, and cumulatively total over $293,000

findings.plain: Half of the board chairpersons did not consistently approve their district managers' timesheets on time, if at all. Of 41 sampled timesheets, 17 (41%) did not comply with the approval procedure, and in 18 instances the Queens Borough President's Office approved timesheets without evidence of the chairperson's sign-off.
findings.quote: did not consistently approve their District Managers’ timesheets in a timely manner, if at all

findings.plain: Community Board 13 could not produce 11 vendor invoices covering 33% of its sampled payments, worth $12,649.24, so auditors could not confirm the goods or services were received or the payments were proper.
findings.quote: Community Board 13 did not provide auditors with 11 vendor invoices, amounting to 33% of the sampled payments and totaling $12,649.24

findings.plain: Community Boards 12 and 14 batched multiple invoices into single payments without recording every invoice number in the Financial Management System, and Board 12 paid one $826.82 invoice twice without clearly demonstrating it recouped the full double payment.
findings.quote: auditors found that Community Board 12 paid $826.82 for one invoice twice on the same payment

findings.plain: No procurement issues were found at 11 of the 14 boards, and sampled micro-purchases totaling $177,790.69 showed the boards are generally buying goods and services for legitimate business purposes.
findings.quote: the Community Boards are generally procuring goods and services for legitimate business purposes

numbers.label: Queens boards with at least one reportable problem
Excess leave accumulated by one district manager
Combined estimated leave payouts for seven managers
Sampled district manager timesheets out of compliance
Board 13 payments not backed by vendor invoices
Invoice Board 12 paid twice

recommendations: All Queens board chairpersons should encourage district managers and staff to use their annual leave, limit authorizations to carry over excess leave where practicable and make sure district managers' timesheets are approved on time and promptly sent to the Queens Borough President's Office.

All Queens boards should actively monitor leave accruals and require written authorization or conversion of excess annual leave to sick leave, obtain and verify vendor invoices before every payment and develop written policies for managing employee leave and purchasing.
Community Board 12 should make sure the $826.82 overpayment is fully recouped.
Community Boards 12, 13 and 14 should record each paid invoice number in the Financial Management System.
Community Board 13 should consider hiring support staff as needed to support the district office's operations.
audits.agency_response: Twelve of the 14 boards sent written responses between February 24 and 27, 2025; many did not directly address the recommendations but their comments implied a general sense of agreement. Community Boards 4 and 13 did not respond.

audits.title: Letter Re: Audit of the Financial and Operating Practices of the 3 Staten Island Community Boards
audits.plain_title: Leave warning as Staten Island community board audit is called off
audits.agency: Staten Island Community Boards
audits.what_they_audited: This is a closure letter, not a full audit report. The Comptroller's office told Staten Island Community Board 2 that a planned audit of the financial and operating practices of the borough's three boards was terminated, and it flagged the district manager's excess annual leave balance.
audits.background: Recent changes to the New York City Charter allow the Comptroller to treat all community boards as a single combined agency, so auditing one board's operations in a four-year cycle now fulfills the mandate. Before the change, the office had to audit all 59 community boards every four years.

findings.plain: The planned audit of the three Staten Island community boards was terminated because charter changes let the Comptroller satisfy the audit mandate by examining a single board in each four-year cycle.
findings.quote: This decision was made based on recent changes to the New York City Charter which allows the Comptroller to treat all Community Boards as a single combined agency.

findings.plain: The district manager of Staten Island Community Board 2 had banked 843.25 hours of annual leave as of November 25, 2024, which is 493.25 hours (70.5 days) over the two-year maximum for managers.
findings.quote: an annual leave balance of 843.25 hours, as of November 25, 2024

findings.plain: Auditors estimated the payout on separation at $61,458.19 with a waiver to carry over the excess and $42,169.57 without one, as much as 41% of the manager's salary and 23% of the board's fiscal year 2025 personal services budget.
findings.quote: These amounts were determined to be $61,458.19 and $42,169.57, respectively.

findings.plain: Under the city personnel order, managers may only bank two years of annual leave unless the agency head grants a waiver; without one, excess leave converts to sick leave that pays out at one-third the balance. Either way, unmanaged accruals can strain a board's small budget.
findings.quote: a Community Board’s budget and fiscal health can be crippled if leave accruals are not effectively managed

numbers.label: Board 2 district manager's annual leave balance
Leave beyond the two-year maximum
Estimated payout if excess leave carries over
Estimated payout if excess leave converts to sick leave

recommendations: Encourage the district manager to use annual leave and shrink the accrued balance to limit the lump sum payment owed when the manager leaves city service.
Limit authorizations to carry over excess annual leave where practicable.
Establish protocols for monitoring future leave accruals and ensure compliance with the personnel order's leave regulations.
