audits.title: Metropolitan Transportation Authority’s Express Bus Accessibility and User Satisfaction
audits.plain_title: Express buses often fail riders who use wheelchairs
audits.agency: Metropolitan Transportation Authority
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Metropolitan Transportation Authority's (MTA) express buses are accessible to riders with disabilities and how satisfied riders are with the service. The review drew on surveys of 458 riders, roundtables with disability advocates and field observations in which wheelchair users attempted to board 25 express buses across all five boroughs.
audits.background: The MTA runs 79 express bus routes between Manhattan and the outer boroughs, many serving neighborhoods without rail service. Unlike low-floor local buses with front-door ramps, express buses are high-floor coaches that wheelchair users can board only via an external lift that the driver must exit the bus to operate.

findings.plain: Wheelchair users could not board six of the 25 express buses tested, either because of lift problems or because drivers failed to stop and pick them up. Some riders had to wait up to an hour before they could board a bus.
findings.quote: Wheelchair users were unable to board six of the 25 (24%) buses

findings.plain: Even when boarding succeeded, nearly half of the boardings were delayed, and the Bus Command Center (BCC) did not send required assistance to any of the drivers struggling with lifts.
findings.quote: Of the 19 instances in which wheelchair users were able to board express buses, nine (47.4%) were delayed.

findings.plain: In 16 of 19 boardings, drivers did not correctly position wheelchairs on the lift or properly secure them inside the bus, and drivers failed to announce stops in nine of 19 instances, a violation of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and MTA rules.
findings.quote: drivers did not correctly position wheelchairs on the lift and/or properly secure wheelchairs once the riders were inside the bus

findings.plain: Riders traveling to or from Staten Island, which relies heavily on express buses to reach Manhattan, fared worst: wheelchair users could not board half of the sampled buses there.
findings.quote: wheelchair users were unable to board five of the 10 (50%) sampled express buses traveling to or from Staten Island

findings.plain: MTA data shows wheelchair lift use on express buses is rare, about 208 deployments per million rides versus about 3,046 on local buses, supporting reports that wheelchair users avoid express buses because of unreliable service and safety concerns.
findings.quote: People who use wheelchairs are 15 times more likely to ride a local bus than an express bus, an enormous disparity.

findings.plain: Training and oversight are inadequate. Despite the MTA saying it increased lift training, several drivers said they had been trained on the lift only once or were operating it for the first time.
findings.quote: several express bus drivers stated that they were trained only once on wheelchair lift operation, or that this was their first time operating the lift

findings.plain: Since 2018 the MTA has piloted only one potentially viable ramp-equipped express bus design and did not adopt it despite positive feedback from wheelchair users, and it surveyed more than 1,000 general riders about new designs but only 10 wheelchair users.
findings.quote: since 2018, the MTA has piloted only one potentially viable ramp-equipped express bus design

numbers.label: Sampled express buses wheelchair users could not board
Successful boardings that were delayed
Boardings where wheelchairs weren't properly secured
How much likelier wheelchair users are to ride local buses
Express bus fare, compared with $2.90 on local buses
Express bus trips canceled, January through September 2024

recommendations: Immediately conduct refresher trainings on wheelchair lift operation and on Americans with Disabilities Act and MTA requirements for serving people with disabilities, including informing the Bus Command Center of lift issues, safely boarding customers, securing wheelchairs, making stop announcements and appropriate etiquette.
Ensure all express bus drivers receive annual hands-on training in operating wheelchair lifts and give drivers field instructions for the lifts.
Report express bus wheelchair lift deployments separately, including the number of failed and successful deployments.
Pilot additional low-floor entry buses or other accessible designs and consider adopting them as vehicles are retired.

Make meaningful efforts to engage the accessibility community on new bus designs, including in selecting pilots and features, and involve enough people with disabilities that their feedback can be projected to the population.
Compare scheduled pickup and drop-off times to actual times and revise schedules so they are realistic and as accurate as possible.
Address driver shortages and mechanical failures to minimize the impact of cancelations, and if shortages cannot be addressed, revise service schedules to minimize cancelations.
Improve the MTA's communication apps so they give customers accurate and timely information on service alerts, bus locations and estimated arrival times.

audits.title: Audit Report on Estate Asset Identification and Management Practices of the Kings County Public Administrator’s Office
audits.plain_title: Weak safeguards for estates at Brooklyn's public administrator
audits.agency: Kings County Public Administrator's Office
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Kings County Public Administrator's Office (KCPA), which administers the estates of Brooklyn residents who die without a will or without heirs willing or able to act, properly researched and identified decedents' assets and accurately accounted for and safeguarded estate assets.
audits.background: New York City has five public administrators, each appointed by the judges of their county's Surrogate's Court. During the period of January 2022 through June 2023, KCPA had 14,258 active estate cases and was managing $106,204,541 in cash for 4,810 estates in interest-bearing bank accounts.

findings.plain: KCPA does not reliably collect or document decedents' personal property. Sixteen of 109 security bags in its vault had no intake sheets, 60 items flagged as missing in a 2019 search were still unaccounted for and staff could not open a safe in the office because no one knows the combination.
findings.quote: the auditors found no intake sheets attached to 16 of the 109 (15%) security bags

findings.plain: At KCPA's warehouse, items were generally untagged and auditors could not find items matching 12 of 15 sampled estates' inventory entries. Paintings were falling apart and goods were covered in dust.
findings.quote: the items in the warehouse were all stored haphazardly and in a manner that provided inadequate protection from breakage or from deterioration

findings.plain: Property sits unsold for years. Among dated inventory entries, 92% entered storage more than five years ago, and 84 entries of stocks, bonds and other financial instruments remained unliquidated, nearly half of them for more than a decade.
findings.quote: 1,096 (92%) of the remaining entries indicate that items entered the inventory more than five years ago

findings.plain: KCPA identified assets worth $580,162 belonging to eight sampled estates but never collected them, skipped required inquiries to 26 financial institutions and left even the unclaimed funds it found at the state comptroller uncollected.
findings.quote: Files for eight sampled estates indicated that assets valued at $580,162 were identified by KCPA, but auditors found no evidence that the assets were collected and deposited into the estate accounts.

findings.plain: Funds totaling $2,556,205 from 676 closed estate cases were never distributed to heirs or the city, and two dormant accounts holding a combined $375,100 have been untouched since 2010.
findings.quote: When closed, the associated fund balances totaled $2,556,205.

findings.plain: Real estate oversight was poor. Property lists were inaccurate, one property sold for $60,420 below its appraised value, a Brooklyn sale was recorded under a Manhattan address and three properties were sold after KCPA's temporary letters of administration had expired, bringing into question the legality of those sales.
findings.quote: three of the sold properties were sold after the temporary Letters of Administration given to KCPA by the Surrogate’s Court had expired

findings.plain: There is a massive backlog: over 10,000 estates had been open more than five years, most without an assigned case manager, and KCPA filed inaccurate or incomplete reports to the Surrogate's Court and the state and city comptrollers.
findings.quote: More than 70% of estates active during the audit scope period had been open for more than five years, and more than half of those had not yet been assigned a case manager.

numbers.label: Identified estate assets that were never collected
Funds from closed estates never distributed
Active estate cases during the audit period
Cases open for more than five years
Cash KCPA managed for 4,810 estates
Amount one property sold below its appraised value

recommendations: Develop a systematic process for clearing the backlog of pending cases, including prioritizing cases by age and value, identifying all related assets, liquidating them and closing cases out.

If feasible, consider hiring vendors to help, including consultant case managers, organizers to link assets to the correct estates, temporary staff to process financial assets and auctioneers to speed the sale of long-held property.
Consider asking OMB to increase KCPA's budget to hire the additional staff needed for effective case management, backlog reduction and a reasonable pace of administering and closing estates.
Maintain an accurate and detailed master inventory of all decedents' personal property and record all of it in the decedents' accounts in the CompuTrust case management system.
Ensure all personal property is inventoried and tagged with the estate number or decedent's name when placed in the vault or warehouse, stored in an organized manner and protected from damage.
Ensure staff follow estate administration policies and procedures, including required searches for decedents' assets, with adequate documented oversight.
Hire a locksmith to open the safe with the unknown combination, account for the coins listed as stored there and reset the code if the safe stays in use.
As funding allows, consider getting appraisals for certain personal property before auctions and record the appraised values in inventory records and CompuTrust.

Routinely check the New York State Comptroller's unclaimed funds office for potential estate assets, conduct new searches every six months until a case closes and its funds are distributed and keep documentation of unclaimed funds in estate files.
Collect all personal and real property known to belong to decedents and record it in the appropriate estate accounts in CompuTrust.
Obtain appraisals before selling properties to establish fair market value and keep all sale documentation, including advertisements, offers and auction records, in estate files and CompuTrust.
Keep all documentation on identifying, collecting and depositing funds and other assets in the estate case file and in CompuTrust.
Maintain an accurate running master list of all decedents' real estate holdings and record every property in decedents' CompuTrust accounts.

Ensure legal documents are completed correctly during real property sales and that sales are accurately recorded in the right property database, such as the city's Automated City Register Information System (ACRIS), and in decedents' accounts.
Keep all case-related documents and information in the estate case files and in CompuTrust.
Establish written policies and procedures giving staff detailed guidance, consistent with the Surrogate's Court Procedure Act and state public administrator guidelines, for performing their duties.
Collect the information needed to use CompuTrust to track cases and monitor lengthy delays in administering any estate.
Accurately report required estate information to the Surrogate's Court, the New York State Comptroller's Office and the New York City Comptroller's Office.
audits.agency_response: In its February 3, 2025 written response, KCPA generally agreed with all 18 recommendations, though it said hiring vendors to clear the backlog "is currently not feasible without additional funding and resources."
audits.implementation_note: This is not a follow-up, but the report notes that five comptroller audits of KCPA since 2005 flagged similar issues, and that a June 2015 follow-up audit found many of the earlier recommendations were not implemented.

audits.title: Audit Report on Estate Asset Identification and Management Practices of the New York County Public Administrator’s Office
audits.plain_title: How Manhattan's public administrator handles estates of the dead
audits.agency: New York County Public Administrator's Office
audits.what_they_audited: The New York County Public Administrator's Office, which manages the estates of Manhattan residents who die without a will and close heirs or without anyone available to administer their affairs. Auditors checked whether the office properly identified, collected, accounted for and safeguarded the assets of the dead.
audits.background: Each county in New York City has a public administrator appointed by Surrogate's Court judges, with a fiduciary duty to find and protect estate assets, pay debts and distribute proceeds to heirs. According to June 2023 bank statements, the Manhattan office was administering $119,189,151 in gross assets, with 4,702 estate cases active at some point between January 2022 and June 2023 and a staff of 21.

findings.plain: Investigators did not consistently document what they found when searching dead people's homes. In all 11 sampled estates where property was collected during initial searches, some items were left off the reports, and items including three Emmy Awards, a laptop and a car never made it onto inventory lists.
findings.quote: one or more items of personal property were not recorded

findings.plain: Some home searches happened months after the office learned of a death. The office has no time target for initial searches, and in one case investigators did not search until more than three months after the death notification.
findings.quote: ranging from five to 131 days (approximately four months)

findings.plain: Collected valuables often sat unappraised for long stretches, in one case a box of jewelry for almost two years and nine months. Delays in appraisal push back crediting assets to estates and distributing money to heirs.
findings.quote: 212 (79%) of these entries pertaining to personal property not appraised for at least four months

findings.plain: The office failed to identify or collect at least $208,584 in assets held at financial institutions and did not check the state comptroller's website for unclaimed funds, where auditors found 22 unclaimed accounts belonging to 12 of the 50 sampled estates.
findings.quote: Six of the assets totaling $208,584 (associated with two estates) were held by financial institutions.

findings.plain: Recordkeeping was poor. Over $1 million in assets recorded as collected and over $2.4 million in recorded deposits lacked documentation showing the money was actually collected and put in the office's bank accounts.
findings.quote: The remaining 18 assets—totaling $1,039,898—lacked sufficient documentation.

findings.plain: Estates lingered. Most of the 50 sampled estates stayed open longer than the two-year benchmark, one for nearly 15 years, and 2,005 of 4,702 active estates were listed as unassigned, most of them for six months or longer.
findings.quote: 31 of them (62%) were opened or re-opened for over two years

findings.plain: The office did not consistently file required reports on open and closed estates with the Surrogate's Court, the state comptroller and the city comptroller, skipping four monthly reports entirely until auditors asked about them.
findings.quote: NYCPA did not include 135 of the 324 closed estates (42%)

numbers.label: Gross estate assets the office was administering
Assets at financial institutions not identified or collected
Collected assets lacking sufficient documentation
Recorded deposits auditors could not confirm
Sampled estates open or reopened for over two years
Active estates listed as unassigned

recommendations: Strengthen oversight of investigators' home searches so everything found is consistently documented on the required reports and inventory records.
Set target timeframes for conducting initial searches of decedents' homes and for appraising collected property that is not on hold.
Keep using the newly adopted tamper-proof sealed bags with pre-printed inventory numbers to secure collected personal property.
Use the CompuTrust case management system to record inventory transactions on time and itemize personal property with detailed descriptions and quantities.

Establish controls so that when assets at a financial institution are identified the office promptly gets the balance, collects the funds and keeps at it until everything is credited to estate accounts.
Routinely check the state comptroller's unclaimed funds website for open cases, pursue collection where possible and document those funds in estate files.
Investigate the three unclaimed accounts the auditors identified and pursue collection where possible.
Keep inventory lists of stocks and bonds up to date, liquidate them and deposit the money promptly, and mark the current status of any that are inactive or have living beneficiaries.

Keep all supporting documents in each estate file, covering searches, asset collection, property sales, payments to creditors and any delays, including explanations when properties go unsold for long periods.
Close estates on time, with reasons for delays clearly documented in the files.
Investigate the unassigned cases the auditors identified, decide whether to administer or close them and update their statuses.
Make sure payments are adequately supported and that accountings and close-out memos are prepared and kept in estate files.
Report open and closed cases to the applicable oversight authorities as required.
audits.agency_response: The office disagreed with most of the findings and did not directly address any of the 13 recommendations, and the comptroller's office said its response questioned the auditors' competency and methodology without providing sufficient evidence to refute any finding. Based on its comments, the office appears to generally agree with two recommendations, partially agree with one and disagree with three.

audits.title: Audit Report on the Department of Housing Preservation and Development’s Administration of the Affordable Neighborhood Co-operative Program
audits.plain_title: Why the city's affordable co-op conversions take so long
audits.agency: New York City Department of Housing Preservation and Development
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Affordable Neighborhood Co-operative Program (ANCP), run by the Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD), is effective at turning city-owned buildings in the Tenant Interim Lease (TIL) program into affordable co-ops owned by their tenants.
audits.background: The Tenant Interim Lease program, created in 1978, let tenants in city-owned buildings buy their apartments for $250 and form low-income co-ops; after many buildings struggled, the housing department restructured it in 2012 into the Affordable Neighborhood Co-operative Program, which fully gut renovates buildings before conversion. When the program began there were 126 buildings waiting to convert, and as of October 2024, 13 conversions had been completed.

findings.plain: Very few buildings have actually become co-ops. Since 2012 only 13 of the 126 eligible buildings have converted, every one of them blew past the department's timing benchmarks and the conversions took six to 11 years each.
findings.quote: with delays ranging from 15 to 87 months, for conversion processes that ranged from 6 to 11 years

findings.plain: Many buildings have not even started. Of 113 buildings still waiting, 45 had no developer assigned as of April 2024, and 1,851 apartments sit in buildings waiting to enter or complete conversion. One building has been waiting for a developer since the program began in 2012.
findings.quote: of the 113 buildings still awaiting conversion, 45 (40%) have not yet been assigned developers

findings.plain: The department has no centralized way to track what is delaying projects or how long problems go unresolved, which keeps it from spotting and dismantling systemic obstacles in the conversion pipeline.
findings.quote: HPD lacks a practical centralized mechanism for tracking and reviewing key performance indicators

findings.plain: The units that did convert are affordable under federal guidelines. Average maintenance charges at converted buildings came in well under the affordability threshold, and the department helped residents with Section 8 vouchers and public financing.
findings.quote: the actual average maintenance charges under ANCP fell well below the affordability threshold set at 40% of AMI

findings.plain: Delays cost the city money. The department paid $31.6 million from 2021 through 2023 to maintain buildings still waiting to convert, and construction cost overruns on two clusters required an extra $1.9 million and $2.6 million in city funds.
findings.quote: From 2021 through 2023, these costs totaled $31.6 million

findings.plain: After buildings converted, the department did not always enforce its own regulatory agreements. Some required annual financial reports were missing and only seven of 23 required annual maintenance fee increases were actually implemented across nine co-ops.
findings.quote: only 30% of the required maintenance fees were implemented

findings.plain: Surveyed tenants raised concerns about higher costs, the slow pace and poor communication. Proposed monthly maintenance fees ran $389 to $959 above the lowest rents tenants had been paying, though still within federal affordability standards.
findings.quote: a percentage increase of 147% to 400%

numbers.label: Share of program buildings converted to co-ops since 2012
Original benchmark for a complete conversion
Waiting buildings with no developer assigned
Units still waiting to enter or complete conversion
City cost of maintaining unconverted buildings, 2021-2023
Rise from lowest rents to lowest proposed maintenance fees

recommendations: Develop a centralized mechanism to readily identify the specific issues delaying each project.
Analyze the most common recurring causes of delay and develop strategies to address them, making programmatic and contractual changes to remove obstacles upfront.
Regularly measure project progress against time benchmarks and act promptly to mitigate delays as they occur.
Update the program brochure on the department's website with the most recent benchmark timeframes and targets for each stage of conversion.
Develop new conversion completion targets for each pending project, share them with tenants and track and report progress against them.
Keep exploring ways to build better communication and relationships with tenants about the conversion process, including possible surveys, and continue soliciting tenant feedback.
Work with other city entities such as the City Council, the Office of Management and Budget and the Department of Buildings to streamline the approval process.
Collect and review all information required after conversion to help keep each building financially solvent and ensure maintenance fees rise with building needs.
audits.agency_response: The department generally agreed with all eight recommendations, agreeing fully with five and partially with three, but disputed any responsibility for significant delays in the conversion process.

audits.title: Status Report on Local Law 42
audits.plain_title: Monitor's full case against parts of the solitary confinement ban
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: The court-appointed independent monitor's comprehensive analysis of Local Law 42, the city law banning solitary confinement and requiring 14 hours of daily out-of-cell time, examining how its rules on restrictive housing, restraints, de-escalation confinement and emergency lock-ins would affect the Department of Correction's operations and its compliance with the Nunez court orders.
audits.background: The City Council passed Local Law 42 on December 20, 2023 and enacted it over the mayor's veto on January 30, 2024. The mayor suspended certain provisions by emergency executive order on July 27, 2024, the City Council challenged that suspension in state court and the federal court directed the monitoring team to analyze how the law intersects with the Nunez court orders. This report captures all of that work to date.

findings.plain: While the monitoring team found some provisions of the law laudable and consistent with sound correctional practice, it has grave concerns about certain sections whose universal application removes discretion or imposes standards it considers impractical or unsafe to operationalize.
findings.quote: the Monitoring Team has grave concerns about the implementation of certain

findings.plain: On restrictive housing, the team found the law denies the department the discretion needed to build a viable model: it bars any restriction on out-of-cell time, sets arbitrary discharge timeframes such as mandatory release within 30 days regardless of behavior, requires protracted placement procedures and prohibits the enhanced restraints that allow safe group programming.
findings.quote: the Law does not permit the Department the necessary discretion to develop

findings.plain: On restraints, the team found that applying the same stringent procedures to routine restraints as to enhanced restraints creates an impractical bureaucratic burden, and that the blanket ban on enhanced restraints for people under 22 overlooks that violent behavior is not exclusive to older people in custody.
findings.quote: ...restraints creates an impractical bureaucratic burden

findings.plain: On de-escalation confinement, the team found the law's fixed time limits, readmission restrictions and universal access requirements impose a one-size-fits-all protocol on situations that require calibrated judgment by correctional managers.
findings.quote: ...managers must have the discretion to use de-escalation confinement absent arbitrary and absolute

findings.plain: On emergency lock-ins, the team found that an absolute time limit for ending lock-ins forecloses the informed judgment of the on-scene manager, and that requirements for more frequent observations, universal tablet access and immediate public notification undercut safe resolution of the emergency.
findings.quote: An absolute, inflexible, and arbitrary time limit to complete emergency lock-ins

findings.plain: The monitor concluded that without modifications the highlighted requirements are inconsistent with sound correctional practice, would worsen already dangerous conditions and would impede compliance with the Nunez court orders, and stated it will not approve department practices that include them.
findings.quote: will only exacerbate the already dangerous conditions

numbers.label: Daily out-of-cell time the law mandates for all incarcerated people
Maximum restrictive housing stay under the law, with no exceptions

recommendations: The specific problematic provisions of Local Law 42 identified in the report should not be implemented pending resolution of the legal issues raised by the monitoring team's findings, with the court and parties determining the appropriate legal pathway to mitigate the potential for harm.

After the court decides on remedial relief in the contempt proceedings, the court should direct the monitor to provide within 30 days a timeline for finalizing specific recommendations on how to address the problematic provisions in a way that is narrowly tailored and permits safe operation of the jails.
audits.agency_response: The department sought the monitor's guidance on the law twice during 2024, and the city told the court it was considering seeking relief, filing a declaration from Commissioner Lynelle Maginley-Liddie stating her belief that many provisions would have deleterious effects on department operations if they took effect.
audits.compliance_note: The monitor assessed that certain Local Law 42 provisions, as designed, would undermine the Nunez court orders' purpose of a constitutionally sufficient level of safety and would impede the department's compliance, and said it will not approve practices incorporating them absent modifications.

audits.title: An Assessment of NYPD's Use of Social Media
audits.plain_title: Police brass posted insults online with no oversight
audits.agency: New York City Police Department
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation's (DOI) Office of the Inspector General for the New York City Police Department (OIG-NYPD) examined NYPD's social media policies and practices and several posts made by NYPD executives on official accounts in the first half of 2024.
audits.background: The investigation followed a May 2024 request from City Council Speaker Adrienne Adams, who alleged the department's official accounts showed a pattern of targeting public officials and members of the public with intimidating invective. OIG-NYPD reviewed all X posts from January 2022 through August 2024 on three accounts the speaker identified.

findings.plain: Certain X posts by NYPD executive staff on official city accounts were unprofessional, encouraged unproductive public discourse and violated department policies requiring courtesy and civility. The posts raise questions about prohibited political activity by city employees, though DOI reached no conclusion on that issue.
findings.quote:
Certain X posts made by members of NYPD’s executive staff  on official City 
accounts were unprofessional and encouraged an unproductive public discourse

findings.plain: Several NYPD social media practices do not comply with the citywide social media policy; for example, some accounts are not registered with the Mayor's Office of Creative Communications and executive accounts other than the commissioner's were created without that office's approval.
findings.quote:
Several of NYPD’s practices regarding social media are not in compliance with the 
Citywide Social Media Policy to which all City agencies are required to adhere.

findings.plain: NYPD's social media policy, dated December 2, 2022, has not been updated for the June 2023 citywide policy and does not describe staff roles, the internal content approval process or how complaints should be handled.
findings.quote:
NYPD’s official use of social media policy (dated December 2, 2022) has not been 
updated to include all of the requirements

findings.plain: The department's policy provides no rules or guidance on what content and language is appropriate for official accounts, and executives run individual accounts without sufficient oversight, outside the supervision of the Deputy Commissioner of Public Information's office.
findings.quote:
NYPD executives with individual social media accounts operate their accounts 
without sufficient oversight

findings.plain: NYPD provides no formal training to executives with individual accounts on appropriate content and public impact, though it does train the Digital Communications Officers who manage command-level accounts.
findings.quote:
NYPD does not provide formal training to NYPD executives with 
individual social media accounts regarding appropriate content for posting

findings.plain: NYPD stopped engaging in discourteous exchanges targeting particular individuals in early May 2024, after public criticism and the speaker's request for a DOI investigation.
findings.quote:
NYPD ceased to engage in social media exchanges that used discourteous 
language and targeted particular individuals in early May 2024

numbers.label: Policy and procedure recommendations issued
Start of the X post review period, running through August 2024

recommendations: Memorialize in writing an internal review and approval process for posts on executive accounts.
Update all relevant Patrol Guide and Administrative Guide sections to align with the citywide social media policy.
Review the citywide social media policy and ensure NYPD complies with all of its requirements.
Update the department's social media use policy to include rules and guidance on appropriate content and language for official accounts.
Assign Digital Communications Officers to all social media accounts, including executive accounts, to keep posts consistent with citywide and department policy, and put the requirement in writing.
Train all staff who use official agency social media on the citywide policy, the department's policy and best practices.
audits.agency_response: The report notes NYPD has refrained from the criticized exchanges since early May 2024 and has taken steps to improve oversight and depersonalize interactions, which the inspector general called steps in the right direction.

audits.title: Status Report on Remedial Measures
audits.plain_title: How a court takeover of Rikers should be built, per the monitor
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: A report from the court-appointed independent monitor in Nunez v. City of New York advising the court on how to structure remedial relief, such as a receivership, for the city jails after the court held the city in contempt, drawing on a review of receiverships in nine other jail and prison systems.
audits.background: After oral argument on the contempt motion, the court's September 26, 2024 order directed the parties to develop remedial proposals through a meet and confer process organized by the monitoring team, including a fully fleshed-out description of the authority and structure of a receivership or other framework and a method for streamlining the court orders in the case.

findings.plain: Reviewing nine correctional receivership cases around the country, the monitoring team found receivers have been used sparingly and that there is no standard model for this kind of relief in jails or prisons.
findings.quote: There is also no standard model for remedial relief that involves receiverships, or

findings.plain: A principal weakness in managing the Nunez reforms has been the lack of continuity in department leadership, so the remedial framework should guarantee consistent leadership with clear reporting lines.
findings.quote: ...managing the Nunez Court Orders has been a lack of continuity of leadership.

findings.plain: The court orders in the case have grown so numerous and interconnected that they no longer provide a workable framework: there are at least ten orders with likely more than 500 provisions, and they need to be organized and streamlined.
findings.quote: There are at least ten Nunez Court Orders representing likely over 500 provisions.

findings.plain: The monitor identified priority areas any remedy must address, including widespread security failures, staff assignment and absenteeism, expanding the supervisory structure from two to three lines, safely managing people who commit serious violence and swifter staff discipline.
findings.quote: The highest priority must be to reduce

findings.plain: Despite years of new policies and procedures, the essential ingredient of culture change in the department has still not happened, and staff must be genuinely engaged in the reform effort.
findings.quote: ...component of culture change has yet to take place.

findings.plain: The monitor concluded no single fix will resolve the department's deeply entrenched problems, and any remedy must define clear, measurable criteria for ending court control and for sustaining reforms afterward.
findings.quote: There is no providential formula

numbers.label: Provisions likely contained across the Nunez court orders
Provisions in the consent judgment alone

recommendations: Structure remedial relief around continuity in managing the Nunez reforms: a practical leadership structure with clear lines of authority, leaders with deep correctional expertise, maximizing work already underway and a willingness to make unpopular decisions.
Define the structure of the relief up front, including specific, measurable criteria for terminating the remedial measure and a design that sustains reforms after court control ends.

Focus the relief on priority areas: sound correctional practice to reduce the risk of harm, streamlined budgeting and hiring, staff assignment and absenteeism, an expanded supervisory structure, managing people after serious violence, staff accountability and engaging staff in reform.
Preserve a neutral and independent assessment of the department's functioning during and after any remedial measure.
Direct the monitoring team to manage the process of streamlining the Nunez court orders, submitting a timeline to the court within 30 days of the ruling on remedial measures.
audits.agency_response: The parties' own remedial proposals are attached to the report, and the parties reported that they consent to the monitoring team's recommended approach for managing the streamlining of the court orders.
audits.compliance_note: The report follows the court's finding of civil contempt and stresses that the department's problems are so deeply entrenched that no single solution will fix them with the speed current conditions demand.

audits.title: Equal Employment Opportunity Policies and Practices at the New York City Board of Elections
audits.plain_title: Elections board chief harassed staff and its EEO program is broken
audits.agency: New York City Board of Elections
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) investigated workplace harassment allegations against Michael Ryan, Executive Director of the New York City Board of Elections (BOE), and reviewed the BOE's Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) policies and practices.
audits.background: The BOE is a non-mayoral city entity that administers elections in New York City, overseen by a ten-member bipartisan Board of Commissioners with a staff of over 900 employees. DOI took the case because an agency cannot impartially investigate its own executive director and the BOE in particular lacked a sufficient process to do so.

findings.plain: DOI concluded that Ryan's conduct constituted harassment and created a hostile work environment for two employees in violation of the BOE's EEO policies, and more likely than not violated state and city human rights laws.
findings.quote:
Ryan’s conduct constituted harassment and created a hostile work environment for these 
two employees in violation of  BOE’s Equal Employment Opportunity (“EEO”) policies.

findings.plain: One employee endured sexually suggestive and ethnicity-based comments over about four months in 2024, causing significant anxiety and contributing to her decision to resign. A second employee described unwanted ethnicity- and gender-based comments during her DOI interview.
findings.quote:
caused Complainant 1 to experience significant anxiety and emotional distress, and 
ultimately contributed to her decision to resign

findings.plain: The BOE's EEO policy lacked a confidential complaint mechanism or an independent investigation protocol for allegations against its executive director and other senior staff.
findings.quote:
the BOE’s EEO Policy lacked a confidential complaint mechanism or independent investigation 
protocol for allegations against its Executive Director and other senior staff.

findings.plain: Unlike other city agencies, the BOE had no EEO Officer handling complaints, investigations, accommodation requests and recordkeeping independently of senior staff, and commissioners and senior staff were confused about whether the citywide EEO policy even applied to the BOE.
findings.quote:
the BOE did not have an EEO Officer who handles routine EEO responsibilities independently of 
other senior staff

findings.plain: DOI told the board that termination or resignation was warranted, but the board instead suspended Ryan for three weeks without pay, ordered sensitivity training and placed him on probation for a year. Ryan had completed the city's EEO and harassment prevention training during the period the conduct occurred.
findings.quote:
The Board declined to terminate Ryan or to give him the opportunity to 
resign; instead, the Board suspended Ryan for three weeks without pay

findings.plain: This is the second set of substantiated allegations DOI knows of involving misconduct by a senior BOE leader implicating its EEO policy, after a previous case involving the BOE's former general counsel that ended in a criminal conviction.
findings.quote:
two such instances make 
clear the need for significant reforms to the BOE’s EEO program.

numbers.label: BOE staff, plus part-time and temporary election workers
BOE personnel interviewed, including commissioners
Policy and procedure recommendations issued

recommendations: Formally appoint a qualified EEO Officer reporting directly to both the executive director and the president of the Board of Commissioners, and properly staff the EEO office with qualified professionals.
Communicate the identity and contact information of the EEO Officer and other EEO professionals to all BOE staff annually and at other appropriate intervals.

Formally adopt the citywide EEO policy as the BOE's own, follow Department of Citywide Administrative Services (DCAS) guidance and include requirements for confidential independent investigations, referral of allegations against top officials to another city entity and detailed complaint and recordkeeping procedures.
Train all BOE personnel, including executive management and commissioners, at regular intervals on the EEO policy and sexual harassment prevention.
Report regularly to an external city entity, such as DCAS, on EEO activities including complaints, investigations, reasonable accommodations and training.
Formally subject the BOE to audits and oversight by the New York City Equal Employment Practices Commission.
audits.agency_response: The board indicated it will "review and update its [EEO] policies and procedures in part based on DOI's recommendation." It declined DOI's view that termination or resignation was warranted, opting for a three-week unpaid suspension, training and a year of probation.

audits.title: Investigation Concerning New York City Police Department Security Details for City Elected Officials
audits.plain_title: Police security details for elected officials still lack clear rules
audits.agency: New York City Police Department
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) investigated how the New York City Police Department (NYPD) runs security details for elected officials and reviewed the status of recommendations from DOI's 2021 report on the subject.
audits.background: DOI's 2021 report concluded that former mayor Bill de Blasio repeatedly misused his security detail for personal benefit in violation of the city's Conflicts of Interest Law, and identified flaws including a lack of rules, minimal officer training and recordkeeping violations. NYPD accepted most of those recommendations and in November 2022 issued written Protection Detail Guidelines.

findings.plain: NYPD has implemented or begun to implement some but not all of DOI's 2021 recommendations, and substantial gaps remain in its policies and procedures for elected officials' security details.
findings.quote:
finding substantial 
and continuing gaps in NYPD’s policies and procedures concerning security details for elected officials

findings.plain: The new Protection Detail Guidelines provide little useful substance for detail officers or protected officials, failing to define "official purposes" or the scope of permitted uses, even though the 2021 report called lack of guidance the root of nearly all the problems it found.
findings.quote:
The PDGs provide little useful information for either members of  
service assigned to security details, or the elected officials afforded protection.

findings.plain: Detectives assigned full time to an elected official's detail received minimal training, two or three total days of dignitary protection training, in some cases a decade or more before their current assignment, and had little or no knowledge of the governing policies.
findings.quote:
two or three total days of dignitary protection 
training, in some cases a decade or more prior to their current protection assignment.

findings.plain: NYPD's security detail training did not cover the ethical and legal restrictions that apply to details for city officials.
findings.quote:
its security detail training did not cover the 
ethical and legal restrictions applicable to security details.

findings.plain: NYPD still does not maintain records recommended in 2021, with officers testifying they keep no trip logs, tour summaries or other records that would establish where details went and what they did.
findings.quote:
they do not maintain trip logs, 
tour summaries, or other records that would establish detail usage, destinations, o r other 
duties undertaken by detail members.

numbers.label: Policy and procedure recommendations in this report
Year of DOI's earlier security detail report

recommendations: Further develop substantive guidance on proper security detail use, updating the Protection Detail Guidelines with executive protection best practices from outside experts and clear rules for officers and protectees reflecting the Conflicts of Interest Law.

Require and provide high-quality executive protection training, ideally from outside experts, to all personnel assigned to elected officials' security details, both inside and outside the Executive Protection Unit.
Maintain appropriate records for all security details, such as detailed memo books and car logs establishing the location and time of each stop and other duties undertaken by detail members.

Promptly review whether written security determinations exist for all elected officials currently assigned details, make and document determinations where they are missing and adjust assignments if needed.
Regularly update written security determinations for elected officials and adjust details to reflect changes in identified threats, given the need to use limited government resources efficiently.
audits.agency_response: NYPD said it could not fully implement the training recommendation as written because outside experts such as the United States Secret Service have limited availability, but planned to extend its Executive Protection Unit training to all detail members. NYPD rejected the recordkeeping recommendation, which DOI called a substantial deviation from the practices of other protective agencies.
audits.implementation_note: The report found NYPD has implemented or begun to implement some but not all of the recommendations in DOI's 2021 report; three of the five new recommendations reiterate and expand on 2021 recommendations not yet fully implemented.

audits.title: Audit Report on the Development and Implementation of the New York City Fire Department’s Fire Inspection Revenue and Enforcement System
audits.plain_title: The Fire Department's $18.4 million inspection software fell short
audits.agency: New York City Fire Department
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Fire Inspection Revenue and Enforcement System (FIRES), the software the Fire Department (FDNY) paid contractor GCOM Software about $18.4 million to build for scheduling inspections, processing violations and collecting fees, meets its goals and handles information reliably and securely.
audits.background: The Fire Department previously ran inspections, violations and billing on paper forms, phone calls, spreadsheets and a 30-year-old unsupported mainframe system. It contracted with GCOM in 2016 to build a replacement, paid Gartner another $5.5 million for quality assurance and project oversight and launched the new system in September 2021.

findings.plain: The department never made its contractor deliver key inspection and enforcement functions required by the contract, yet still gave the vendor positive performance ratings across seven evaluations.
findings.quote: FDNY gave GCOM ratings of satisfactory, good, or excellent, and did not hold GCOM accountable for its performance.

findings.plain: Automated inspection scheduling and routing was never fully built. Supervisors still juggle Outlook calendars and spreadsheets, the system automatically cancels inspections nobody finalizes within 45 days and a May 2024 report showed 49,834 inspections past due.
findings.quote: 49,834 inspections are past due

findings.plain: Enforcement work is still largely manual. Summonses are issued on paper and hand-delivered to court, and the department paid in full for a $190,500 electronic interface for hearing dispositions that was never implemented.
findings.quote: GCOM received full payment for this work, which was not performed.

findings.plain: The department could not show the system was properly tested before launch. The only test report provided said testing could not be completed because of significant defects, and there was no documented approval of final test results.
findings.quote: due to the unacceptable amount of defects, lack of confidence of the stakeholders and untested functionalities, it was decided that there will be another round of SIT and UAT

findings.plain: When the scope of work was cut, the department did not reduce the contract price. Instead $506,928.44 was shifted to vaguely defined enhancements without the price and cost analysis city rules require.
findings.quote: the $506,928.44 was reallocated to milestones 17–20

findings.plain: Users are unhappy. About a quarter of surveyed department staff and public users were dissatisfied overall, a third of staff said the system does not let them work easily and efficiently and inspectors reported frequent connectivity failures in the field, which auditors also observed.
findings.quote: approximately 25% of respondents were overall dissatisfied or very dissatisfied with FIRES

findings.plain: The system ran on an unsupported software version for two years after launch, missing vendor updates that included stronger password enforcement and multi-factor authentication and exposing sensitive data to greater risk.
findings.quote: FDNY did not update FIRES for two years and operated in an unsupported version of Accela

numbers.label: Paid to GCOM to build the system
Paid to Gartner for quality assurance and oversight
Inspections past due as of May 2024
Paid for an electronic interface never implemented
Reallocated in the contract without required cost analysis
Staff saying the system is not easy or efficient to use

recommendations: Consult with legal counsel about available contract remedies for system functions that were paid for under the contract but never developed, tested or approved.

Consult with the fire prevention and fire operations bureaus on business needs, fully implement automated inspection scheduling and routing based on inspector availability and require all units to use it.
Add a feature that automatically alerts units when an inspection needs scheduling and disable the feature that cancels inspections not assigned within a set time.

Consult with the Bureau of Legal Affairs and implement functions and two-way interfaces to automate summons issuance and transmission, court date and inspector scheduling, hearing disposition updates and appeals.
Conduct refresher training for all system users.
Consider the survey results, solicit more feedback from internal and external users and promptly address concerns about ease of use, functionality, connectivity and customer service.
Ensure future system development and testing contract requirements are fully met and results are approved and documented before deployment.
Ensure department information systems continuously receive updates to improve functionality and optimize workflow.
audits.agency_response: The Fire Department agreed with four recommendations, partially agreed with one and disagreed with three, and it disputed the audit's findings on system testing and the security risk of running unsupported software.
